core_claim: A single positive stepsize schedule, fixed before knowing the objective or stopping time, makes gradient descent reach the accelerated silver convergence rate at every stopping time.

metainfo.paper: Anytime Acceleration of Gradient Descent

nl_proof:
The argument exhibits one explicit schedule and one constant that work simultaneously for every objective and every stopping time, and then bounds the suboptimality at an arbitrary iterate.

Foundations. The analysis rests on the standard first-order inequalities valid for any 1-smooth convex function: interpolation inequalities between any two iterates, the descent bound that a gradient step decreases the value by at most (α²+2α)/2 times the squared gradient norm, and the fact that at the minimizer the gradient vanishes. A schedule of positive stepsizes is called primitive when the associated potential, combining the weighted value gap, a weighted squared terminal gradient, and half the squared distance to the optimum, is controlled by half the squared initial distance; this immediately yields a last-step guarantee of the form value gap at the terminal index bounded by the initial squared distance divided by the accumulated stepsize sum, and a terminal squared gradient bounded by that distance over the square of the sum.

Concatenation. A key structural tool (adapted from prior work on long-step schedules) shows that two primitive schedules can be joined into a single longer primitive schedule by inserting one carefully chosen join stepsize given by an explicit function of the two aggregate stepsizes. Iterating this, the silver schedules — obtained by recursively concatenating a schedule with a copy of itself — are primitive; the order-i silver block has length two-to-the-i minus one and aggregate stepsize equal to the i-th power of the silver ratio minus one.

Construction. The proposed anytime schedule concatenates, for increasing orders j, a geometrically growing number of copies of the order-j silver block, each concatenation again inserting a join stepsize. By the concatenation lemma this infinite schedule and all its finite prefixes are primitive, and every stepsize is strictly positive. A counting lemma establishes two quantitative facts: the accumulated stepsize sum after t steps grows at least like a fixed power of t with exponent (c+log₂ρ)/(c+1), where c is a free construction parameter, and the order reached by step t grows only like t to the power 1/(c+1).

Controlling intermediate iterates. Because the schedule is non-monotone, the value at a general index between two join steps must be handled separately. Refined lemmas, again exploiting primitivity of each silver block together with the join-step magnitudes, bound the terminal squared gradient of a primitive block by a constant multiple of the squared initial stepsize times the incoming squared gradient, and bound the value increase across an entire silver block by a fixed constant (432) times the squared initial stepsize times the incoming squared gradient. This is where controlling the gradient magnitudes prevents intermediate overshoot.

Assembling the rate. Fix a stopping time and locate the largest join step below it, which terminates a primitive prefix. Primitivity of that prefix bounds both the value gap and the squared gradient at the join step by the initial squared distance divided by the accumulated sum (respectively its square). The join stepsize inserted there is shown, via the explicit join function, to lie between a lower bound of the form (√2−1) times the following block's aggregate plus √2 and an upper bound of order the silver ratio to the current order; the lower bound lets the refined block lemma apply, while the upper bound, combined with the counting lemma, converts the block increase into a bound decaying like the initial squared distance over a power of the index with exponent 2c/(c+1). Adding the value gap at the join step, whose decay exponent is (c+log₂ρ)/(c+1), gives an overall bound governed by the smaller of the two exponents.

Optimizing the parameter. Choosing the construction parameter c equal to log₂ρ equalizes the two exponents, both becoming ϑ = 2log₂ρ/(1+log₂ρ). The very first few indices are checked by hand using the descent inequality. This produces a single predetermined positive schedule and a single constant for which the value gap at every stopping time is at most that constant times the squared initial distance divided by the stopping time raised to ϑ.
nl_theorem: Let F be a real Hilbert space. There exist a stepsize schedule α : ℕ → ℝ with α t > 0 for every t, together with a constant C > 0, such that the following holds. For every function f : F → ℝ that is Fréchet-differentiable everywhere, convex on all of F, and whose gradient ∇f is 1-Lipschitz, and that attains a global minimum at some point x* ∈ F, for every initialization x₀ ∈ F, and for every stopping time T ≥ 1, the gradient descent iterates x_t defined by x₀ and x_{t+1} = x_t − α_t · ∇f(x_t) satisfy f(x_T) − f(x*) ≤ C · ‖x₀ − x*‖² / T^ϑ, where ϑ = 2·log₂(1+√2) / (1 + log₂(1+√2)) is the silver convergence exponent.

core_claim: Every finite election admits, for each positive slack, a small dominating committee together with a candidate distribution keeping every candidate's expected pairwise support close to one half.

metainfo.paper: Approximately Dominating Sets in Elections

nl_proof:
The argument builds the committee and distribution by sampling from a maximal lottery, so it proceeds in three stages: producing the lottery, controlling how much an empirical sample distorts each voter's view, and reading off the size, domination, and expectation guarantees.

First, the paper invokes the maximal lottery of the election. This is the equilibrium distribution over candidates arising from the two-player zero-sum game in which one player picks a candidate a, the other picks b, and the payoff is the vote margin of a over b. By the minimax property of this symmetric game, there is a distribution over candidates such that, for every candidate a, the expected fraction of voters preferring a to a random draw b from the lottery is at most one half. Rephrased through the notion of rank (a voter's rank of a with respect to a distribution is the probability that the voter prefers a to a sample from it), the average rank of any candidate under the maximal lottery is at most one half.

Second, the paper isolates the statistical tool that avoids a logarithmic dependence on the number of candidates. It records the expected one-sided gap between the empirical distribution function of k independent uniform samples on the unit interval and the uniform distribution function itself. Using Massart's sharp form of the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality, which gives a Gaussian tail bound on this supremum deviation, and integrating that tail bound, the expected supremum gap is at most (1 + o(1)) times the square root of π/(8k). The point is that this single quantity simultaneously controls all rank changes for a fixed voter, because a voter's ranks of the candidates always follow that voter's linear order.

Third comes the sampling construction. One draws k candidates independently from the maximal lottery and lets D be their empirical (uniform-over-the-multiset) distribution; its support S therefore has at most k candidates. From the perspective of a single voter, sampling from any distribution can be modeled by cutting the unit interval into segments whose lengths are the candidates' probabilities, ordered by that voter's preference, and drawing a uniform point; a candidate's rank is the left endpoint of its segment. Under this coupling, the voter's rank of a candidate under the empirical distribution equals the fraction of the uniform sample points falling below its rank under the maximal lottery. Hence the largest increase, over all candidates, of that voter's rank in passing from the maximal lottery to the empirical distribution is bounded by exactly the one-sided empirical-versus-uniform supremum deviation. Taking expectations, the expected largest rank increase for each voter is at most the DKW bound, and by linearity the expected average of these increases over all voters is also at most that bound. By the probabilistic method there is a concrete sample for which the average rank increase over voters is at most the bound.

For that sample, the average rank of any candidate a under the empirical distribution is at most its average rank under the maximal lottery plus the average increase, hence at most one half plus (1 + o(1)) times the square root of π/(8k). Since the average rank equals the expected fraction of voters preferring a to a draw from the distribution, choosing k on the order of (1 + o(1))π/(8ε²) makes this at most one half plus ε for every candidate, and the support size then satisfies the stated bound with a remainder tending to 0 as ε tends to 0 from the right. Finally, the domination property follows from the expectation bound: for a candidate a outside S, strict totality of each voter's order gives that the fraction preferring b to a is one minus the fraction preferring a to b, so the distribution-weighted fraction of voters preferring the sampled candidate to a is at least one half minus ε; consequently some member of S with positive probability is preferred to a by at least a (one half minus ε) fraction of voters, making S a (one half minus ε)-dominating committee.
nl_theorem: There exists a function r from the reals to the reals with r(ε) tending to 0 as ε tends to 0 from the right, such that for every ε > 0, every finite nonempty voter set V, every finite nonempty candidate set C, and every family (≻_v)_{v ∈ V} of strict total orders on C, there exist a committee S ⊆ C and a function D : C → ℝ forming a probability distribution supported on S (nonnegative, summing to 1, and vanishing off S) with the following properties: the cardinality of S is at most (1 + r(ε)) · π / (8 ε²); the committee S is (1/2 − ε)-dominating, meaning that for every candidate a not in S there is some b ∈ S for which at least a (1/2 − ε) fraction of voters prefer b to a; and for every candidate a, the D-weighted sum over candidates b of the fraction of voters preferring a to b is at most 1/2 + ε.

core_claim: For a sufficiently small tolerance and any fixed failure level, directional halfspace classes over finite pools admit proper tolerant pool-based learners whose query count meets the stated minimum-times-logarithm budget.

metainfo.paper: Actively Learning Halfspaces without Synthetic Data

nl_proof:
The argument establishes the tolerant learner by reducing directional halfspace learning to a one–versus–many monotonicity problem and combining three ingredients: a black-box exact learner for "shuffled monotone" labelings, a randomized one-dimensional tolerant learner, and a sampling test for monotonicity.

Setup and reduction. Each unit direction in the pool orders the points by the size of their projection onto that direction, yielding one permutation of the pool per direction. A labeling comes from a halfspace with a given direction exactly when it is non-decreasing along that direction's ordering. Hence, if the observed labeling is within the allowed tolerance of some halfspace in the class, then along at least one of the orderings (the one matching that halfspace's direction) the labeling is close to a genuinely monotone function on the line. The whole task therefore becomes: identify a direction whose induced one-dimensional labeling is nearly monotone, and then tolerantly recover a monotone labeling along it.

Choosing tolerance and failure level. The failure level is treated as a fixed positive constant, and the tolerance constant is taken small enough (a fixed fraction of the failure level) so that the guaranteed distance of the observed labeling to some halfspace is a small multiple of the accuracy times the failure level. This is what lets the sampling arguments below go through with room to spare.

Identifying a good direction. The learner repeats a voting round on the order of the logarithm of (number of directions over failure level) times. In each round it draws a batch of independent uniform sample points from the pool, of size proportional to one over (accuracy times failure level), and runs the exact shuffled-monotone learner on the labeling restricted to that batch; this exact learner uses a number of queries on the order of the minimum of (directions plus inverse-accuracy logarithm) and (one over accuracy times failure level). For every direction it then records a vote of plus one if the recovered restricted labeling is non-decreasing along that direction and minus one otherwise. After all rounds it selects the direction with the largest vote total.

Why the selected direction is nearly monotone. The key intermediate claim is that, with high probability, the selected direction's one-dimensional labeling is within a small multiple of accuracy-times-failure-level of monotone. For the correct direction, the small set of points on which the observed labeling disagrees with a nearby monotone function is a tiny fraction of the pool; a random batch misses this disagreement set with probability comfortably above nine tenths (this uses that a small per-point miss probability raised to the batch size stays bounded below by a constant), and when the batch misses it, the batch restriction is truly monotone, the exact learner reproduces it, and the correct direction receives a plus-one vote. For any direction that is far from monotone, a property-testing fact about monotone functions guarantees that a batch of that size exhibits a monotonicity violation with constant probability, so such a direction fails to earn a plus-one vote with constant probability. Comparing the vote difference between a far direction and the correct one, each round contributes an independent bounded increment with strictly negative expectation; summing over the logarithmically many rounds and applying a Hoeffding concentration bound makes the probability that any fixed far direction outscores the correct one at most failure-level-over-number-of-directions. A union bound over the far directions shows the selected direction is nearly monotone except with probability at most the failure level.

Tolerantly recovering the labeling along the chosen direction. On the chosen direction the learner runs a randomized binary search tailored to tolerant monotone learning. That subroutine, proved separately, takes a one-dimensional labeling within some distance of monotone and, using a number of queries on the order of the inverse-accuracy logarithm plus the inverse-failure logarithm, returns a monotone labeling whose distance to the input is within a constant-over-failure-level multiple of the input distance, succeeding with high probability. Its analysis performs binary search by repeatedly splitting the live interval into thirds and querying a uniformly random point of the middle third, which shrinks the interval by a constant factor each step (bounding the number of queries) and keeps each query's chance of landing in the rare disagreement set small; a union bound over the few queries shows that with the target probability every query avoids the disagreement set, so the recovered function stays close to the nearby monotone function and hence, by the triangle inequality, close to the input. Feeding the chosen direction's labeling into this subroutine at the appropriate internal accuracy yields a monotone one-dimensional labeling within the target accuracy of the observed labeling along that ordering.

Conclusion. Because the recovered labeling is monotone along one of the orderings, composing it back with that direction's ordering gives an actual halfspace in the class, so the learner is proper. Combining the failure probability of selecting a good direction with that of the binary search via a union bound gives overall success with the stated failure probability. Every query is a label query to a point already in the pool, and the total query count is the product of the logarithmic number of voting rounds and the per-round exact-learning cost, which matches the claimed budget of a constant times the minimum of (directions plus inverse-accuracy logarithm) and (one over accuracy), multiplied by the binary logarithm of the number of directions.
nl_theorem: Consider Boolean labelings of a finite pool of points in Euclidean space, where a directional halfspace class is the set of labelings of the form "the strict threshold comparison of the inner product with a chosen unit direction exceeds a chosen real cutoff," the direction ranging over a given finite set of unit vectors. Learning is pool-based: a randomized learner is a probability distribution over deterministic label-query trees that query only labels of pool points. The normalized Hamming error between two labelings is the fraction of pool points on which they differ, and the tolerant targets at tolerance c and accuracy ε are the labelings lying within normalized Hamming distance c·ε of the class. Then there exists a constant c₀ with 0 < c₀ < 1 such that for every tolerance c with 0 < c ≤ c₀ and every failure level δ with 0 < δ < 1, there is a constant K > 0 with the following property: for every dimension d, every finite pool X in that Euclidean space, every finite set V of unit directions, and every ε with 0 < ε < 1, the directional halfspace class over X with directions V is properly tolerantly learnable in the sense that some distribution over query trees outputs, for every c·ε-tolerant target, a member of the class using at most K · min(|V| + log(1/ε), 1/ε) · L(|V|) queries (where L is the clipped binary logarithm), and the probability mass of trees whose output has normalized Hamming error exceeding ε is at most δ.

core_claim: Proximal gradient descent with silver stepsizes achieves, at every dyadic horizon, an accelerated objective gap bounded by an explicit constant times the smoothness parameter and squared initial distance to a minimizer.

metainfo.paper: Accelerating Proximal Gradient Descent via Silver Stepsizes

nl_proof:
The paper deduces this convergence rate from an exact "multi-step descent certificate," an algebraic identity that holds along the whole proximal gradient trajectory. Writing F = f + h, the update x_{t+1} = x_t − α_t(g_t + s_{t+1}) with the M-normalized silver stepsizes (and the optimality condition g_* + s_* = 0), the certificate asserts the existence of coefficient arrays λ and μ and a symmetric slack matrix S such that

  Σ λ_{ij} Q^f_{ij} + Σ μ_{ij} Q^h_{ij} = (2ρ^k − 1)(F_* − F_n) + (ρ/(2√2)) M‖x_0 − x_*‖² − ½(‖u‖² + Tr(V S Vᵀ)),

where the Q^f_{ij} and Q^h_{ij} are the co-coercivity (interpolation) quantities of f and h, and u and V are explicit vectors built from the iterates, gradients, and subgradients. Throughout, M is set to 1 without loss of generality by rescaling f and h by 1/M.

Granting this identity, the theorem follows immediately. The co-coercivities Q^f_{ij} and Q^h_{ij} are nonnegative because f is convex and smooth and h is convex (the standard interpolation inequalities), and the multipliers λ_{ij}, μ_{ij} are nonnegative for i ≠ j while the diagonal terms vanish; hence the left-hand side is nonnegative. On the right-hand side, ‖u‖² is a square and Tr(V S Vᵀ) is nonnegative because S is positive semidefinite, so the whole bracketed term is nonnegative. Rearranging yields F_n − F_* ≤ (ρ/(√2(4ρ^k − 2))) M‖x_0 − x_*‖². Finally, since n = 2^k − 1 gives ρ^k = (n+1)^{log_2 ρ} and one checks n^{log_2 ρ} ≤ ρ^k − 1, the denominator satisfies 4√2·n^{log_2 ρ} ≤ √2(4ρ^k − 2), which upgrades the estimate to the stated bound ρ/(4√2·n^{log_2 ρ}) M‖x_0 − x_*‖².

The bulk of the work is establishing the certificate, which is done by induction on k, with the three ingredients proved separately.

First, the multipliers are built by "recursive gluing." For f, the array λ^{(k+1)} is the same one used in the analysis of plain gradient descent: it is the sum of a recursion component that stitches together two copies of λ^{(k)} (one for the first half of the trajectory, one for the second, scaled by ρ²), a sparse correction touching O(1) entries, and a low-rank correction affecting O(1) rows built from the stepsize vector π^{(k)}. The array μ^{(k)} for h is new and is constructed analogously from a recursion component gluing two copies of μ^{(k)}, a three-entry sparse correction, and a low-rank correction assembled from linear combinations of π^{(k)} and the auxiliary sequence c^{(k)}. Nonnegativity of the off-diagonal entries follows by induction: all pieces are manifestly nonnegative except the entries μ_{n,j} for 1 ≤ j < n, where a possibly negative low-rank term is added; a direct computation shows μ_{n,j} equals a positive multiple of (c^{(k)}_j − π^{(k)}_j), which is nonnegative because c^{(k)} ≥ π^{(k)}. The needed properties of the schedules—Σπ^{(k)} = ρ^k − 1, the concatenation π^{(k+1)} = [π^{(k)}, ρ^{k−1}+1, π^{(k)}], Σc^{(k)} = 2(ρ^k − 1), and c^{(k)} ≥ π^{(k)}—are recorded as helper lemmas.

Second, the slack matrix S^{(k)} is shown to be positive semidefinite via a Laplacian structure. One defines a recursively built matrix L^{(k)} and proves by induction that its off-diagonal entries are nonpositive (again using c^{(k)} ≥ π^{(k)}) and that every row sum is zero, so L^{(k)} is a graph Laplacian and hence positive semidefinite. Since the top-left entry of S^{(k)} is the positive number 1/√2, positive semidefiniteness of S^{(k)} reduces to that of its Schur complement, which is itself shown to be Laplacian (its off-diagonal entries stay nonpositive because c^{(k)}_1 ≥ √2 and its row sums remain zero), completing the proof.

Third, the descent identity itself is verified by induction on k, checking that coefficients match on both sides. The base case k = 1 is an explicit elementary identity checked by matching coefficients. For the inductive step, the terms are organized through a bookkeeping decomposition into a recursion part R (which glues the two level-k identities applied to the two halves of the trajectory, valid because the silver schedule concatenates), terminal rows T^f and T^h, and correction terms C^f and C^h coming from the sparse and low-rank pieces. The identity splits into a linear form in the function values {f_i}, {h_i} and a quadratic form in the gradients {g_i}, subgradients {s_i}, and the initial gap x_0 − x_*, and these two forms are handled independently. In the linear form, the {f_i} coefficients coincide with the gradient-descent analysis and are inherited from prior work, while the {h_i} coefficients are matched by expanding the co-coercivities and collecting terms (a cancellation using Σc^{(k)} = 2Σπ^{(k)} appears). For the quadratic form, rather than checking the Θ(n²) pairwise coefficients directly, the key observation is that after grouping terms in the right order both sides become succinct quadratics in a constant number of aggregated vectors γ and σ (weighted sums of gradients and subgradients). One then verifies a constant number of coefficient identities: the (g,g) block matches the gradient-descent computation, the (g,s) and (s,s) blocks match after using the Pell recurrence ρ² = 2ρ + 1 and the recursive Laplacian structure of S (which supplies exactly the residual squares needed), and the blocks involving x_0 − x_* and s_* match by inspection. Assembling the matched linear and quadratic forms proves the inductive identity, and together with the base case this establishes the certificate and hence the theorem.
nl_theorem: Let E be a real Hilbert space, let k be a natural number with k > 0, put n = 2^k − 1, and let M > 0. Let f : E → ℝ be convex with a specified gradient g that is M-Lipschitz, let h : E → ℝ be convex, and let F = f + h. Suppose x_* is a global minimizer of F over E, and that the sequence (x_t) is generated from x_0 by proximal gradient descent using the M-normalized silver stepsize schedule α_t = (ρ^{ν₂(t+1)−1} + 1)/M, where ρ = 1 + √2 is the silver ratio and ν₂ is the 2-adic valuation; that is, each x_{t+1} is the proximal point of x_t − α_t g(x_t) for h at scale α_t for all t < n. Then F(x_n) − F(x_*) ≤ ρ / (4√2 · n^{log₂ ρ}) · M‖x_0 − x_*‖².

core_claim: A cooling online algorithm run on a Gaussian matrix produces a bounded-integer output whose contraction ratio stays small except with failure probability that decays exponentially in the target dimension times a logarithmic factor.

metainfo.paper: Adaptive Robustness of Hypergrid Johnson-Lindenstrauss

nl_proof:
The paper proves the guarantee by controlling separately the numerator and denominator of the contraction ratio for the online algorithm's output, and then bounding a failure probability by a union over the cooling stages.

First, the denominator is easy to bound from below. During the initial block of steps the temperature is held at its top value B, so every coordinate committed there has absolute value B. Since this block occupies at least half of the n steps, the output vector already has squared Euclidean norm at least of order B²·n, so its norm is at least about B·√(n/2). This lower bound holds deterministically and does not depend on what happens later; consequently it suffices to show that, with high probability, the final state vector has Euclidean norm of order m, because then the ratio is of order m/(B√n).

The core of the argument is the analysis of how the Euclidean norm of the running state evolves under one update. When the current column a is added or subtracted with amplitude b, the algorithm greedily picks the sign minimizing the new norm. Decomposing a into its component along the current state y and its orthogonal complement, and applying the Pythagorean theorem, the paper writes the updated squared norm as (‖y‖ − b·|N|)² + b²·Q, where N is a standard normal (the component along y) and Q is an independent chi-square variable with m−1 degrees of freedom (the squared orthogonal part); this uses the spherical symmetry of the Gaussian column. Writing L for ‖y‖, this gives the one-step recurrence L' = √((L − b|N|)² + b²·Q).

The paper then extracts two comparison bounds for the increment. Using √(1+x) ≤ 1 + x/2, when L is at least about 2bm the update has negative drift: L' is stochastically dominated by L − b·D, where D is a variable independent of L with mean at least 1/4 and constant subexponential tails. This "type-B" comparison variable is defined explicitly (essentially |N| minus a normalized chi-square term, with a correction on the rare event that |N| exceeds m); its mean bound is verified by standard Gaussian and chi-square moment facts together with Cauchy–Schwarz, and its subexponential tail is verified by a case analysis of large-deviation bounds. Separately, by the triangle inequality the update can never increase the norm by more than b·A, where A is a "type-A" variable distributed like the norm of a standard Gaussian vector (square root of a chi-square with m degrees of freedom), of mean at most √m and with subgaussian fluctuations. These two bounds cover the negative-drift regime and the small-norm or atypical regime, respectively.

Next comes the single-block evolution estimate: for a stretch of steps run at a fixed temperature b, if the norm starts at most 8bm then after at least Km steps it is at most 4bm, except with probability exponentially small in m. This is proved by looking at the last time the norm dips below 2bm. If it never dips that low, the norm is dominated by the starting value minus a long sum of independent type-B increments, and since these have positive mean the sum exceeds 4m with only exponentially small probability once the block is long enough (of length a large constant times m). Otherwise, after the last dip the process is dominated by 2bm plus a single type-A increment minus the subsequent type-B increments; summing over all possible last-dip times and applying tail bounds for the type-A upper tail and for prefix sums of type-B variables, each term is exponentially small, and the geometric series over the times converges. Together these give the exponentially small bound for one block.

Finally, the whole schedule is a sequence of constant-temperature blocks with geometrically decreasing temperatures B, B/2, B/4, …, 1. Starting from the block at temperature B, the block estimate shows the norm ends at most 4Bm = 8·(B/2)·m, which is exactly the admissible starting condition for the next block at temperature B/2; that block ends at most 4·(B/2)·m = 8·(B/4)·m, and so on. Chaining these implications through all the cooling stages, the very last block brings the final state norm to at most 4m. Since there are on the order of log B stages, a union bound over their individual failure probabilities yields a cumulative failure probability of order (log B)·2^{−Ω(m)}. On the complementary event the numerator is at most order m while the denominator is at least order B√n, so the contraction ratio is of order m/(B√n), which is exactly the claimed guarantee with absolute constants for the ratio, the failure prefactor, and the exponential rate.
nl_theorem: There exist a natural-number threshold K0 and positive real constants C_ratio, C_fail, and c such that the following holds. For all natural numbers m, n, B, K with m < n, with B a power of two and at least 2, with K0 at most K, and with 2·K·m·log2(B) at most n, consider a matrix whose n columns are independent standard Gaussian vectors in dimension m, and let x be the output of the COOL online algorithm run with parameters B and K. Under the corresponding Gaussian matrix law, the probability of the bad event—that the contraction ratio ‖Ax‖/‖x‖ exceeds C_ratio·m/(B·√n)—is at most C_fail·log2(B)·exp(−c·m).

core_claim: Under smoothness, contractivity, covariance, and sample-size assumptions, multipass preconditioned stochastic gradient descent satisfies the stated closed-form upper bound on its on-average squared parameter stability after a fixed number of iterations.

metainfo.paper: On-Average Stability of Multipass Preconditioned SGD and Effective Dimension

nl_proof:
The paper proves the bound by tracking the coupled evolution of two runs of the algorithm: one on the original data set and one on the data set in which the i-th point has been replaced by an independent copy, driven by the same random index sequence. Writing the quantity of interest as the expected squared M-distance between the two parameter trajectories, the argument establishes a one-step recurrence and then solves it.

For the one-step recurrence, one conditions on the index drawn at the current step. With probability one minus one over n the two runs read the same data point; on this event the assumed r-contractivity of the preconditioned update immediately contracts the current squared distance by the factor one minus the step size times r. With probability one over n the two runs read different points; here the update difference is split, by adding and subtracting the population-gradient version of the step, into a population-gradient part and a noise part. Contractivity handles the population-gradient part, and a weighted quadratic (Young) inequality with a free parameter handles the remaining cross term. Averaging over the index and then over the data and the replacement point yields a recurrence of the form: next distance is at most a contraction factor times the current distance, plus a coefficient times the step size squared over n times the expected squared PMP-norm of the noise term.

The noise term is then controlled distribution-dependently. Adding and subtracting the appropriate population gradients splits it into four pieces; a four-term quadratic inequality bounds the whole by four times the sum of the pieces. Two pieces are centered gradient fluctuations, whose expected PMP-quadratic form equals a covariance trace and is bounded by the trace of PMP times Sigma using the covariance assumption; the other two are same-datum gradient differences, bounded by smoothness transferred into the preconditioned geometry, which produces the spectral factors: the largest eigenvalue of HPMP and of the product of M inverse with H, multiplied by beta squared and the current squared distance. This gives the noise term at most eight times the trace of PMP times Sigma, plus eight times beta squared times those two spectral factors times the current distance.

Substituting this back and choosing the free Young parameter equal to n times the step times r over two, the contraction coefficient is shown to be at most one minus the step times r over four: the extra instability contribution is absorbed precisely because the sample-size condition guarantees that beta times the square root of the two spectral factors divided by n is at most r over eight. The additive term becomes eight times step squared times the trace over n plus sixteen times step times the trace over n squared times r.

Using that one minus a nonnegative quantity is at most its exponential, the recurrence reads: next distance is at most the exponential of minus step times r over four times the current distance, plus the additive term. Unrolling from the initial distance, which is zero because both runs start at the same point, gives the current distance as a sum over past steps of exponentially memory-weighted additive terms. The step-squared contributions assemble exactly into the memory-weighted step quantity times eight times the trace over n. The remaining single-step contributions form a lower Riemann sum of the integral of the decaying exponential over cumulative time; bounding that integral yields the factor one minus the exponential of minus cumulative time times r over four, divided by n squared times r squared, times sixty-four times the trace. Combining the two contributions produces the stated closed-form upper bound on the on-average squared parameter stability.
nl_theorem: Let d, n, t be natural numbers, let Q be a probability measure on a measurable space Z, fix an index i in Fin n, let X be a subset of R^d, and let g be a jointly measurable gradient field from R^d × Z to R^d. Fix a starting point x0 in X. Let H, P, M be positive-definite d×d real matrices with the largest real spectral value of H equal to 1, let Sig satisfy on X the gradient-covariance bound (each g(x,·) is in L^2(Q) and Sig minus the gradient covariance of g at x is positive semidefinite), and let β, ηbar, r be positive reals. Assume g is β-smooth relative to the H-geometry on X, and every P-preconditioned update with step size at most ηbar is r-contractive in the M-quadratic form on X. Suppose the step schedule η satisfies 0 ≤ η s ≤ min(ηbar, r⁻¹) for all s, and that for every dataset S, every s ≤ t, and every index sequence the corresponding PSGD iterate lies in X. Assume the inner expectation (over the replacement point) and the outer expectation (over the dataset) of the coupled squared M-distances are Bochner integrable. If 8·β·√(λmax(HPMP))·√(λmax(M⁻¹H))/r ≤ n, then the on-average squared parameter stability after t iterations is at most 64·(η̄_t/(8n) + (1 − exp(−T_t·r/4))/(n²·r²))·tr(P M P Sig), where T_t is the cumulative step sum and η̄_t is the memory-weighted step sum.

core_claim: For every number of centers at least two, some randomized word-RAM algorithm runs within the stated near-linear-plus-polynomial time using logarithmic words and, with high probability, outputs the prescribed mixed approximation to k-center.

metainfo.paper: Beyond 2-Approximation for k-Center in Graphs

nl_proof:
The paper obtains the algorithm and its high-probability guarantee by reducing the optimization statement to a radius-gap decision procedure and then running a binary search over the radius guess.

Reduction to a decision procedure. The core object is a randomized procedure that, given an integer radius guess R and the graph, decides with high probability between the two cases R_k(G) > R and R_k(G) ≤ 2R − ⌊R/(2k−1)⌋. Once such a procedure exists, one binary-searches over the polynomially many possible integer values of R. Let R be the least guess accepted with the second outcome. Because the two ranges overlap, this R satisfies R ≤ R_k(G) and the returned centers cover every vertex within 2R − ⌊R/(2k−1)⌋ ≤ 2R_k(G) − ⌊R_k(G)/(2k−1)⌋. Writing R_k(G) = (2k−1)q + r with 0 ≤ r < 2k−1 and multiplying through by 2k−1 turns the covering-radius bound into (2k−1)·R̃ ≤ (4k−3)·R_k(G) + (2k−2), which is exactly the claimed mixed guarantee; equivalently R̃ ≤ (2 − 1/(2k−1))R_k(G) + (1 − 1/(2k−1)). The additive term vanishes when R_k(G) is divisible by 2k−1, giving a pure multiplicative factor 2 − 1/(2k−1) in that case.

The decision procedure. Set α = ⌊R/(2k−1)⌋ and assume R_k(G) ≤ R with optimal centers c_1,…,c_k. First all pairwise shortest-path distances are computed in O(mn) time. Then a random vertex set S of size O(√n log n) is drawn. A sampling lemma shows that either S already contains k vertices covering all of V within radius 2R − α (which can be tested directly over all k-tuples of S in time about n·|S|^k = Õ(n^{k/2+1})), or, with high probability, the farthest vertex w_1 from S and the collection W_1 of its √n nearest vertices contain a point s_1 with d(s_1, c_1) ≤ α. The high-probability part comes from S hitting, for every vertex, its √n nearest neighbours, which forces W_1 to contain a suitable point on a shortest path from w_1 toward a nearby optimal center.

Recursive covering. The procedure then extends the partial center set one vertex at a time. The key recursive lemma states that if we hold vertices s_1,…,s_i with each d(s_j, c_j) suitably bounded, and we look at the uncovered region U (the complement of the balls of radius R + r about the chosen points) together with the relaxed region Y (the complement of the balls of radius 2R − α), then one of two things happens for the farthest point w_{i+1} of U from S. Either w_{i+1} is far from S, in which case the hitting-set argument again places a new approximate center s_{i+1} in the √n nearest neighbours of w_{i+1} with d(s_{i+1}, c_{i+1}) growing by a controlled additive amount; or every uncovered point is close to S, in which case k − i points of S already cover Y within radius 2R − α. The proof of the second alternative uses a triangle-inequality argument along a shortest path from a center to a point of Y, isolating the first vertex on that path lying in U and bounding its distance to the center by r + α using integrality. Iterating this yields, after enough steps, vertices s_1,…,s_i with d(s_j, c_j) ≤ (2j−1)α.

The final step. Carrying the recursion all the way to k centers would only give distance bound (2k−1)α and hence a factor 2 − 1/(2k) approximation. To reach 2 − 1/(2k−1), the last stage is handled differently, mirroring the two-center warm-up: given the first k−1 approximate centers, either the √n nearest neighbours of the farthest uncovered point contain a final center s_k with a small distance to c_k, or the intersection Q of the radius-R balls around the sampled uncovered points is nonempty and any point of Q, together with s_1,…,s_{k−1}, covers everything within radius 2R − α. Trying both options completes the k-tuple whenever the required sampling events hold, which they do with high probability.

Running time and word size. Enumerating tuples at level i costs Õ(n^{(k−i)/2+1}), and each level recurses over the √n candidates in W_{i+1}, giving the recurrence T_i = Õ(n^{(k−i)/2+1}) + √n · T_{i+1}, which solves to T_0 = Õ(n^{k/2+1}). Adding the O(mn) cost of the initial all-pairs distance computation yields the overall Õ(mn + n^{k/2+1}) bound. Since all quantities manipulated (distances, indices, addresses) are polynomially bounded in n, each machine word uses O(log n) bits. The union of the finitely many sampling events fails with only polynomially small probability, so the whole procedure, and hence the binary-search algorithm built on it, succeeds with high probability.
nl_theorem: Fix an integer k with k ≥ 2. Then there exists a randomized word-RAM k-center algorithm A (a single finite program together with, for every encoded finite undirected graph and every uniform random seed of its prescribed length, a certified halting execution on the canonical graph encoding) satisfying all three of the following. First, its word-width envelope A.wordBits k is O(log(n+2)); that is, the real function n ↦ A.wordBits k n is big-O of n ↦ log(n+2). Second, its running-time envelope A.steps k is Õ(mn + n^(k/2+1)); that is, there exist a natural number d and a constant C ≥ 0 such that, for all sufficiently large n and every m ≤ C(n,2), A.steps k n m ≤ C·((m·n + n^(k/2+1))·log(n+2)^d). Third, A attains the mixed approximation with high probability: there exist an integer c > 0 and a threshold N such that, for every n ≥ N and every encoded n-vertex graph G, the proportion of uniform seeds whose decoded output C is a set of exactly k vertices satisfying R_k(G) ≤ covering radius of C and (2k−1)·(covering radius of C) ≤ (4k−3)·R_k(G) + (2k−2) is at least 1 − n^(−c).

core_claim: Every edge-weighted graph excluding a fixed complete-graph minor has bounded epsilon-scatter dimension, controlled both by an explicit closed-form function of the clique size and accuracy, and by a uniform doubly-exponential estimate.

metainfo.paper: Bounding ε-scatter dimension via metric sparsity

nl_proof:
The paper proves the explicit bound and its doubly-exponential consequence by adapting three tools from the theory of sparse graph classes to graph metrics: weak coloring numbers, flatness, and a "no long ladder" argument. The overall route builds these in order and then combines them.

Step 1 (weak coloring numbers). For an edge-weighted graph one partitions the vertex set and totally orders the parts. A part Y is weakly r-reachable from a part X if there is a path of length at most r from a vertex of X to a vertex of Y that stays inside the union of parts not preceding Y; the weak coloring number is the maximum, over all X, of the number of parts weakly r-reachable from X. The paper shows that for a K_h-minor-free graph and any target part-diameter ρ, one can build a partition into parts of diameter at most ρ together with an ordering such that, for every scale r larger than ρ, this weak coloring number is at most a value c(h, r/ρ) equal to a binomial coefficient in ⌈4h·(r/ρ)⌉ times a linear factor in r/ρ times (h−1). This is proved using a buffered cop decomposition of the minor-free graph (radius Δ = ρ/4, buffer Δ/h, at most h−1 shortest-path skeleton leaves per supernode). Each supernode is refined into balls around a maximal Δ-scattered subset of its skeleton, giving parts of diameter at most ρ, and the parts are ordered by the ancestor relation in the decomposition's partition tree. The count of reachable parts is split into two factors: the number of ancestor supernodes within reachability distance, controlled by a counting lemma for buffered cop decompositions (the binomial factor), and the number of reachable parts inside a single supernode, controlled by the at-most-(h−1)-leaf shortest-path skeleton (the linear factor).

Step 2 (flatness). Starting from an ordered partition whose weak coloring number at scale r is at most c, the paper shows that any collection A of parts with at least (2mc)^{c+1} members contains a "separator" set S of at most c parts and a subcollection B ⊆ A∖S with at least m parts such that any two distinct parts of B are more than r apart once the parts of S are deleted. The argument is a greedy two-phase procedure: first repeatedly move into S a "hub" part that is weakly r-reachable from at least a 1/(2mc) fraction of the current A, shrinking A each time (at most c iterations, since the accumulated hubs stay inside the intersection of reachable sets); then greedily select parts of the remainder whose weakly reachable sets are pairwise disjoint, which forces any short connecting path to reveal a common reachable part and hence keeps selected parts far apart after deleting S.

Step 3 (no long ladder). Fix ε > 0 and scales r > ρ > 0 with ρ ≤ (ε/3)·r, a partition with parts of weak diameter at most ρ, and an ordering whose weak coloring number at scale 3r equals c. The paper proves that every ε-ladder of width r has length below (6c·(r/ρ + 2)^c)^{c+1}. Assume otherwise. The first ladder points x_i satisfy dist(x_i, x_j) > ε·r ≥ 3ρ (from the triangle inequality applied to the ladder conditions), so they lie in distinct parts X_i; collect these into A. Applying the flatness statement at scale 3r with m = 3·(r/ρ + 2)^c yields a separator S and a subcollection B whose parts are more than 3r apart after deleting the parts of S. Assign to each part of B a distance profile to S, recording ⌊dist/ρ⌋ (capped once the distance exceeds r); there are at most (r/ρ + 2)^c profiles, so by pigeonhole three indices i < j < k in B share a profile. Shortest paths from x_j and from x_k to p_i each have length at most r, so their concatenation is a path of length at most 2r between two parts of B; since those parts are more than 3r apart off S, one of these paths meets a part of S. Equality of the profiles then transfers the relevant distance bound from x_j (or x_k) to x_i, and combining the segment lengths through the meeting point yields dist(x_i, p_i) ≤ (1 + ε)·r, contradicting the strict diagonal inequality of the ladder.

Step 4 (conclusion). To bound the ε-scatter dimension it suffices to bound the length of an arbitrary ε-ladder, which has some positive width r. Feed the partition and ordering produced in Step 1 with the choice ρ = (ε/3)·r into the no-long-ladder lemma. Then the reachability scale 3r gives ratio 3r/ρ = 9/ε, so the weak coloring number is c(h, 9/ε), which equals the stated constant with binomial argument ⌈36h·ε⁻¹⌉ and linear factor (12 + 72·ε⁻¹) times (h−1). The lemma's length bound then becomes exactly (6c·(9·ε⁻¹ + 2)^c)^{c+1}, valid for every integer h ≥ 1 and every real ε > 0, establishing the explicit bound. Finally, estimating this closed form — the constant c is at most a simple-exponential expression in h·ε⁻¹ raised to a power linear in h, and the outer tower adds one more exponential — shows the whole quantity is at most a doubly-exponential expression; choosing a large enough absolute constant in the exponent's base makes this bound uniform in all admissible h and ε, which yields the second, normalized 2^{(h·ε⁻¹)^{O(h)}}-style guarantee.
nl_theorem: Fix the following data on ε-ladders and induced graph metrics. A metric space V has ε-scatter dimension at most B if, for every natural number ℓ and every pair of maps x, p : Fin ℓ → V that form an ε-ladder (meaning there is a width r > 0 with (1+ε)·dist(p i)(x i) exceeded, i.e. (1+ε)·r < dist(p i)(x i) for all i, and dist(p i)(x j) ≤ r whenever i < j), one has ℓ ≤ B. An edge-weighted graph on V consists of a simple graph together with a positive symmetric weight on adjacent vertices such that the ambient distance between any two points is exactly the minimum weighted length of a connecting walk. The graph is K_h-minor-free if there is no family of h pairwise disjoint, connected, pairwise-adjacent branch sets. Write c(h,ε) = C(h−2 + 2·⌈36·h·ε⁻¹⌉₊, h−1) · (12 + 72·ε⁻¹) · (h−1) and scatterBound(h,ε) = (6·c·(9·ε⁻¹ + 2)^c)^(c+1) (real powers). Then both of the following hold. First, for every integer h ≥ 1, every real ε > 0, every metric space V, and every edge-weighted K_h-minor-free graph on V, the ε-scatter dimension of V is at most scatterBound(h,ε). Second, there exists an absolute constant C > 0 such that, under the same hypotheses, the ε-scatter dimension of V is at most 2^((max{2, h·ε⁻¹})^(C·h)).

core_claim: A valid partition hierarchy satisfying simultaneous mixing with one congestion parameter and a path-based flow condition with another yields a cut collection that approximates congestion with quality quadratic in the number of levels.

metainfo.paper: Congestion-Approximators from the Bottom Up

nl_proof:
The paper proves the congestion-approximator guarantee in two layers: a reduction to a "pseudo" statement, and an iterative construction that establishes the pseudo statement level by level.

Reduction. The paper first proves a weaker-looking claim: for every demand b that respects the cut budget on every set of the collection, one can produce another demand b' bounded entrywise by the boundary-degree weighting of the top partition together with a flow of congestion 16L²αβ routing b − b'. From this the theorem follows immediately: since the top partition is the single cluster containing all vertices, no edge crosses it, so its boundary-degree weighting is identically zero; the bound |b'| ≤ 0 forces b' to vanish, and the constructed flow already routes b itself with congestion 16L²αβ. As b was an arbitrary demand meeting the cut constraints, the collection is a congestion-approximator of that quality.

Structure of the common refinements. Two elementary observations organize the argument. First, for i < j the common refinement of the partitions from level i onward refines the one from level j onward, so each part of the later refinement is a disjoint union of parts of the earlier one; consequently boundaries only grow as i decreases. Second, any crossing edge of the level-i refinement that is not a crossing edge of the level-(i+1) refinement must already be a crossing edge of the i-th partition itself. These facts let boundary and cut quantities be transferred cleanly between consecutive refinement levels.

Iteration. The pseudo statement is proved by running L−1 rounds. One maintains a sequence of demands b_1 = b, b_2, …, together with flows f_1, …, f_{L−1}, so that each f_i routes b_i − b_{i+1} with congestion 16Lαβ, each b_i is bounded entrywise by the boundary-degree weighting of the level-i refinement, and the aggregate demand of b_i on every part of every later refinement matches that of b (hence still obeys the cut budget). The base case holds because the singleton clusters lie in the collection, so |b(v)| is at most the degree of v. Summing the L−1 flows telescopes to a flow routing b − b_{L−1} whose congestion is at most (L−1)·16Lαβ ≤ 16L²αβ, and the final residual b_{L−1} is bounded by the boundary-degree weighting of the top partition; this is exactly the pseudo statement with b' = b_{L−1}.

The single-level transfer. Each round is a technical lemma: given a vector s bounded by the level-i refinement boundary degrees and satisfying the cut budget on every part of the level-(i+1) refinement, one builds a flow of congestion 16Lαβ routing s − t, where t is bounded by the level-(i+1) refinement boundary degrees and s − t has zero aggregate on every part of that refinement. The vector t is defined explicitly: on each part C of the level-(i+1) refinement it spreads the total s(C) across the vertices of C in proportion to their boundary degrees; because the vertex boundary degrees inside C sum to the cut value δC, the cut hypothesis makes t respect the degree bound, and by construction t(C) = s(C), so s − t is a valid demand with zero mass on each such part.

Routing s − t. The remaining demand s − t (scaled by one half) is fed into a core helper claim, which produces a nonnegative-shaped correction y bounded by 2·(boundary degree of partition i) + 2Lβ·(boundary degree of partition i+1), with (½(s−t) − y) having zero aggregate on every cluster of the (i+1)-st partition, and a flow of congestion 4Lβ routing ½(s−t) − y. Scaling this flow by two gives a flow of congestion 8Lβ routing s − t − 2y. It then remains to route 2y. Since s − t and ½(s−t) − y both have zero aggregate on each cluster C of the (i+1)-st partition, y also has zero aggregate on C, and inside C one has |y(v)| ≤ 2·deg_{∂P_i}(v) + 2Lβ·deg_{∂C}(v) ≤ 4Lβ·deg_{∂P_i ∪ ∂C}(v). Hence (1/4Lβ)·y restricted to C is a demand dominated by the weighting deg_{∂P_i ∪ ∂C}|_C. The simultaneous-mixing hypothesis then supplies one flow routing the sum over all clusters, i.e. (1/4Lβ)·y, with congestion α; scaling by 8Lβ yields a flow of congestion 8Lαβ routing 2y. Adding the two flows routes s − t with congestion 8Lβ + 8Lαβ ≤ 16Lαβ.

The core helper. The correction y is obtained through a chain of subclaims. From the flow hypothesis at level i one gets, for any nonnegative s ≤ deg_{∂P_{i+1}}, a target t ≤ ½·deg_{∂P_i} and a flow of congestion β routing s − t; this is read off from the hypothesized flow by taking a path decomposition and deleting or shrinking paths so each vertex is the source of exactly s(v). A downward induction from level L to level i then routes, for nonnegative x ≤ deg_{∂R_{≥i}}, the difference x − y' with y' ≤ 2·deg_{∂P_i} and congestion (2L−2i)β: at each step one splits x proportionally toward the next refinement's boundary degrees, applies the inductive flow, and then applies the flow-hypothesis flow (scaled) to move the leftover mass toward partition i, using the boundary-difference observation to control x − x' by deg_{∂P_i}. A further step localizes the endpoints inside the clusters of the (i+1)-st partition: taking a path decomposition and truncating each path at the first boundary edge of its starting cluster keeps every path's endpoints in the same cluster, changes each vertex's received mass by at most 2Lβ·deg_{∂P_{i+1}}, and yields the stated bound on y with the zero-aggregate-per-cluster property, at congestion 2Lβ. Finally, splitting an arbitrary x into positive and negative parts, applying this localized construction to each, and taking the difference of the two flows gives the general helper claim at congestion 4Lβ. Assembling these pieces completes the single-level transfer, the iteration, and hence the theorem.
nl_theorem: Let V be a finite vertex set and let c assign a real capacity to each unordered pair of vertices, where W ≥ 1 and every pair has capacity either 0 or lying in the interval [1, W]. Let α ≥ 1 and β ≥ 1, let L ≥ 1, and let P be a sequence of finite partitions of V. Suppose the partitions form a valid hierarchy, meaning P 1 is the partition into singletons (⊥) and P L is the single-cluster partition (⊤). Suppose further that the mixing hypothesis holds with congestion α: for every level i in [1, L−1], the family of restricted weighted-degree weightings over the clusters of P (i+1) mixes simultaneously in the graph with congestion α. Suppose also the flow hypothesis holds with congestion β: for every level i in [1, L−1] there is a finite nonnegative weighted family of directed paths, all positive-weight paths having distinct endpoints, whose gross source mass equals the boundary degree of P (i+1) at every vertex, whose gross receipt mass at each vertex lies between 0 and half the boundary degree of P i, whose gross edge load on each pair is at most β times its capacity, and which satisfies the endpoint-coverage condition at level i. Then the cut collection, formed as the union over i in [1, L] of the parts of the common refinement of P i, …, P L, is a congestion-approximator of quality 16·L²·α·β: for every demand b summing to zero such that the absolute value of the sum of b over each cut C in the collection is at most δC, there exists an antisymmetric flow of congestion 16·L²·α·β routing b.

core_claim: For weakly dependent real variables whose mixed moments follow a prescribed formula, the joint cumulant admits explicit upper bounds, one when the third set family is nonempty and another when it is empty.

metainfo.paper: Computational barriers for permutation-based problems, and cumulants of weakly dependent random variables

nl_proof:
The argument treats the joint cumulant as a value of a bivariate power series in the two dependence parameters and quantifies how nearly the prescribed mixed moments factorize.

First, the joint cumulant is rewritten through the Möbius (moment–cumulant) inversion formula, which expresses it as an alternating sum, indexed by set partitions of the variable index set, of products of mixed moments weighted by the Möbius coefficients. Because the mixed-moment formula depends on the two parameters only through explicit rational factors, each mixed moment is promoted to a bivariate function of two formal variables that specialize to the given parameter values. The corresponding partition sum defines a bivariate series whose specialization is exactly the cumulant to be bounded; this series is well defined as long as the first parameter stays below the reciprocal of the total support size.

The key device is a quasi-factorization quantity: for each subset of indices one forms the alternating product of the moment series over all its subsets. When the underlying variables split into two independent blocks, so that the mixed moments factorize across the blocks, this quantity equals one; correspondingly the cumulant vanishes, recovering the fact that uncorrelated variables have zero joint cumulant. The proof establishes a non-asymptotic, quantitative refinement of this principle, adapting the weighted-dependency-graph theory of the small-cumulant/quasi-factorization result to a setting where the moments are viewed as series rather than as asymptotic quantities.

Concretely, one lower-bounds the order (the lowest total degree of a nonvanishing term) of the quasi-factorization function and, through it, of the cumulant series, so that the near-factorization forces the cumulant to start only at a controlled order in the small parameters. The combinatorial gain in this order is governed by how the supports of the variables meet the sets of the third family: the number of connected components of the graph whose vertices are the variable indices and whose edges join two indices exactly when their supports both meet a common set of that family determines the exponent by which the ratio of the two parameters is suppressed. Bounding the remaining coefficients of the series term by term, using the explicit form of the rational moment factors together with the smallness conditions on the parameters relative to the squared total support size, yields the stated numerical inequality in the first case, with its factorial-type prefactor, the power of the first structural parameter, the power of the squared-support times the second parameter, and the power of the parameter ratio raised to the component count minus one.

The second case, where the third family is empty, is handled by the same scheme with the roles simplified: the graph and the associated ratio factor disappear, and the same order control and coefficient estimates, now under the smallness condition on the squared support times the single remaining parameter, produce the second inequality. Together the two cases give the asserted conjunction.
nl_theorem: Let ℓ, q, r be natural numbers with ℓ ≥ 1, and let μ be a probability measure on Ω. Let Z index real-valued functions by Fin ℓ, and let I, A, B be families of finite subsets of ι indexed by Fin ℓ, Fin q, Fin r respectively, each family pairwise disjoint. Assume η, x₀, y₀ ≥ 0 and that the variables satisfy the general mixed-moment hypothesis, meaning that for every subset Δ of Fin ℓ the product of the Z t over t in Δ is integrable and its integral equals η raised to the cardinality of the union of the I t over Δ, times the product over j of the reciprocal factor ∏_{k=1}^{|I_Δ∩A_j|−1}(1−k x₀)⁻¹, times the product over i of the direct factor ∏_{k=1}^{|I_Δ∩B_i|−1}(1−k y₀). Write L for the cardinality of the union of all I t, cum for the joint cumulant defined as the partition sum ∑_π (−1)^{|π|−1}(|π|−1)! ∏_{C∈π}∫∏_{t∈C}Z t dμ over set partitions π of Fin ℓ, and cc(𝓑) for the number of connected components of the simple graph on Fin ℓ whose distinct vertices t, t' are adjacent exactly when some i makes both I t ∩ B i and I t' ∩ B i nonempty. Then both of the following hold: (1) if r ≥ 1, y₀ > 0, 2 L² y₀ ≤ 1, and 2 x₀ ≤ y₀, then |cum| ≤ 4 ℓ^{2ℓ} η^L (L² y₀)^{ℓ−1} (x₀/y₀)^{cc(𝓑)−1}; and (2) if r = 0 and 2 L² x₀ ≤ 1, then |cum| ≤ 2 ℓ^{2ℓ} η^L (L² x₀)^{ℓ−1}.

core_claim: For every admissible contract instance with a submodular inspection cost, an optimal incentive-compatible inspection scheme with small support exists, and a uniform polynomially bounded value-oracle solver producing such schemes also exists.

metainfo.paper: Contract Design Beyond Hidden-Actions

nl_proof:
The paper proves both parts of the claim through a single constructive algorithm, together with structural facts about submodular cost functions.

The central preliminary tool is a marginal-realization lemma. Given any target marginal inspection probabilities for the actions, submodularity guarantees that the cheapest inspection distribution consistent with those marginals is obtained by a nested (chain) construction: order the actions so their target marginals are nondecreasing, and place mass only on the "suffix" sets of that ordering, with the mass of each suffix equal to the successive gap between consecutive marginals (and the remainder on the empty set). One shows this reproduces exactly the prescribed marginals, keeps total mass fixed, and, by an exchange/telescoping argument that uses decreasing marginals, has expected cost no larger than that of any other distribution with the same marginals. Crucially, this distribution is supported on at most n+1 sets, and any two marginal vectors sharing the same relative order yield distributions with the same support.

The algorithm builds the optimal scheme from this. First, one uses the observation that, without loss of generality, one may inspect the suggested action only as a singleton and otherwise inspect only sets not containing it; monotonicity of the cost shows this reshuffling never raises expected cost and preserves the agent's incentives. This lets the problem of finding the best incentive-compatible scheme that recommends a fixed action i be written as a program whose objective is the payment term plus expected inspection cost, and whose incentive constraints, rewritten in terms of marginal inspection probabilities, take the form of lower bounds on each competing action's marginal (functions of the payment and of the probability of inspecting i). Since the null action is available, one may also impose that the payment is at least the ratio needed to make i individually rational, which lets one discard or simplify the constraints.

Next, for each recommended action the payment interval is partitioned into a polynomial number (order n squared) of subintervals by the finitely many payment values at which two of these marginal-threshold functions cross. Within each subinterval the relative order of the thresholds is fixed, so the set of nested support sets produced by the marginal-realization lemma is fixed as well. Because the problem is a minimization, each competing marginal is driven to the smaller of zero and its threshold, and applying the lemma on the actions other than i collapses the exponentially many inspection variables into a program in only two variables, the payment and the probability of inspecting i. This program is solved in closed form: substituting the reciprocal of the payment turns the objective into a term of the form constant-over-variable plus a linear term in the two variables over a bounded polygon; since the inspection probability of i enters only linearly, an optimum lies on an edge, and on each edge one minimizes a one-variable ratio of a quadratic over a linear function, which has an explicit closed-form optimizer.

Correctness is established by showing a two-way correspondence: the optimal solution of the full program for a recommended action, lying in some payment subinterval, corresponds to a feasible solution of the matching simplified program with the same objective value (using the order-preservation within the subinterval and the lemma's structural guarantee), and conversely any feasible solution of a simplified program yields, via the lemma, a feasible distribution for the full program with no larger cost and the same payment. Enumerating all recommended actions, all payment subintervals, and all threshold-sign cutoffs, and returning the best scheme found, therefore yields a genuinely optimal incentive-compatible scheme.

The support bound follows because the returned distribution consists of the singleton of the recommended action plus the nested support produced by the lemma on the remaining actions, which has at most n sets, giving at most n+1 sets overall. Finally, the resource analysis gives the second conclusion: the procedure runs three nested loops (over the actions, the payment subintervals, and the threshold cutoffs), each of polynomial size, so it terminates in time polynomial in the number of actions; and since the sets whose cost is queried are the same across the innermost loop, only a polynomial number of value queries to the cost function are needed. Thus an optimal incentive-compatible scheme with support at most n+1 exists and can be computed by a polynomial-time algorithm using only value-query access, establishing the existence of the abstract value-query solver as well.
nl_theorem: Fix a finite action type A with decidable equality, and contract data d consisting of an action cost, a success probability, an inspection-cost function on subsets, and a distinguished null action. Assume d is admissible (costs and inspection costs nonnegative, success probabilities in the unit interval, inspection cost normalized to zero on the empty set and monotone, and the null action costless) and that its inspection-cost function is submodular (has decreasing marginals). Then two things hold simultaneously. First, there exists an inspection scheme (a suggested action, a payment, and an inspection distribution over subsets) that is optimal — feasible with payment in the unit interval and incentive-compatible, and maximizing the principal's utility among all feasible schemes — whose inspection distribution is supported on at most the number of actions plus one subsets. Second, the type of abstract submodular value-oracle solvers is nonempty: there exists a triple of uniform maps assigning to every finite action type, contract datum, and action encoding an inspection scheme, a finite adaptive transcript of queried sets, and an amount of charged work, such that replacing the cost oracle by any function agreeing on the transcript leaves transcript, work, and output unchanged; there are constants C and k, independent of the action type and instance, bounding both the work and the number of queries by C times (number of actions plus one) to the power k on every valid encoding; and on every admissible submodular instance the output is optimal with inspection support of cardinality at most the number of actions plus one.

core_claim: A universal constant exists so that, for every accuracy and every non-degenerate matrix, a dual local-relative-smoothness run computes the unique Lewis weights within a stated iteration bound, each iteration using leverage scores of a rescaled matrix.

metainfo.paper: Computing Lewis weights to high precision using local relative smoothness

nl_proof:
The paper establishes the claim by analyzing the multiplicative iteration as gradient descent on a matrix potential, using a locally relative-smoothness convergence framework.

Setup of the dual potential. One works with the strictly convex objective over positive definite matrices M given by minus the log-determinant of M plus a normalized sum over rows of the powers (a_i^T M a_i)^{1+β}, where β = (p-2)/2 is the reciprocal of α_p. Direct differentiation gives explicit gradient and Hessian formulas; the Hessian is positive definite, so the objective is strictly convex and has a unique minimizer M_*. The stationarity condition shows M_* is the inverse of A^T V_* A, where the diagonal V_* is built from the rescaled Lewis weights v_* = σ_p(A)^{1/(1+α_p)}. This simultaneously exhibits the Lewis-weight vector as encoded by M_* and yields its uniqueness (also classically known), since a distinct Lewis-weight vector would give a distinct minimizer of the strictly convex potential. A minimax/duality argument relates this matrix problem to the vector potential used in prior work.

Relative convexity and a local smoothness framework. The potential is shown to be one-strongly convex relative to the reference function h(M) = minus log-determinant of M, because the extra Hessian term is positive semidefinite. The core analytic tool is an extension of relatively-smooth gradient descent in which the smoothness inequality need only hold along the segment between each pair of consecutive iterates ("local relative smoothness between iterates"). Using the three-point property of Bregman divergences, one proves a per-iteration contraction of the Bregman distance to any comparison point, and hence linear convergence: the Bregman divergence from the minimizer decreases by a factor (1 - μ/L) each step, together with control of the function-value gap.

Identifying the algorithm as this descent. The mirror-descent step for this potential and reference function, solved in closed form, is exactly the algorithm's multiplicative update, and every iterate M^{(t)} has the form (A^T V^{(t)} A)^{-1} with positive diagonal V^{(t)}. In the rescaled coordinates this is the stated coordinatewise update driven by the ratios ρ_i (equivalently their 1/α_p powers Φ_i).

Verifying local smoothness along the trajectory. A monotonicity argument shows the geometric invariant that the maximum of Φ over coordinates stays bounded (by a constant multiple of max{1,β}) throughout, starting from its value at the all-ones initialization. Because consecutive iterates change each coordinate by only a constant factor, the matrices A^T V A along a segment are spectrally within constant factors of one another; combined with Kronecker-product monotonicity and the Φ-bound, this yields that the potential is L-smooth relative to h between consecutive iterates for L on the order of p·max{1,β}. Choosing the step-size parameter L of this order makes the relative-smoothness constant at most L.

Convergence and conversion to an estimate. Applying the local-smoothness convergence proposition with strong-convexity parameter one and this L, after a number of iterations of order L·log(m/accuracy) the Bregman divergence from M_* is driven below a small target. A technical lemma converts small Bregman divergence in the log-determinant geometry into a two-sided spectral (multiplicative) approximation: closeness in divergence forces the eigenvalues of the relative matrix near one. Consequently the ratios of the relevant quadratic forms a_i^T M a_i to their optimal values are within the required tolerance for every row, so the returned vector, obtained by raising the final leverage-based quantities to the power 1+α_p, is an ε-estimate of σ_p(A).

Iteration count and per-iteration structure. Substituting the chosen L and the target accuracy gives the total iteration bound of order p^2·log(m p α_p / ε), matching the stated uniform bound with a universal constant. Finally, each iteration only needs the quantities a_i^T (A^T V A)^{-1} a_i, which are precisely the leverage scores of the diagonally rescaled matrix D A with D = V^{1/2}, establishing that every iteration is implemented by one leverage-score computation.
nl_theorem: There exists a constant C > 0 with the following property. For every natural numbers m and n, every real p > 2, every real ε > 0, and every non-degenerate matrix A in R^{m×n} (meaning the map x ↦ Ax is injective and every row of A is nonzero), there exists a vector σ : Fin m → ℝ such that: (1) σ is an ℓ_p-Lewis-weight vector of A, that is, every coordinate of σ is positive and σ equals the leverage-score vector of Diag(σ_i^{1/2−1/p})·A, where the leverage score of a matrix B at row i is (B_i)ᵀ(BᵀB)⁻¹(B_i); (2) σ is the unique such Lewis-weight vector; and (3) there exists a trace of the dual local-relative-smoothness algorithm satisfying its execution certificate relative to σ, whose output is an ε-estimate of σ (each coordinate positive and lying between (1−ε)σ_i and (1+ε)σ_i), whose iteration count is at most C·p²·max{1, log(m·p·α_p/ε)} with α_p = 2/(p−2), and every one of whose iterations computes the leverage scores of Diag(d)·A for a diagonal scaling d with d_i = (v_i)^{1/2}.

core_claim: For every time-constructible growth function there exist an efficient binary error-correcting code and a concept family satisfying the complete computational-statistical tradeoff package derived from the assumed hardness of nondeterministic time.

metainfo.paper: Computational-Statistical Tradeoffs from NP-hardness

nl_proof:
The argument builds one explicit code and one explicit concept family and then verifies each part of the package in turn.

Fixing the construction. The paper first sets up a general recipe: for any language L decided by a time-bounded verifier V that uses short certificates, and for any efficient binary error-correcting code with expansion factor c and decoding radius ε*, it defines a concept for each string z. If z is not in L the concept is identically zero; otherwise, taking w* to be the lexicographically first accepting certificate for z, the concept maps an input of the form (z,i) to the i-th bit of the encoding of w* and maps every other input to zero. Inputs whose prefix equals z are called useful, the rest useless. The concept family collects these concepts over all z. To prove the theorem for a given growth function p, one instantiates this recipe with the universal padded language consisting of pairs of a nondeterministic machine and an input that the machine accepts within p(|input|) steps, together with the verifier that simulates the machine for that many steps. Because a p-step nondeterministic machine can be simulated with only a logarithmic overhead, this verifier runs in time on the order of p times log p and uses certificates of size p, placing the language in the nondeterministic-time class with the stated time and certificate bounds. Any efficient binary code (assumed to exist) supplies c and ε*.

Bounded VC dimension. A single useful example (z,i) at a coordinate where the codeword is 1 is shattered, so the dimension is at least one. No two points can be shattered: two points with different prefixes are never simultaneously labeled 1, and two points with the same prefix realize only the all-zero labeling and the single labeling dictated by that prefix's codeword, so the all-ones labeling is missing. Hence the dimension is exactly one.

Enumerability and small representations. Each concept has a small decision-tree form: the tree first reads the prefix bits and rejects (outputs 0) as soon as they disagree with z, then reads the index bits and outputs the corresponding coordinate of the encoding of w*; its size is linear in p. Given z and w*, this tree is produced in polynomial time, and the encoding is computed in polynomial time. To find w* nondeterministically-efficiently, the paper introduces an augmented language that asks whether a certificate of bounded lexicographic rank exists; this augmented language stays in the same nondeterministic-time class, and binary search over the rank finds the lexicographically first certificate using about p oracle calls. The resulting decision tree is output in polynomial time, establishing that the family is enumerable by an oracle for that nondeterministic-time class and simultaneously that every concept is a decision tree, hence a circuit, of size linear in p.

The two upper bounds. For very few samples: after receiving a single useful example the learner recovers z, brute-forces the lexicographically first certificate in exponential-in-p time, and outputs the exact concept; if no useful example appears it outputs the zero function. A concentration bound shows that if useful inputs carry probability at least ε, then a fresh sample of size on the order of 1/ε contains one with high probability, so this learner achieves error ε with about 1/ε samples and runtime exponential in p. For many samples: the concepts are p-sparse, and a general lemma about sparse classes shows an empirical risk minimizer that outputs the observed 1-inputs learns any p-sparse class to error ε with sample complexity and runtime both on the order of p/ε, via a union bound over the at most 2^p possible hypotheses.

The few-sample collapse. This is the main reduction, proved by contrapositive. Suppose a learner uses m samples, runs in time t, and reaches error ε* with high probability. The paper builds an Arthur–Merlin protocol for the language: Arthur draws m random useful indices, Merlin supplies their labels, the learner is run on this random labeled sample to produce a hypothesis, Arthur evaluates the hypothesis on all coordinates of the prefix z to read off a noisy codeword, decodes it, and runs the verifier on the recovered string. If z is in the language, Merlin's honest labels make the sample a genuine draw from the uniform distribution over useful inputs, so with high probability the hypothesis has error at most ε*, the read-off word is within the code's decoding radius of the true codeword, decoding returns w*, and the verifier accepts. If z is not in the language, no certificate is accepting, so the protocol rejects for every Merlin response, giving perfect soundness. The runtime is p times t log t plus a polynomial in p plus the verifier time, and the protocol uses only m bits of nondeterminism. A separate simulation shows that a perfectly sound Arthur–Merlin protocol using p bits of nondeterminism can be turned into a one-sided randomized algorithm by brute-forcing over all Merlin messages, at a multiplicative cost of two-to-the-number-of-nondeterminism-bits. Applying this to the protocol yields a one-sided randomized algorithm for the language running in time two-to-the-order-m times t log t times a polynomial in p. Because the chosen universal language is hard for the whole nondeterministic-time class (any such language reduces to it by pairing its verifier with the input), this places the entire nondeterministic-time class inside randomized time with the stated bound, which is exactly the few-sample containment claimed.

Assembling the package. Collecting these facts—VC dimension one, oracle enumerability with a learner of the stated sample and runtime bounds, the few-sample randomized containment, the linear-in-p/ε learner, and the small decision-tree and circuit representations—shows that the instantiated code and concept family satisfy every component of the tradeoff package, which proves the existence claim.
nl_theorem: Let p be a function from natural numbers to natural numbers that is a growth function (monotone with n ≤ p(n) for every n) and time-constructible, and assume that at least one efficient binary error-correcting code exists. Then there exist an efficient binary error-correcting code `code` and an indexed concept family C over the certificate-point domains determined by p and `code` such that C satisfies the complete computational-statistical tradeoff package: the low-sample item (VC dimension exactly one at every positive input length, NTIME(p·log p, p)-enumerability by an oracle machine, and a uniform PAC learner using O(1/ε) samples with constant-factor linear sample cost and post-sample time 2^{O(p(n))}); the few-sample lower bound stating that any m(n)-sample, time-t(n) learner at the code's error ε* whose induced two-trial public-coin simulation runtimes are stable under polynomial padding yields the language-by-language randomized containment of NTIME(p,p) in the stated tradeoff runtime; a many-sample uniform learner with sample complexity and runtime both O(p(n)/ε); and O(p(n)) decision-tree and circuit representations of every concept.
