core_claim: Two irreducible square matrices over a field share all corresponding principal minors exactly when a short chain of cut-transpose operations turns one into something diagonally equivalent to the other.

metainfo.paper: Characterizing and Testing Principal Minor Equivalence of Matrices

nl_proof:
The equivalence is proved by establishing the two implications separately.

Easy direction (a short cut-transpose chain forces equal principal minors). One first shows that a single cut-transpose operation preserves every principal minor: after reindexing so that the chosen cut sits in the top-left block, any principal submatrix splits into a two-by-two block form with rank-one off-diagonal blocks, and an explicit determinant expansion (via the generalized Laplace expansion, fixing the rows on one side of the cut) shows that the determinant of that block form is unchanged when the operation swaps the crossing rank-one factors and transposes the complementary block. Diagonally similar matrices trivially share all principal minors, and transposition leaves each principal minor fixed, so diagonally equivalent matrices are principal-minor equivalent. Chaining these facts along the sequence, each step preserving all principal minors and the final diagonal equivalence contributing none, gives that the endpoints of any short chain are principal-minor equivalent.

Hard direction (equal principal minors produce a short chain). This is proved by reducing to a convenient normal form and then by induction on the order.

Reduction to nonzero off-diagonal entries. Using the transformation sending a matrix to the adjugate of a diagonal shift, one can assume all off-diagonal entries are nonzero: for an irreducible matrix a suitable diagonal shift makes this adjugate have no zero off-diagonal entry; the transformation preserves principal-minor equivalence, preserves the set of cuts, and commutes (up to diagonal similarity) with the cut-transpose operation. Hence a chain for the transformed pair yields one of the same length for the original pair, and it suffices to treat matrices with nonzero off-diagonal entries.

Base cases. If the order is at most three, or the order is at least four but the first matrix has no cut, then a previously established characterization shows the two matrices are already diagonally equivalent, giving an empty chain. For order four with a cut, a case analysis, carried out by equating the sums of weights of Hamiltonian cycles of the associated digraphs over all index subsets (an equivalent restatement of principal-minor equality), shows that either the two matrices are diagonally equivalent, or they share a common cut and applying one cut-transpose along any common cut makes the first matrix diagonally equivalent to the second.

Obtaining a common cut. In general one takes an inclusion-minimal cut of the first matrix. If its size exceeds two, it is automatically a cut of the second matrix; the argument decomposes along smaller index sets, uses that minimal larger cuts leave certain principal submatrices without cuts, and applies the no-cut characterization to force the crossing rows and columns to be proportional. If the minimal cut has size two and fails to be a cut of the second matrix, one analyses ratios of crossing entries and identifies a cut of the second matrix such that one cut-transpose along it produces a matrix in which the size-two set is a cut. In every case one reduces to the situation where the two matrices share a common cut.

Decomposition and induction. Given a common cut, each matrix is split into two overlapping principal submatrices, one supported on the cut plus one outside index and one on the complement plus one inside index. Principal-minor equivalence is inherited by the corresponding pieces. Minimality of the cut forces the smaller piece on the cut side to have no cut, hence to be diagonally equivalent to its counterpart. Applying the induction hypothesis to the complementary pieces yields a cut-transpose sequence relating them. This sequence is lifted to the full matrices: each cut in the sequence is either enlarged by the common cut or kept unchanged, according to whether it contains the distinguished overlap index, and one verifies at every step that both the common cut and the lifted cut are genuine cuts and that applying the lifted operation restricts correctly to the smaller matrices while keeping the common cut minimal.

Final step and length bound. After this lifting, the transformed first matrix agrees, up to diagonal equivalence, with the second matrix on the complement side. A concluding lemma shows that from here either the two full matrices are already diagonally equivalent or one further cut-transpose along the complement of the common cut makes them so; when the alignment is with the transpose one works with the transpose of the second matrix. Counting the operations, the lifted induction contributes at most twice the order minus two steps, possibly one extra step is used to create the common cut, and possibly one final step is needed, so the total number of cut-transpose operations is strictly less than twice the order. This produces the required short cut-transpose chain and completes the equivalence.
nl_theorem: Let 𝔽 be a field and let A and B be n×n matrices indexed by Fin n over 𝔽, each irreducible (its index type is nonempty and, for every ordered pair of indices, there is a reflexive-transitive walk along nonzero off-diagonal entries). Then A and B are principal-minor equivalent (for every index subset S, the determinants of the principal submatrices A[S,S] and B[S,S] agree) if and only if there is a short cut-transpose chain from A to B: an integer k < 2n and a sequence of matrices (A_i) with A_0 = A such that for each i < k the pair (A_i, A_{i+1}) is a single cut-transpose step (A_{i+1} is the normalized cut-transpose of A_i at some cut), and A_k is diagonally equivalent to B (diagonally similar to B or to its transpose).

core_claim: There exists a positive absolute constant for which partially augmented projection density estimators attain the stated expected squared error bound, combining an invariant dimension term with a group averaging term.

metainfo.paper: Data Augmentation: A Fourier Analysis Perspective

nl_proof:
The paper proves the density statement by combining two building blocks: a baseline variance bound for unaugmented projection estimators and an exact identity for random group averaging, glued together by an orthogonal decomposition of the error.

Setup and reductions. Because the finite-dimensional hypothesis space is closed under the isometric group action, each lifted operator that sends a function to its transform is unitary, and the full group-averaging operator (the expectation of these operators over a uniform group element) is exactly the orthogonal projection onto the invariant subspace. The augmentation hypothesis is that this projection fixes the projection of the target onto the hypothesis space; consequently the projection of the target onto the invariant subspace coincides with its projection onto the whole hypothesis space. The paper names two intermediate targets: the projection of the true density onto the hypothesis space, and its further projection onto the invariant subspace, which under the stated hypothesis are the same invariant function.

Step 1 (estimation inside the invariant subspace). The paper first records that an unaugmented projection density estimator built from an orthonormal basis has expected squared excess error over its span equal to the sum of the coordinate-wise variances of the empirical coefficient averages. Each such variance is at most the second moment of a basis function under the true density, which is bounded by the essential supremum of the density times the unit basis normalization. Summing over the coordinates of the invariant subspace shows that the ideal estimator using full group averaging has expected squared error at most a constant times the density's essential sup times the invariant dimension divided by the sample size.

Step 2 (replacing full averaging by averaging over the sampled subset). Because projection estimators are linear in the data, augmenting each sample by the transforms coming from the sampled group elements is equivalent to applying the empirical averaging operator over that subset to the unaugmented estimator; full augmentation corresponds to the exact group projection. Conditioning on the base samples, the paper invokes its random-averaging identity: decomposing the hypothesis space into isotypic components, the exact projection keeps the invariant part and kills every nontrivial irreducible block, while the empirical average over an independent uniform subset has, on each nontrivial block, mean zero (by Schur's lemma and character orthogonality, the group mean of a nontrivial irreducible representation vanishes). A direct variance computation, with cross terms vanishing, shows that the expected squared discrepancy between the subset average and the exact projection equals the squared norm of the non-invariant part of the input divided by the subset size. Applying this to the unaugmented estimator, and using that the invariant intermediate target is annihilated by the complementary projection so that the residual is controlled by the deviation of the estimator from the projection of the target onto the whole space, the paper bounds the expected squared gap between the augmented estimator and the ideal fully-averaged estimator by a constant times (dimension of the hypothesis space) divided by (sample size times subset size), again using the baseline variance bound applied to the full space.

Step 3 (combining the two errors). Writing the total error as the sum of the gap between the augmented estimator and the ideal fully-averaged estimator plus the estimation error of the ideal estimator inside the invariant subspace, and applying the elementary inequality that the squared norm of a sum is at most twice the sum of the squared norms, the two bounds add. This yields an absolute constant times the sum of the essential-sup-weighted invariant-dimension term over the sample size and the full-dimension term over the sample size times the subset size, which is exactly the claimed guarantee for a suitable positive constant.
nl_theorem: There exists a real constant C > 0 that is an admissible density-estimation constant in the following sense. For every probability space (X, μ); every finite group G acting on X so that each element acts by a μ-preserving map; every dimension r and family φ = (φ_ℓ) that is L²(X,μ)-orthonormal with each φ_ℓ ∈ L²(X,μ); every representation ρ of G on Rʳ that implements the lifted action (so that ιφ(ρ(g)c)(x) = ιφ(c)(g⁻¹·x) pointwise); and every measurable f* : X → ℝ that is nonnegative μ-almost everywhere, lies in L²(X,μ), has finite essential supremum with (essential supremum) value at most 1, whose density measure f*·μ is a probability measure, and whose projected-target coefficient vector θ(f*) is fixed by the invariant projection Π_{FG}: for all natural numbers n, m with n > 0 and m > 0, the expectation over n i.i.d. samples from the density law (and over an i.i.d. uniform augmentation set S of size m from G) of the squared L²(X)-distance between the partially augmented projection density estimator and Π_{FG} θ(f*) is at most C · ( ‖f*‖∞ · dim(Rʳ)ᴳ / n + r / (n·m) ).

core_claim: A universal constant makes the ratio-class minimum-distance estimator achieve, with high probability, squared Hellinger risk bounded by the best logarithmically weighted model approximation plus a VC-dimension complexity term.

metainfo.paper: Density estimation for Hellinger via minimum-distance estimators: mixtures of Gaussians, log-concave, and more

nl_proof:
The argument mirrors the classical minimum-distance-estimator proof for total variation distance, but replaces the total-variation ingredients with a modified Hellinger-type distance over the ratio class together with a reverse data processing inequality. Throughout write H² for squared Hellinger distance and d_H for the modified distance that takes the supremum, over concepts in the ratio class, of one half the squared difference of the square roots of the two masses assigned to the concept event.

Two elementary structural facts about d_H drive the proof. First, d_H(p,q) ≤ H²(p,q) always: on any single event the contribution is bounded by the local Hellinger integral, which is at most the whole integral. Second, d_H obeys an approximate triangle inequality, d_H(a,c) ≤ 2(d_H(a,b) + d_H(b,c)), coming from inserting an intermediate square root and using (u+v)² ≤ 2(u²+v²). One also uses that both H² and d_H lie in [0,1].

Step one applies the approximate triangle inequality to the target loss through any model density g: H²(f, hat) ≤ 2(H²(f,g) + H²(g, hat)).

Step two controls H²(g, hat) by d_H(g, hat). Here the reverse data processing inequality is essential: for any two densities there is a likelihood-ratio threshold whose induced two-point (Bernoulli) distributions retain a constant-over-logarithm fraction of the Hellinger distance, giving d_H(g, hat) ≥ H²(g, hat) / (50 log(4/H²(g, hat))). This is combined with a scalar monotonicity lemma: since the map x ↦ x·log(e/x) is nondecreasing on [0,1], the bound x ≥ y/(50 log(4/y)) forces y ≤ 100·x·log(e/x). Applying it converts the reverse inequality into H²(g, hat) ≤ 100·d_H(g, hat)·log(e/d_H(g, hat)).

Step three works with the entropy-type envelope z(x) = x·log(e/x), which is nondecreasing on [0,1], is zero at zero, and satisfies the approximate subadditivity z(x) ≤ 2(z(a)+z(b)) whenever x ≤ 2(a+b) with all arguments in [0,1]. Repeatedly inserting f and then the empirical distribution and applying this subadditivity, together with symmetry of d_H, rewrites the bound entirely in terms of z evaluated at d_H(f,g), d_H(f, f_n), and d_H(f_n, hat). The defining property of the minimum-distance estimator, d_H(f_n, hat) ≤ d_H(f_n, g) (with an additive slack for an approximate minimizer), lets the last term be replaced by a term through g, and then again through f. Collecting the constants yields H²(f, hat) bounded by a constant multiple of z(H²(f,g)) plus a constant multiple of z(d_H(f, f_n)); using z(x) ≤ constant·x·log(2/x) and d_H ≤ H² identifies the first piece with the logarithmically weighted approximation penalty H²(f,g)·log(2/H²(f,g)).

Step four bounds the empirical fluctuation term z(d_H(f, f_n)) using a second-order (normalized) uniform convergence estimate for VC classes: with probability at least 1 − δ, uniformly over all concepts in the class, the difference of the square roots of the empirical and true counts is at most a multiple of the square root of d·ln(2n+1) + ln(8/δ). Dividing by the sample size and translating into d_H shows that, on this high-probability event, d_H(f, f_n) is at most a radius of order (d·log(2n+1) + log(1/δ))/n; feeding this into z and bounding the resulting logarithmic factor by log n produces the complexity term (d·log n + log(2/δ))·log n / n. The additive optimization slack, being at most 1/n, is likewise absorbed into this term.

Since the resulting bound holds simultaneously for every g in the model on the same high-probability event, one passes to the infimum over g, obtaining that with probability at least 1 − δ the squared Hellinger loss of the estimator is at most an absolute constant times the sum of the best logarithmically weighted approximation error and the VC complexity term. Choosing that absolute constant establishes the stated existence claim; the hypothesis that the target law is atomless and that n ≥ 2 supports the uniform convergence step, and no assumption that f belongs to the model is needed.
nl_theorem: There exists a positive real constant C such that the following holds. For every measurable space Ω, measure μ on Ω, natural numbers n and d, real δ, target density f on μ, and family F of densities on μ, if n ≥ 2, d ≥ 1, 0 < δ < 1, and F is nonempty, then for every real ε with ε ≤ 1/n and every map hat sending samples of size n to densities: if the probability measure represented by f is atomless (every measurable set of positive measure has a measurable subset of strictly smaller positive measure), the ratio class of F is countable and has VC dimension d, hat is an ε-approximate minimum-distance estimator with respect to that ratio class, and the map x ↦ H²(f, hat x) is measurable, then under the law of n i.i.d. observations from f the event that H²(f, hat x) ≤ C·(inf over g in F of H²(f,g)·log₂(2/H²(f,g)) + (d·log₂ n + log₂(2/δ))·log₂ n / n) has probability at least 1 − δ.

core_claim: Any shallow fully connected ReLU network that exactly computes the coordinate maximum on the unit hypercube must have width at least an explicit growing power of the input dimension.

metainfo.paper: A Depth Hierarchy for Computing the Maximum in ReLU Networks via Extremal Graph Theory

nl_proof:
The paper proves the bound by induction on the depth k, reducing a depth-k network to a shallower one that computes a lower-dimensional maximum, and invoking a classical density theorem from extremal graph theory (Turán's theorem: a graph on d vertices with no clique of size r has at most (1 − 1/(r−1))·d²/2 edges).

Setup and normalization. A preliminary structural proposition shows that any ReLU network agreeing with the coordinate maximum on the unit hypercube can be replaced by one of the same depth and at most twice the width that computes the maximum on all of real d-space, and whose every first-hidden-layer neuron has a weight vector with at least two nonzero coordinates. This is obtained by first shifting the network with a random bias so that it computes the maximum in a neighborhood of the origin, then successively "homogenizing" it: neurons with negative bias become inactive near the origin and are deleted (propagating zeros forward), while neurons with positive bias are each replaced by two unbiased neurons together with a compensating adjustment of the next layer's biases. Because each neuron is replaced by at most two, the width at most doubles; the resulting network is positively homogeneous and coincides with the maximum near the origin, hence, by homogeneity of both sides, coincides with the maximum everywhere. A probability-one choice of the random shift guarantees the two-nonzero-coordinate property.

Base case (depth 3). Here one shows width at least roughly d²/8, and in particular at least 0.1·d² once d ≥ 256, which matches the claimed exponent 1 + 1/(2^{1} − 1) = 2. Assume a too-narrow depth-3 network; apply the normalization above. Form a graph on the d input coordinates by starting from the complete graph and, for each first-layer neuron, deleting the edge joining the two smallest indices of its nonzero weights. Since each neuron deletes at most one edge, the graph retains at least C(d,2) minus the width many edges, which for a sufficiently narrow network exceeds the Mantel/Turán threshold and forces a triangle. Every neuron therefore still has a nonzero weight on some coordinate outside this triangle (otherwise its two nonzero coordinates would lie inside and would have deleted a triangle edge). Substituting exponentially increasing negative values for the coordinates outside the triangle makes, in each neuron, the term of largest nonzero index dominate the preactivation; consequently every first-layer neuron keeps a fixed sign, hence a fixed activation state, over the whole unit cube in the three clique coordinates. The first layer is then purely linear there and can be absorbed into the second layer, collapsing the network to a depth-2 network computing the maximum of three coordinates on the unit cube. This contradicts the separately established fact that no depth-2 ReLU network computes the maximum of three inputs on the cube (proved by characterizing the nondifferentiable set of a depth-2 network as an arrangement of at most width-many hyperplanes and showing the maximum's ridge set cannot arise from such an arrangement).

Inductive step. Set α_k = 1/(2^{k-2} − 1), so the target width is 0.1·d^{1+α_k}. The hypothesis 3 ≤ k ≤ log₂(log₂ d) yields d ≥ 256 and d^{α_k} ≥ 16. Suppose for contradiction that a depth-k network computes the maximum on the cube with width below 0.1·d^{1+α_k}. Normalize it as above to a network of width below 0.2·d^{1+α_k} computing the maximum on all of real d-space with the two-nonzero-coordinate property. Build the same first-layer weight graph; it has at least C(d,2) minus one-fifth d^{1+α_k} edges, which after using d^{α_k} ≥ 16 exceeds the Turán threshold for a clique of size r = ⌊2.1·d^{1-α_k}+1⌋ ≥ 2.1·d^{1-α_k}. As before, each neuron has a nonzero weight outside this size-r clique. Substituting exponentially increasing negative values for the non-clique coordinates makes the largest-index nonzero term dominate each preactivation, fixing every first-layer activation over the unit cube in the r clique coordinates; the first layer becomes linear and is absorbed into the next, producing a depth-(k−1) network of width still below 0.2·d^{1+α_k} that computes the maximum of r coordinates on the unit r-cube.

Closing the contradiction. The induction hypothesis applied at depth k−1 and dimension r forces this reduced network to have width at least 0.1·r^{1+α_{k-1}}. Using r ≥ 2.1·d^{1-α_k} and the algebraic identity (1 − α_k)(1 + α_{k-1}) = 1 + α_k, one computes 0.1·r^{1+α_{k-1}} ≥ 0.1·2.1·d^{1+α_k} = 0.2·d^{1+α_k} + 0.01·d^{1+α_k} ≥ 0.2·d^{1+α_k} + 2, so the reduced width strictly exceeds 0.2·d^{1+α_k}. This contradicts the width bound established for the reduced network, completing the induction and proving that width at least 0.1·d^{1+1/(2^{k-2}-1)} is necessary.
nl_theorem: Fix natural numbers d and k with 3 ≤ k and k ≤ log₂(log₂ d). Consider a fully connected feed-forward ReLU network of depth k mapping ℝ^d to ℝ, where each hidden layer applies an affine map followed by coordinatewise ReLU and the single output neuron applies an affine map, its width being the largest number of neurons in any hidden layer (zero if there are no hidden layers). Suppose this network, evaluated at every point x of the unit hypercube [0,1]^d, equals the maximum of the coordinates of x. Then the width of the network is at least (1/10)·d^(1 + 1/(2^(k-2) − 1)), where the exponent uses real powers and k − 2 is truncated natural subtraction.

core_claim: Every binary hypothesis class has a worst-case data-selection regret sequence satisfying exactly one of three regimes: always one, linear between explicit bounds, or eventually zero.

metainfo.paper: Data Selection for ERMs

nl_proof:
The argument links the worst-case selection regret to the combinatorial theory of epsilon-nets, and it splits into four case analyses governed by two complexity parameters of the class: its VC dimension and its star number. Recall that the star number is the largest number of points that can be arranged so that each individual point can be singled out (flipped) by some hypothesis while the others keep a fixed pattern, and the VC dimension is the largest number of points shattered by the class. The proof uses two known facts about epsilon-nets: for any distribution, if the relevant set family has finite star number s then an epsilon-net of size at most s exists for every epsilon, and if the family has finite VC dimension d then an epsilon-net of size O((d/epsilon)·log(1/epsilon)) exists.

First, suppose the star number is finite. Given any dataset, pass to a maximal subdataset that is perfectly classifiable within the class; the optimal loss on the whole dataset equals the excluded fraction. Form the family of error sets of the hypotheses restricted to this subdataset; its star number is bounded by the star number of the class. Taking the uniform distribution on the subdataset, the first epsilon-net bound yields, for every epsilon, an epsilon-net of size at most the star number. Feeding this net to any empirical risk minimizer produces a hypothesis with restricted loss at most epsilon, hence total loss at most the optimum plus epsilon. Since epsilon is arbitrary and the net size does not grow with the budget, once the budget reaches the star number the regret is zero, giving the zero-rate regime.

Second, suppose the star number is infinite. For each budget n, take a star configuration of n+1 points whose center hypothesis realizes the labeling; this dataset is realizable. Choose an empirical risk minimizer that, whenever it sees a proper subset, outputs a hypothesis inconsistent with at least one of the n+1 points. Then it misclassifies at least one point, forcing regret at least 1/(n+1); this supplies the linear lower bound.

Third, suppose the VC dimension is finite and equal to d. The argument mirrors the finite-star case but invokes the VC-based epsilon-net bound instead, producing for budget n an epsilon-net with epsilon of order (d/n)·log n; applying any empirical risk minimizer to it yields loss at most the optimum plus this quantity, hence the upper bound of order (d·log n)/n, matching the linear-rate regime's upper bound.

Fourth, suppose the VC dimension is infinite. For any budget n and any small epsilon, take a shattered set of size n/epsilon, label all its points positively, and use a learner that predicts the negative label on every point outside its training subset; shattering guarantees this choice is realizable within the class. It classifies only the n selected points correctly and errs on the remaining fraction 1-epsilon, so letting epsilon tend to zero forces regret at least 1, giving the trivial rate.

Finally, these four conclusions are combined. The conditions infinite VC dimension, finite VC dimension together with infinite star number, and finite star number are mutually exclusive and exhaustive (finiteness of the star number implies finiteness of the VC dimension). In the first situation the trivial-rate bounds apply, in the second the matching lower bound of order 1/n and upper bound of order (log n)/n hold, and in the third the regret eventually vanishes. Hence exactly one of the three regimes holds for every hypothesis class.
nl_theorem: Let X be any domain and let H be any hypothesis class of binary hypotheses X → Bool. Consider the worst-case selection regret sequence R(n) defined as the supremum, over all learning rules A that are empirical risk minimizers over H and all finite nonempty datasets D, of the minimum selection regret: the infimum over training samples S of length n whose entries all occur in D of the empirical loss of A(S) on D minus the best loss in H on D. Then exactly one of the following three statements holds, meaning one holds and the other two fail: (1) the trivial rate, R(n) = 1 for every natural number n; (2) the linear rate, there exist constants C₁, C₂ > 0 (independent of n) such that C₁/n ≤ R(n) ≤ C₂·log(n)/n for every integer n ≥ 2; (3) the zero rate, there exists n₀ such that R(n) = 0 for every n ≥ n₀.

core_claim: For finitely many agents, at least one, and finitely many indivisible chores with nonnegative additive costs, some assignment is simultaneously envy-free up to one chore and Pareto optimal.

metainfo.paper: Existence of Fair and Efficient Allocation of Indivisible Chores

nl_proof:
The paper proves existence by combining a fixed-point argument with a discrete transfer algorithm; the target statement is exactly this existence result for additive chore costs.

Preliminary reductions. First, any chore that some agent values at zero cost can be handed to that agent and deleted, so one may assume all single-chore costs are strictly positive. Second, the argument passes to a perturbed instance whose costs are multiplied by tiny prime powers. Three perturbation estimates show that for a sufficiently small perturbation the instance becomes non-degenerate (no alternating cost cycle in the complete agent–chore bipartite graph has cost-product ratio equal to one), that any allocation which is envy-free up to one chore in the perturbed instance stays envy-free up to one chore in the original, and that any fractionally Pareto optimal allocation in the perturbed instance is Pareto optimal in the original. Hence it suffices to produce an allocation that is simultaneously envy-free up to one chore and fractionally Pareto optimal in a non-degenerate instance.

Linear-programming characterization. A classical welfare characterization says an allocation is fractionally Pareto optimal exactly when it minimizes a positively weighted total cost; equivalently, it is an integral optimum of a transportation-type linear program with weight vector having strictly positive entries. The dual assigns each chore a price; complementary slackness makes every assigned chore tight, and dual feasibility bounds each price by the weighted cost. A key lemma shows that if an optimal primal allocation is price-envy-free up to one chore (each agent's own bundle price, after removing one chore, is at most any other agent's bundle price), then, using tightness on the removed subbundle and dual feasibility on the other bundle and cancelling the positive weight, the allocation is envy-free up to one chore.

Finding the right weights via a fixed point. To locate weights guaranteeing a price-envy-free structure, the weights are taken from the standard simplex and slightly shrunk by a small parameter so that they stay strictly positive; the shrunken program still has an integral optimum that is fractionally Pareto optimal and a unique strictly positive dual price vector. A lemma shows that for every simplex weight vector and every optimum, some agent with positive weight is price-envy-free, because an agent carrying enough weight can receive no chore without contradicting optimality. Defining, for each agent, the closed set of weight vectors admitting an optimum in which that agent is price-envy-free, the covering hypothesis of the Knaster–Kuratowski–Mazurkiewicz lemma is met, so the sets share a common weight vector: at this weight, every agent is price-envy-free in some optimal allocation.

Discrete algorithm producing price-envy-freeness up to one chore. Fixing this weight and its dual prices, the tight bipartite graph of agent–chore incidences is a forest by non-degeneracy (a cycle would force a cost-product ratio of one). Degree-one chores are pre-assigned, leaving a residual forest with fewer chores than agents, in which a matching covers all remaining chores by Hall's condition. Using the per-agent totals of forced degree-one chores, one sets up two invariants: agents attaining the maximum forced total receive at most one residual chore, and every agent's bundle price is at least this maximum. An initial optimal allocation satisfying both invariants exists. While the current allocation is not price-envy-free up to one chore, there is a shortest alternating path from an unmatched maximum-total agent to a violating agent; transferring chores along this path (choosing the appropriate cutoff index) removes a chore from the violator while preserving both invariants and optimality. Termination is proved by a potential function built from agent and chore "levels" (half the length of the shortest alternating path from unmatched agents), which are shown to be non-decreasing, so the potential strictly decreases each iteration; the process halts in polynomially many steps at a price-envy-free-up-to-one-chore optimum.

Conclusion. That final allocation is fractionally Pareto optimal (being an optimum of the positively weighted program) and, by the price-to-envy lemma, envy-free up to one chore, in the non-degenerate perturbed instance. By the perturbation lemmas, for small enough perturbation the same allocation is envy-free up to one chore and Pareto optimal in the original instance, giving the desired allocation.
nl_theorem: Let the agents and the chores be finite types, with at least one agent, and let each agent assign a nonnegative additive cost to every chore (formally, a function sending each agent and each chore to a nonnegative real, the cost of a chore to that agent). Consider allocations that assign each chore to exactly one agent, where the bundle of an agent is the set of chores assigned to it, and the cost to an agent of a bundle is the sum of that agent's costs over the chores in the bundle. Then there exists such an allocation that is simultaneously envy-free up to one chore and Pareto optimal, where: envy-free up to one chore means that for every ordered pair of agents such that the first agent's cost for its own bundle exceeds its cost for the second agent's bundle, there is a chore in the first agent's bundle whose removal makes the first agent's cost for its remaining bundle at most its cost for the second agent's bundle; and Pareto optimal means that no allocation Pareto dominates it, where one allocation Pareto dominates another when every agent's own-bundle cost is no larger under the first and strictly smaller for at least one agent.

core_claim: Folded Reed-Solomon codes over a finite field, built from a multiplicative generator and appropriate evaluation points, are list-decodable up to the relaxed generalized Singleton radius with the prescribed list size.

metainfo.paper: Explicit Folded Reed-Solomon and Multiplicity Codes Achieve Relaxed Generalized Singleton Bounds

nl_proof:
The paper proves the list-decodability bound by contradiction, reducing it to a single combinatorial–geometric statement about the coefficient vectors of message polynomials, and then establishing that statement through a root-counting argument controlled by a novel "loss" bound.

Overview of the main argument. Suppose the code failed to be list-decodable at the stated radius. Then there would be a received word together with L+1 distinct message polynomials of degree less than k whose codewords all lie within relative Hamming distance ρ of that word. For each such polynomial let its agreement set be the collection of blocks on which its codeword matches the received word. Because ρ equals (L/(L+1))(1 − sR/(s−L+1)), each agreement set has size at least n/(L+1) + Lk/((L+1)(s−L+1)); summing the L+1 lower bounds and subtracting n shows that the total "excess agreement" is large.

To organize this excess the paper introduces a geometric agreement hypergraph: the vertices are the coefficient vectors of the L+1 polynomials, and for each block there is a hyperedge consisting of those vectors whose codewords agree with the received word on that block. The weight of the hypergraph is the sum over blocks of (size of hyperedge − 1), truncated at zero; the distance computation gives weight at least Lk/(s−L+1). The theorem then follows from a key lemma: if such a hypergraph on m ≥ 2 vertices has weight at least (m−1)k/(s−m+2), the vertices cannot be distinct. Applying it with m = L+1 contradicts the assumed distinctness, finishing the proof.

Proof of the key lemma. One first passes to an inclusion-minimal vertex subset that still has weight at least its own threshold (m′−1)k/(s−m′+2) while every proper subset of size at least two is strictly below its threshold. Translating so that one vertex becomes the origin keeps the translated vectors distinct. To each set of vectors the paper attaches a geometric polynomial, defined as a scaled determinant of the folded Wronskian of a basis of their span; using the folded Wronskian criterion for linear independence and the fact that a change of basis multiplies the determinant by a nonzero scalar, this polynomial is well-defined and nonzero, with degree at most ℓ(k−1), where ℓ is the dimension of the span.

Two quantitative ingredients then collide. First, a root-counting result shows that the geometric agreement hypergraph forces many roots of the geometric polynomial: a hyperedge whose vectors span an affine subspace of dimension t contributes multiplicity at least t at each of the s−ℓ+1 evaluation points γ^0 α, …, γ^{s−ℓ} α associated with its block. This is because t linearly independent difference vectors vanish at all shifts of that block's point, so a common linear factor appears in t columns of the Wronskian; expanding along those columns yields the multiplicity, and appropriateness of the evaluation points guarantees that the roots coming from different blocks are distinct and hence add up. Thus the polynomial has at least (s−ℓ+1) times the sum of affine dimensions of the hyperedges as its root count.

Second, the paper bounds how much the affine dimension of a hyperedge can fall short of its size minus one. It defines a loss function measuring exactly this shortfall and proves that, under the strict weight condition on all proper subsets, the total loss is at most (m′−1−ℓ)k/(s−m′+2). The engine here is a partition lemma from matroid theory: the translated vertex set admits a partition into ℓ+1 parts such that choosing one representative from each part always yields affine dimension exactly ℓ. Consequently the affine dimension of any hyperedge is at least the number of parts it meets minus one, which converts the loss into a sum of part-restricted weights; the strict weight bounds on each part, together with the identity that the part sizes minus one add to the total, give the loss bound. This loss control is the decisive improvement that drives the list size down to its optimal value.

Combining the two ingredients, the number of roots of the geometric polynomial is at least (s−ℓ+1) times (weight minus total loss), which is at least (s−ℓ+1)((m′−1)k − (m′−1−ℓ)k)/(s−m′+2) = ℓk. But the polynomial has degree at most ℓ(k−1) < ℓk, so it must be identically zero, contradicting its nonvanishing. Hence the vertices cannot be distinct, which establishes the key lemma and therefore the claimed list-decodability.
nl_theorem: Let F be a finite field with cyclic multiplicative group of units, and let s, n, L be positive integers with a positive integer k satisfying k ≤ n and L ≤ s. Suppose γ is a unit of F that generates the group of units (every unit lies in the subgroup of integer powers of γ), and suppose the tuple α = (α₁, …, αₙ) in Fⁿ is appropriate for (s, γ), meaning the map sending a pair (i, j) with 0 ≤ i < s and 1 ≤ j ≤ n to γ^i · α_j is injective. Consider the (s, γ)-folded Reed-Solomon code whose codewords are, for each polynomial f over F of degree less than k, the length-n word whose j-th symbol is the s-tuple (f(α_j), f(γα_j), …, f(γ^{s-1}α_j)) in F^s. Let R = k/(sn) be its rate and let ρ = (L/(L+1))·(1 − sR/(s−L+1)) be the relaxed generalized Singleton decoding radius, all computed over the reals with division by zero giving zero. Then this code, viewed as a block-length-n code over the alphabet F^s, is (ρ, L) list-decodable: for every received word y, the number of codewords whose Hamming distance to y is at most ρ·n is at most L.

core_claim: Every property that is sample-testable with bounded proximity, sample count, and circuit size sits between itself and its neighborhood inside a structured symmetric property whose part count and partition complexity satisfy universal exponential bounds.

metainfo.paper: Efficient and Private Property Testing via Indistinguishability

nl_proof:
The paper fixes a valid randomized circuit tester T of size at most s for the property P: it accepts every function in P with probability at least two thirds and accepts every function outside the ε-neighborhood with probability at most one third. The plan is to build a structurally simple simulator of T, use it to define the sandwiching property Q, and read the partition off the simulator's internal form. Two regularity-type tools drive the argument.

The first tool is the complexity-theoretic regularity lemma: any target function admits a low-complexity simulator, expressible as a clipped weighted sum of a bounded number of distinguisher functions, whose error correlates only negligibly with every distinguisher in a prescribed family. The second, stronger tool is the supersimulator lemma, an iterative strengthening that lets the simulator fool a family of distinguishers that are permitted to grow more complex than the simulator itself, at the cost of choosing the simulator's size within a bounded interval that may depend on the target.

Two intermediate lemmas connect these tools to testing. The oracle simulation lemma states that replacing the true labeling function f by any simulator f̃ that is regular with respect to the family of one-way restrictions of the tester (the functions obtained by hard-wiring all but one input of the tester) changes the tester's acceptance probability by at most 2mδ, where δ is the regularity error. Its proof is a hybrid argument that swaps the m labels one at a time from true labels to modeled labels drawn from the Bernoulli distribution with mean f̃, together with the standard rewriting that turns a distinguisher on a labeled sample into a linear expression in the label, exposing exactly a one-way restriction. The tester simulation lemma states that if a candidate simulator T̃ is regular for the tester's mean function with respect to the consistency indicators of a family F (functions checking that all m labeled samples are consistent with some thresholded member of F), then for every f̃ in F the expected outputs of the mean tester and of T̃ on samples labeled by f̃ agree up to 2^m·γ, where γ is the regularity error. Its proof rewrites Bernoulli labels via uniform random thresholds, relates the acceptance on such labels to acceptance on fully uniform labels through the 2^{-m} probability that uniform labels match, and applies regularity against the consistency indicator, incurring the 2^m factor.

The main construction combines these. Using the supersimulator lemma with a growth function that outputs the consistency indicators of structured sums of restrictions of T and of the current approximation, the paper obtains a simulator T̃ of the tester's mean function that fools consistency indicators of functions slightly more complex than both T and T̃; this extra power over the ordinary regularity lemma is exactly what is needed, since the modeled labeling functions are marginally larger than the testers. Separately, the ordinary regularity lemma supplies, for the labeling function f, a low-complexity simulator f̃ that is regular with respect to the restrictions of both T and T̃. Chaining the two intermediate lemmas gives a comparison, for every labeling function f: the tester's acceptance probability equals its value on modeled labels up to 2mδ (oracle simulation), which equals T̃'s value on modeled labels up to 2^m·γ (tester simulation), which equals T̃'s value on true labels up to a further 2mδ (oracle simulation again). The total discrepancy is 4mδ + 2^m·γ, which is made smaller than one sixth by choosing δ of order 1/m and γ of order 1/2^m.

The property Q is then defined as the set of functions on which T̃ accepts in expectation with value at least one half. Because a function in P is accepted by T with probability at least two thirds, T̃'s value on it is at least two thirds minus one sixth, hence at least one half, so P is contained in Q; because a function outside the ε-neighborhood is accepted by T with probability at most one third, T̃'s value on it is below one half, so Q is contained in the ε-neighborhood. This establishes the sandwiching.

Structured symmetry is read off the explicit form of the supersimulator: T̃ is a clipped scaled sum of at most about 1/γ² terms, each a signed consistency indicator of a function f_j that is itself a bounded structured sum of restrictions. Consequently T̃'s expected output depends on the labeling function only through the densities of f over the sets defined by thresholding each f_j at fixed levels, for the m sample slots. Intersecting these at most mk thresholded sets yields a partition into at most 2^{mk}, and hence 2^{2^{O(m)}}, parts on which Q is invariant, giving the doubly exponential bound on the number of parts. Finally, a gate-counting lemma shows, by induction on the number of terms, that a single classifier circuit can compute all the thresholded indicator bits: since T has size s its one-way restrictions also have size s, and each new term adds only polynomially many gates and restrictions, so the classifier has size at most 2^{O(m)}·s. This produces the required bound on the partition complexity, and taking the two suppressed constants as fixed absolute numbers yields the doubly exponential part bound and the exponential-times-s complexity bound simultaneously, completing the proof.
nl_theorem: There exist absolute natural-number constants c1 and c2 with the following property. For every input length n, every sample count m, every size bound s, every real number ε with ε ≥ 0, and every property P of Boolean functions on {0,1}^n, if P is sample-testable with proximity ε using m samples and a randomized Boolean circuit of size at most s, then there exist a natural number k, a property Q of Boolean functions on {0,1}^n, and a natural-number bound b such that P ⊆ Q ⊆ P_ε, the property Q is k-part symmetric with partition complexity at most b, the number of parts satisfies k ≤ 2^(2^(c1·(m+1))), and the partition complexity satisfies b ≤ 2^(c2·(m+1))·s. Here sample-testability means there is an m-sample randomized circuit tester of size at most s accepting every f in P with probability at least 2/3 and accepting every f outside the ε-neighborhood of P with probability at most 1/3, probabilities being expressed by exact inequalities between uniform finite counts; P_ε is the set of functions ε-close in normalized Hamming distance to some member of P; and Q being k-part symmetric with partition complexity at most b means there is a classifier of {0,1}^n into k parts, computed by a Boolean circuit of size at most b, under all of whose within-part permutations Q is invariant.

core_claim: For sufficiently small bounded step sizes, the tau-leaping sampler started from the uniform law achieves data-recovery error controlled, up to an absolute constant, by the score error, an exponential horizon term, and a discretization term.

metainfo.paper: Efficient Sampling with Discrete Diffusion Models: Sharp and Adaptive Guarantees

nl_proof:
The argument bounds the error of the terminal output by an analysis of the whole trajectory and then splits the resulting quantity into an initialization piece, a score-approximation piece, and a discretization piece, each controlled separately.

Step 1 (reduction to a path comparison). Since the output distribution is the terminal marginal of the sampler's trajectory and the data distribution is the terminal marginal of the reversed noising trajectory, the data-processing inequality bounds the divergence of the data distribution from the output by the divergence between the two full path laws over the time grid. The chain rule for divergence of Markovian path laws then decomposes this into the divergence at the initial grid point, namely the divergence of the terminal noising law from the uniform law, plus the sum over the grid intervals of the expected conditional divergence between the reverse transition kernel and the sampler transition kernel, the expectation taken over the reverse marginal at the left endpoint.

Step 2 (initialization term). The first piece, the divergence of the terminal noising law from the uniform law, is handled by a log-Sobolev inequality for the uniform noising process, whose modified log-Sobolev constant equals two. This gives exponential contraction of divergence to the uniform stationary law, so the terminal divergence is at most the exponential factor exp(-T) times the initial divergence of the data distribution from the uniform law, and the latter is at most the dimension times the logarithm of the vocabulary size. Hence this piece is bounded by exp(-T) times d times log S.

Step 3 (Girsanov change of measure for each interval). Writing each conditional divergence as the time integral of the derivative of divergence between the conditional reverse marginals and the conditional sampler marginals, a Girsanov-type change-of-measure identity for continuous-time Markov chains expresses the derivative through the off-diagonal rates. This turns each interval contribution into an integral, weighted by the reciprocal vocabulary size, of the expected sum over coordinates and replacement tokens of the exact score times a Bregman divergence between the frozen learned score at the left endpoint and the exact score at the current time. The Bregman divergence here is the standard convex generator, ratio minus one minus the logarithm of the ratio.

Step 4 (law of cosines splitting). For the inner sum, the Bregman three-point identity (the law of cosines for Bregman divergence) decomposes each summand into three parts. The first is the score-entropy expression evaluated entirely at the frozen left-endpoint time, comparing the learned and exact scores. The second is a cross term, a difference of scores multiplied by the logarithm of the learned score. The third is a telescoping difference between a quantity at the current time and the same quantity at the left endpoint, built from minus the logarithm of the exact score summed over one-coordinate neighbors; here one uses the algebraic fact that the expectation over neighbors of the generator function of the exact score equals the expectation of minus the logarithm of the exact score.

Step 5 (controlling the three parts).
First part: after taking the expectation over the reverse left-endpoint marginal and integrating over each interval, the leading term is exactly the step-weighted score-entropy loss at the reverse grid times, whose sum is bounded by the aggregate score error assumption, contributing at most ε_score.
Second part: a martingale property of the exact score along the reverse process forces the cross term to vanish once the expectation over the current state, conditioned on the left-endpoint state, is taken; the score is a reverse-time martingale, so its expected increment against the frozen log-score is zero.
Third part: introduce the function φ(t) equal to the reciprocal vocabulary size times the expected sum of minus the logarithm of the exact score over one-coordinate neighbors. The interval contributions telescope into differences φ(T−t) minus φ(T−t_k). One shows φ is nonnegative (by Jensen) and, using a pointwise logarithmic bound on the exact score of order log S plus the positive part of log(1/t), that φ(t) is of order d times (log S plus max{log(1/t),0}); φ is also nonincreasing in t. Splitting the grid at a point where the remaining reverse time is comparable to the maximum step Δ, and combining the bound on φ near zero with monotonicity for the telescoping tail, bounds the total telescoping contribution by a constant times Δ times d times log(S/Δ).

Step 6 (assembly). Adding the three contributions to the initialization term yields a bound of the divergence of the data distribution from the output by an absolute constant times the sum of ε_score, exp(-T) times d times log S, and Δ times d times log(S/Δ). Because the maximum step is bounded by the fixed cap B in the unit range and the vocabulary size is at least one, the discretization term is nonnegative and the constant depends only on that cap, which is the claimed guarantee.
nl_theorem: Fix a step cap B with 0 < B ≤ 1. Then there exists a constant C > 0 (depending only on B) such that the following holds for every vocabulary size S with S > 0, every dimension d, every step count N, every data distribution q_data on the state space [S]^d, every family (q_t) that is the uniform noising process started from q_data, every learned score function, every time grid times : Fin (N+1) → ℝ, every horizon T, maximum step Δ, and aggregate error ε_score, every family of transition kernels, and every output distribution p_output, subject to: the times form a uniform time grid with horizon T, maximum step Δ, and step bound B (so 0 = t_0 < ⋯ < t_N = T with adjacent gaps positive and at most Δ, some gap equal to Δ, and Δ ≤ B); (q_t) is the uniform noising process from q_data; the learned score is strictly positive on every genuine one-coordinate replacement at each reverse grid time; the aggregate score-estimation error is at most ε_score; the kernels form the frozen-score tau-leaping transition kernels; and p_output is the tau-leaping output law started from the uniform distribution on [S]^d. Under these hypotheses, the Kullback–Leibler divergence of q_data from p_output is at most C · (ε_score + e^{−T} · d · log S + Δ · d · log(S/Δ)), where the right-hand side is embedded into the extended nonnegative reals.

core_claim: One universal set of positive constants turns any specialized product-distributional communication protocol into a randomized reporting data structure achieving the stated space, preprocessing-time, and expected-query-time bounds derived from the protocol's cost, time, soundness, and false-positive parameters.

metainfo.paper: A Framework for Building Data Structures from Communication Protocols

nl_proof:
The argument is a single explicit construction that turns the assumed protocol into the required data structure, with one fixed family of positive constants (the exponent multipliers in the space, preprocessing, and query bounds and the linear factors for false positives, soundness, and output) chosen once and for all, independently of the domains, the target function, the protocol, the resource bounds, and the error parameters.

Given a finite dataset, the key idea is to run the protocol with the input distribution equal to the uniform distribution over the dataset. Because the protocol is guaranteed to work under any product-type input distribution, it in particular works for this data-dependent uniform choice, and the choices of the public and private coins of the randomness party serve as the preprocessing seed. Under fixed distribution and coins, the messages of the randomness party are completely determined by the transcript, so a transcript is captured by the messages of the sender, the querier, and the prover.

Preprocessing builds a protocol tree. Each node corresponds to one step: at a sender node one stores all possible sender messages, each pointing to a child; likewise at a querier node and at a prover node; at a randomness-party node one stores the single determined message and continues to the unique child; and each root-to-leaf path is a complete transcript, labeled by the protocol's Boolean output. There are exponentially many leaves in the total number of bits sent by the sender, querier, and prover. At every accepting leaf one stores exactly those dataset points whose sender messages are consistent with that transcript when the querier and prover send the messages recorded along the path.

To answer a query, the construction enumerates every possible prover message and, for each, walks the tree: at sender nodes it recurses into all children, at querier nodes it follows the single child determined by the query and the current transcript, at prover nodes it follows the child selected by the fixed prover message, and at randomness-party nodes it reads the stored message. On reaching an accepting leaf it scans the stored points and emits those actually satisfying the predicate.

Correctness uses that the protocol only makes false-positive errors under the distinguished prover advice: whenever a dataset point matches the query, the protocol accepts it under the unique distinguished advice for every coin realization. Since the query enumeration includes that distinguished advice, the point lies in a visited accepting leaf and is emitted. Conversely, since the query re-checks the predicate before emitting, only genuine matches are output, so the returned set is exactly the set of matching dataset points.

The space bound follows because there are exponentially many leaves in the combined sender, querier, and prover bit counts; storing the tree costs this many cells, storing the randomness party's messages along each path costs a factor proportional to its bit count, and each leaf stores at most as many points as the dataset size, giving an overall bound exponential in those three costs times the dataset size plus the randomness-party cost. The preprocessing time follows because, for each leaf and each dataset point, one simulates the sender, querier, and randomness-party message construction, whose combined time is bounded by the sum of the three construction-time parameters, multiplied by the dataset size and the number of leaves.

For the expected query time, the number of accepting leaves reached, summed over all prover messages, is exponential only in the sender and prover bit counts; reaching them costs the tree height plus the querier's per-leaf simulation time, giving the exponential traversal term times the sum of the four costs and the querier time. Enumerating stored points is split into three contributions: the genuine matches cost proportionally to their number; under the distinguished advice, the expected number of erroneously stored non-matching points is bounded, by the false-positive guarantee and the uniform distribution, by a constant times the false-positive parameter times the dataset size; and for each of the exponentially many non-distinguished prover messages, the soundness guarantee bounds the private-coin acceptance probability of each point, so in expectation these contribute the exponential-in-prover-cost factor times the soundness parameter times the dataset size. Averaging over the preprocessing seed by linearity of expectation, and adding a fixed initialization-and-halting cost, yields exactly the claimed expected-query bound. Together with exact reporting and the space and preprocessing estimates, this produces a data structure meeting all the stated guarantees.
nl_theorem: There exists one record of positive natural-number constants (six values, each strictly positive) such that the following holds for all types X and Y, every function f : X → Y → Bool, every specialized product-distributional protocol on X and Y, all natural numbers c_a, c_b, c_c, c_m, t_a, t_b, t_c, and all real numbers ε and δ. If the protocol has (c_a, c_b, c_c, c_m)-cost and (t_a, t_b, t_c)-time along every execution, has false-positive error at most ε under its distinguished advice (with ε ≥ 0), has only type-I error under that advice (every input in the distribution's support with f(x,y)=1 is accepted for all Carol coins), and has soundness at most δ (with δ ≥ 0, every non-distinguished advice accepts with private-coin probability at most δ on the support), then there exists a randomized reporting data structure over the atomic reporting cells that satisfies all reduction guarantees for these same constants: it reports exactly the matching dataset elements; every preprocessing execution uses resident space at most 2^(K_s·(c_a+c_b+c_m))·(|D|+c_c); every preprocessing execution costs at most 2^(K_p·(c_a+c_b+c_m))·|D|·(t_a+t_b+t_c)+2 primitive instructions; and for every dataset and query the expected certified query cost is at most 2^(K_q·(c_a+c_m))·(c_a+c_b+c_m+c_c+t_b) + K_ε·ε·|D| + 2^(K_δ·c_m)·δ·|D| + K_o·n_y + 2, where n_y is the number of matches.

core_claim: Every randomized dynamic filter with one-sided error, bounded capacity, a vanishing false-positive rate, a sufficiently large universe, and superlinear update support must use nearly optimally many bits of internal state.

metainfo.paper: Fingerprint Filters are Optimal

nl_proof:
The argument establishes the space lower bound by a one-way communication reduction: a filter using few bits would let a sender transmit a random sequence of keys to a receiver too cheaply. It is built in three stages, each removing an assumption, and all keeping the same skeleton.

Warmup stage (assuming the filter is history independent and monotone). The sender wants to convey a uniformly random sequence of n distinct keys. By an entropy argument the message must carry at least the logarithm of the falling factorial of the universe size to order n, which is essentially n·log|U| bits. To send them cheaply, the sender first transmits one filter F holding all n keys (costing the space bound in bits) while the receiver keeps an empty filter G. The keys are then sent one by one: for each key the sender first transmits a heavily biased indicator bit for whether it lies in the accepted set of G (entropy at most the binary entropy of ε), and then names the key inside the set of accepted-by-F-but-not-by-G elements, which typically costs about log(ε|U|) bits. After each key, the receiver either inserts it into G or deletes it from F, shrinking the effective universe of remaining keys. The protocol sends the smallest keys for a while, then switches to sending the largest keys; the switch index s is a parameter depending only on the filter. Introducing normalized increments a_k of the expected accepted-set sizes (nonnegative and summing to at most one by monotonicity and the one-sided error guarantee), the per-key cost is bounded, via concavity of the logarithm and a conditional-expectation inequality, in terms of partial sums of the a_k. Comparing total cost against the entropy lower bound shows the space bound is at least n·log ε⁻¹ minus a sum of logarithms of these partial sums, plus o(n). The key technical lemma shows that some choice of s makes that sum at most −n·log e + o(n); it is proved by induction on n, reducing to a normalized suffix, and applying Karamata's majorization inequality to the concave increasing function log(1−2^{−x}), together with Stirling's approximation to identify the bound with log(n!/n^n). This yields the space bound of at least n·log ε⁻¹ + n·log e − o(n), and the protocol uses only O(n) updates.

Removing history independence (still assuming a generalized monotonicity for self-contained operation suffixes). Now the two filters F_k and G_k reached with the same key set are distinct states, so their accepted-set sizes need not agree, which would break the cost analysis. To fix this, the keys are split into b batches (b superconstant, growing slowly) drawn from a random partition of the universe into equal pieces, and the operation history is replaced by an obfuscation sequence generated by a random depth-b obfuscating tree: each node has a uniformly random number of children in a range up to M, edges are labeled by key sequences (the rightmost path labeled by the actual batches), and a depth-first traversal inserts on descent and deletes on ascent. The filters F_k and G_k are prefixes of this traversal, so that G's prefix stays a prefix of F's with a self-contained difference, preserving monotonicity. Two claims control the cost: one shows the partition piece U_k can be treated as essentially independent of the accepted-set difference (bounding the intersection using that the tree has few edges), and a coupling claim shows the obfuscation makes the expected accepted-set size of F_k within an additive (1−ε)n+ε|U| over M of that of G_k, because conditioning on the number of children of the rightmost node shifts one distribution into the other. Choosing M and b with M = 4^b and 9^{b^2} = o(ε|U|/n) makes the error terms negligible; an entropy bound identical in form to the warmup follows, and the same choice-of-s lemma (with a supporting lemma showing the extra additive 2/4^b inside each logarithm does not change the −b·log e + o(b) bound) delivers the same conclusion. The obfuscation sequence has at most n·M^{b+1}/b operations, which is ω(n) but can be kept below any prescribed superlinear budget by taking b to grow slowly enough.

Removing monotonicity. For a general filter the accepted set need not be monotone, so the accepted set is replaced everywhere by a reconstructible set: a key belongs to it if some operation sequence conforming to the partition reaches a filter with the same memory representation and the same key-set size in whose true key set the key lies. It is shown that the true key set is contained in the reconstructible set, the reconstructible set is contained in the accepted set (so the one-sided error rate ε is preserved and it contains all stored keys), and the reconstructible set is monotone along the relevant prefixes, because concatenating a reconstruction sequence with a self-contained difference that inserts keys from later partition pieces stays self-contained and conforming. With these properties the entire history-dependent argument goes through verbatim with reconstructible sets in place of accepted sets, completing the proof that every such dynamic filter must use at least n·log ε⁻¹ + n·log e − o(n) bits of space.
nl_theorem: Let the universes be a family of finite types indexed by the natural numbers, and let ε be a false-positive rate sequence. Suppose ε is vanishing (eventually strictly between 0 and 1 and little-o of 1), the universe cardinalities grow faster than n over ε (that is, n·ε⁻¹ is little-o of the universe cardinality), and A is a space-accounted randomized dynamic-filter family whose internal state space at each n has at most 2 to the power of its advertised space bound in bits. Suppose further that A implements a dynamic filter with capacity n and false-positive error rate ε, meaning that after every legal update sequence of length at most its update budget every stored key gets a positive answer with probability one and every non-stored key gets a positive answer with probability at most ε(n), and that A supports superlinearly many updates (n is little-o of its update budget). Then A satisfies the space lower bound: there exists a sequence r that is little-o of n such that, eventually, n·log₂(ε(n)⁻¹) + n·log₂(e) − r(n) is at most the advertised space bound of A at n.

core_claim: Some fixed constant works so that on every point count at least one, convex point configurations admit two non-crossing spanning trees whose flip distance exceeds fourteen-ninths of the count minus that constant.

metainfo.paper: Flipping Non-Crossing Spanning Trees

nl_proof:
The published statement asks for an absolute constant C so that for every n at least one there are n points in convex position carrying two non-crossing spanning trees whose flip distance is at least (14/9)n − C. The paper obtains this through a general reduction from flip distance to an auxiliary directed "conflict graph", followed by one explicit small example.

Setup and the conflict graph. Fix two non-crossing trees T, T' on convex points and cut the convex order open into a linear order p_1, …, p_n, drawing edges as arcs over a spine. Each of the n−1 gaps between consecutive points is covered by a unique shortest edge of each tree, which yields a canonical bijection (a pairing) between the edges of T and those of T'. Classify each edge relative to its gap as short, near, or wide, and split the pairs accordingly; the interesting pairs are the near–near ones. The conflict graph H(T,T') has one vertex per near–near gap, with a directed edge from g_i to g_j whenever the presence of the edge at g_i obstructs directly flipping the edge at g_j to its partner — this happens in three explicitly listed geometric situations (a crossing, or one of two covering configurations). Write las(H) for the size of a largest vertex subset inducing an acyclic subgraph.

The key lower-bound tool. The central intermediate result is: whenever H(T,T') is non-empty, there is a constant c depending only on T and T' such that for all m ≥ 1 the diameter of the flip graph on m convex points is at least (2 − las(H)/|V(H)|)·m − c. The paper proves this by "blowing up" the fixed example. For a parameter k, in each near–near gap one inserts k new points and attaches them as a fan of k pendant edges to the appropriate endpoint, in T using the edge e and in T' using its partner e'. The blown-up trees have m_k = n + k·|P_N| points. The crucial geometric fact is that a directed edge g_i → g_j of H forces every fan edge at e_i to cross every fan edge at e'_j in the blow-up. Now consider any flip sequence between the two blown-up trees. For each near–near pair one records the moment its fan is fully removed and calls the pair direct or indirect according to whether the target fan has already appeared by then. Using the forced crossings, the direct pairs are shown to admit a consistent ordering, so their number δ never exceeds las(H). Each indirect pair, by contrast, is shown to force the appearance of almost k intermediate edges belonging to neither tree (via a connected subgraph containing that pair's inserted points and having only a bounded number of components), and these costs for distinct indirect pairs cannot be shared. Counting, every flip sequence has length at least (k − 2n)(δ̄ + |P_N|), where δ̄ = |P_N| − δ is the number of indirect pairs. Dividing by m_k and using δ ≤ las(H) and |V(H)| = |P_N| gives the claimed bound (2 − las(H)/|V(H)|)·m_k − c for the special sizes m_k. A monotonicity lemma — adding one point together with a common boundary edge cannot decrease the flip-graph diameter, since a common boundary edge stays fixed in some shortest flip sequence and can be contracted — extends the bound from the discrete sizes m_k to all m.

The explicit example. It remains to exhibit one pair with a small acyclic ratio. The paper displays two trees on 13 linearly ordered points whose conflict graph is a single 9-cycle in which every edge is bidirected. Hence |V(H)| = 9, and because a largest acyclic subset of a 9-cycle can contain at most every other vertex, las(H) ≤ ⌊9/2⌋ = 4. Therefore 2 − las(H)/|V(H)| ≥ 2 − 4/9 = 14/9.

Conclusion. Feeding this example into the key tool produces a constant C such that the flip-graph diameter on n convex points is at least (14/9)n − C for every n ≥ 1. Since the diameter is the maximum flip distance over all tree pairs, this simultaneously provides, for each such n, an explicit convex point configuration and two non-crossing spanning trees on it whose flip distance meets the required (14/9)n − C, which is exactly the asserted lower bound.
nl_theorem: There exists a real constant C such that for every natural number n with 1 ≤ n there is an indexed family of n points p(0), …, p(n−1) in the plane that is in convex position (convex independent) together with two non-crossing spanning trees T and T' on those points for which the flip distance between T and T' — the shortest-path distance in the flip graph whose vertices are the non-crossing spanning trees and whose edges join trees differing by a single edge exchange — is at least (14/9)·n − C.

core_claim: Every Boolean matrix with bounded factorization norm contains a large all-zero or all-one rectangle, with row and column densities controlled by a universal cubic-exponential bound in the norm.

metainfo.paper: Factorization Norms and an Inverse Theorem for MaxCut

nl_proof:
The paper proves the statement with an explicit cubic exponent, so it suffices to exhibit a universal constant C for which the guaranteed density is 2^(-C·γ³). The argument proceeds through several reductions and a core density-decrement engine.

First reduction (to square matrices). Given an m-by-n Boolean matrix M with factorization norm at most γ, one forms the blow-up obtained by repeating every row n times and every column m times. This is an (mn)-by-(mn) Boolean matrix with the same factorization norm, and any large monochromatic square submatrix of the blow-up collapses, after deleting duplicated rows and columns, to a monochromatic rectangle of the required relative densities in M. Hence it is enough to treat square matrices.

Second reduction (to all-zeros submatrices in sparse matrices). It suffices to prove: every n-by-n Boolean matrix whose fraction of ones is at most one half, and whose factorization norm is at most γ, contains an all-zeros square submatrix of side n·2^(-O(γ³)). Indeed, if a Boolean matrix has at most half of its entries equal to one, this statement applies directly; if it has more than half ones, one applies the statement to the complement matrix (all-ones minus M), whose factorization norm exceeds that of M by at most one, producing a large all-ones submatrix of M.

Third ingredient (sparsification). A discrepancy-based lemma shows that if a Boolean matrix has bounded factorization norm and its density of ones is bounded away from one, then it has large discrepancy: the cut norm of the centered matrix is, by Grothendieck's inequality, comparable to the dual factorization norm, and evaluating the dual norm on the rescaled factorization vectors gives a discrepancy lower bound proportional to the number of ones divided by the norm. Combined with a halving lemma that passes to a quarter-sized submatrix of strictly smaller density, iterating drives the density down geometrically. Consequently one can pass to a submatrix of relative size 2^(-O(γ)) in which every row and every column has only a small fraction of one entries.

Core density-decrement lemma. The heart of the proof shows that any nonzero square Boolean matrix with factorization norm at most γ and at most half ones contains a square submatrix, still of relative size 2^(-O(γ)) and with at most half ones, whose factorization norm has dropped to γ − Ω(1/γ). To prove this, one first sparsifies as above and fixes a factorization whose row and column vectors have squared Euclidean norm at most γ. A "brilliant" row (or column) is one whose factor vector has total squared inner product with all other row (resp. column) factor vectors at least the number of ones in that row (resp. column). A Frobenius-norm identity, using that the inner product of the rank-one matrices built from two vectors equals the squared inner product of the vectors, shows that the nonnegativity of a certain squared Frobenius norm forces the existence of a brilliant row or a brilliant column. One then repeatedly projects the row (or column) factor vectors onto the orthogonal complement of a brilliant vector, simultaneously discarding the columns (or rows) where the brilliant vector had a one entry; this keeps the matrix a submatrix while each projection step decreases the total squared Frobenius mass of the factor by at least the number of removed lines divided by γ. When the process stops, a counting argument shows a definite total mass has been removed, so retaining the rows or columns whose factor vectors have small squared norm yields a large submatrix admitting a factorization of cost γ − Ω(1/γ), while sparsity keeps its density at most one half.

Iteration and conclusion. Starting from the original matrix and applying the core lemma repeatedly, the factorization norm decreases by Ω(1/γ) at each step, so after O(γ²) steps it must reach zero, meaning the current submatrix is all zeros. Each step shrinks the side length by a factor 2^(-O(γ)), so after O(γ²) steps the surviving all-zeros square submatrix still has side length n·2^(-O(γ³)). Undoing the two reductions produces, for an arbitrary Boolean matrix with factorization norm at most γ, an all-zeros or all-ones submatrix with both relative side lengths at least 2^(-O(γ³)), which is exactly the claimed universal constant C in the exponent.
nl_theorem: There exists a universal constant C > 0 such that for every natural numbers m and n, every real number gamma, and every m-by-n real matrix M whose entries are all either 0 or 1 and whose gamma-two factorization norm is at most gamma, the matrix M has a monochromatic rectangle at densities 2^(-C*gamma^3) in both directions. Here the gamma-two factorization norm is the infimum, over all natural numbers k and all factorizations M = U V through k-dimensional real space, of the product of the maximum Euclidean norm of a row of U and the maximum Euclidean norm of a column of V; and M has such a monochromatic rectangle when there exist a set I of rows and a set J of columns with all entries of M on I-by-J equal to 0 or all equal to 1, with |I| at least 2^(-C*gamma^3) * m and |J| at least 2^(-C*gamma^3) * n.

core_claim: A near-optimally trained minimum-aggregation graph network reproduces iterated Bellman-Ford shortest-path features on every admissible graph up to a controlled multiplicative error determined by the total reachable training nodes and the optimality gap.

metainfo.paper: Graph neural networks extrapolate out-of-distribution for shortest paths

nl_proof:
The argument proceeds in four stages: constructing a sparse exact implementation of Bellman–Ford, proving a matching sparsity lower bound that pins down the global minimum and forces a rigid parameter structure, collapsing that structure to a scalar recurrence, and finally bounding the error on arbitrary graphs.

Stage 1 (a sparse implementation exists). One first exhibits an explicit choice of weights, with exactly mL + mK + K nonzero entries and all biases zero, that makes the L-layer network compute K Bellman–Ford steps exactly on every admissible graph. The first K layers are message-passing layers whose aggregation map adds the incoming node value and the incident edge weight into a single coordinate; the last L − K layers copy that coordinate forward. Because edge weights and features are nonnegative and no parameter is negative, all ReLU gates act as the identity, so each of the first K layers realizes the min-over-neighbors relaxation and the tail layers preserve it. This network has zero training error, hence regularized loss exactly η(mL + mK + K).

Stage 2 (sparsity is necessary, and the minimum is η(mL + mK + K)). One shows that any network with loss close to this value must have at least mL + mK + K nonzero parameters arranged in a specific pattern, using the distinguished training graphs. On the single-edge graph, if some update map were constant then a vertex-swapping automorphism would force the two endpoint features to coincide, producing a unit label error; avoiding this makes every update map nonconstant, which needs at least one nonzero weight in each of its m layers, i.e. mL parameters. On the special two-branch hop graph, an induction shows that unless a layer's aggregation map depends on both its node component and its edge component, the two symmetric branches keep identical features; distinguishing the two terminal vertices, whose true distances differ by one, therefore requires at least K such edge-dependent message-passing layers, and each contributes at least one nonzero weight per layer plus an extra one in its first layer, totaling mK + K. A single misclassified reachable node contributes at least 1/M to the mean absolute error, and the chosen bounds on ε and η make 1/M exceed η(mL + mK + K) + ε, so a near-optimal network cannot afford any unit error. Combined with the upper bound from Stage 1, this forces exactly mL + mK + K nonzero parameters, exactly K message-passing layers, all biases zero, exactly one nonzero weight per update layer, exactly one per aggregation layer beyond the first, and exactly two sharing a row in each first aggregation layer. It also shows η(mL + mK + K) is the global minimum, so a network within ε of the minimum has loss below η(mL + mK + K + 1).

Stage 3 (reduction to a scalar recurrence). Under this sparsity the nonzero weights must also be nonnegative, since a negative weight would make a ReLU output identically zero and hence make some map constant, contradicting Stage 2. Because every layer transmits information through a single coordinate, the features are effectively one-dimensional.
