core_claim: The minimax regret of any class of joint distributions over length-n sequences is bounded, up to a constant and logarithmic factors, by one plus an optimized sequential square-root entropy tradeoff.

metainfo.paper: On the Minimax Regret of Sequential Probability Assignment via Square-Root Entropy

nl_proof:
The paper bounds the minimax regret, expressed as the logarithm of the Shtarkov sum, by an entropy tradeoff, and the argument proceeds through several coordinated stages.

First, the minimax regret is rewritten in a dual form. Using a minimax (von Neumann) argument and the compactness and convexity/concavity structure of the game, the regret equals the supremum over joint distributions p of the expected value, under y drawn from p, of the pointwise regret that compares the best distribution in the class against p. The optimal inner forecaster is p itself. It therefore suffices to bound this expected pointwise regret uniformly over all p.

Second, the conditional probabilities are truncated. Both p and every distribution in the class are replaced by versions whose one-step conditional probabilities are bounded away from zero and one, living in an interval of width controlled by a scale parameter. Two lemmas show that this truncation changes the regret only by additive terms proportional to n times the alphabet size times the truncation scale (and a logarithmic correction). Choosing the truncation scale of order one over n squared times the alphabet size makes these losses only logarithmic in n and the alphabet size, so the remaining task is to bound the expected pointwise regret for truncated distributions.

Third, an offset Rademacher process is constructed by symmetrization. A specially designed transformation is introduced that behaves like twice the square-root deviation for small arguments and like a logarithm for large arguments, and that satisfies three properties: it dominates the logarithm up to a negative quadratic offset over the relevant range; the associated expression induces a nonnegative divergence when averaged over the sampling distribution; and it is Lipschitz with respect to the square-root map, so differences of the transform are controlled by differences of square roots of conditional probabilities. Applying the logarithm-domination property, adding a copy of the nonnegative divergence, and then symmetrizing through a coupling that uses Rademacher signs to select between two independent draws (a selectors argument) yields an upper bound consisting of two offset Rademacher processes, each carrying a negative quadratic penalty scaled by the reciprocal of a logarithmic factor.

Fourth, the offset process is analyzed by chaining. Fixing a geometrically spaced sequence of scales and, at each scale, a smallest sequential square-root cover, the process is decomposed into three parts: an approximation at the finest scale, a telescoping sum of differences between consecutive covers, and a residual on the coarsest cover that retains its quadratic offset. A dedicated lemma shows that one can choose cover representatives so that the quadratic offset is preserved under chaining, by selecting a representative whose squared coefficients are dominated by those of the true distribution or replacing it by p itself. Two finite-class inequalities are the workhorses. An offset inequality bounds an offset sequential Rademacher process by the logarithm of the class size divided by twice the offset weight, regardless of how large the (predictable) coefficients are, proved by a martingale exponential argument. A non-offset inequality, derived from it by optimizing the offset weight, bounds a sequential Rademacher process by the square root of twice the log-cardinality times the expected supremum of the sum of squared coefficients. The essential point is that although the coefficients are unbounded, their squared increments are small in expectation because the sampling distribution appears in the denominator; using the Lipschitz property and the covering guarantee, the expected sum of squared increments at scale alpha is bounded by four times n times the square of that scale times the alphabet size.

Fifth, these ingredients are combined. The finest-scale approximation term is controlled by Cauchy–Schwarz and gives a contribution of order n times the smallest scale times the square root of the alphabet size. Each telescoping increment is a sequential Rademacher process bounded via the non-offset inequality by the scale times the square root of n times the alphabet size times the square-root entropy at that scale. The coarsest residual is an offset process bounded via the offset inequality by a logarithmic factor times the entropy at the coarsest scale.

Finally, choosing the scales dyadically, the telescoping sum is recognized as a Riemann-type sum that is dominated by the integral of the square root of the sequential square-root entropy over the interval between the two scale endpoints, using monotonicity of the entropy in the scale. Setting the finest and coarsest scales to the chosen delta and gamma yields, for every admissible pair delta less than gamma, the bound consisting of the term n times delta times the square root of the alphabet size, the term square root of n times the alphabet size times the entropy integral from delta to gamma, and the entropy at gamma, all multiplied by an absolute constant and a power of the logarithmic factor in n and the alphabet size. Taking the infimum over all pairs with gamma greater than delta greater than zero, and adding the constant plus one to absorb the truncation losses, produces the stated upper bound.
nl_theorem: There exist a real constant C greater than 0 and a natural number exponent k such that, for every natural number n with n at least 7, every finite alphabet Y, and every set Q of joint probability distributions on the length-n sequences over Y, the minimax regret of Q (defined as the logarithm of the Shtarkov sum, itself the sum over all paths of the supremum over Q of the path probability) is at most C times (1 + log n + log of the cardinality of Y) raised to the power k, times (1 plus the optimized entropy tradeoff of Q). Here the optimized entropy tradeoff is the infimum, over all pairs 0 < δ < γ, of the quantity n·δ·√|Y| + √(n·|Y|) times the integral from δ to γ of the square root of the sequential square-root entropy of Q at scale α, plus the sequential square-root entropy of Q at scale γ, where the sequential square-root entropy at scale α is the logarithm of the least size of a family of joint distributions that forms a sequential square-root cover of Q at that scale.

core_claim: A deterministic machine exists that, for all admissible multiset inputs and every positive accuracy, outputs a sparse vector approximating their convolution within the stated additive error, sparsity, and time bounds.

metainfo.paper: New Applications of 3SUM-Counting in Fine-Grained Complexity and Pattern Matching

nl_proof:
The result is established by explicitly constructing the deterministic algorithm and verifying that the vector it produces meets the required accuracy, sparsity, and running-time guarantees; there is no nonconstructive step, so exhibiting the algorithm and its analysis is the whole proof.

The construction proceeds in two layers.

First layer: a weaker auxiliary routine. Here one wants, given multisets A and B and a candidate index set C, a value g(c) for each c in C that always overestimates the true convolution coefficient, while the total overestimation summed over C is at most the smaller of ε times |B| times |C| and |A| times |B| times log N. This is obtained by a fully deterministic hashing scheme in the spirit of the modular sieving used in earlier derandomizations of convolution-style problems. One builds a modulus m as a product of several small primes, chosen greedily. In each greedy step a prime is picked from a fixed interval so that (i) the number of collisions among elements of the still-unresolved part of C is reduced by a controlled factor, and (ii) the number of "pseudo-solutions" — triples that satisfy the sum equation only modulo m — is minimized; both quantities are computable, the latter via fast Fourier transform in time proportional to m. A crude form of the prime number theorem guarantees enough primes exist in the interval, and a Markov-inequality argument (applied to a uniformly random prime) shows a suitable prime always exists; the algorithm derandomizes this by testing all candidate primes and taking the best. Once the modulus isolates a constant fraction of the still-unresolved indices, those isolated indices are assigned the count of solutions modulo m obtained by fast Fourier transform, and are removed; because at least half of the remaining indices become isolated each round, the process terminates in at most log N rounds. Overestimation holds because every genuine solution is also a solution modulo m, and the total excess is exactly the number of pseudo-solutions, which the greedy choice keeps below the target. Choosing the branching parameter as two to the power of the square root of log N makes the modulus, and hence the running time, subpolynomial in N.

Second layer: the main algorithm, built recursively to also control the maximum coordinate error and the sparsity. In the base case, when N is below a fixed constant, the problem is solved trivially. In the recursive case one picks a parameter r, sets a reduced universe size N' equal to N over r, forms the folded multisets A' and B' obtained by reducing all elements modulo N', and recursively computes a vector f' approximating the convolution of A' and B' with a tightened error parameter (a constant fraction of ε). The reduced instances keep the same cardinalities, so the recursion does not enlarge A or B. To lift the folded approximation back to the full universe, the algorithm forms a candidate set consisting of the support of the folded solution together with all its shifts by multiples of N', applies the auxiliary routine to A, B, and this candidate set with a suitably scaled error parameter to obtain overestimates g, and then for each candidate index passing a consistency test — namely that the folded value agrees with the summed lifted values up to the allowed slack — assigns to each of the corresponding full-universe indices the value g thresholded at half of ε times |B| (values below the threshold are set to zero). Indices failing the test remain for later rounds.

The three guarantees are then verified. Correctness of the maximum-norm bound is proved by induction on the universe size, splitting into the case where an index lies outside the lifted candidate range (where the induction hypothesis forces the true coefficient to be tiny, so the assigned value zero is within tolerance) and the case of a thresholded assignment (where a contradiction is derived from the overestimation property together with the consistency test, using that the auxiliary routine never underestimates). The number of outer rounds is again bounded by log N: calling an index "bad" when its lifted overestimate exceeds the truth by too much, the total-error guarantee of the auxiliary routine caps the number of bad indices at half, and every good index passes the consistency test and is removed. The sparsity bound follows because in each round the total mass added is at most order |A| times |B| times log N (again from the auxiliary routine), so across the log N rounds the total assigned mass is order |A| times |B| times log squared N; since every nonzero entry is at least half of ε times |B| due to the thresholding, the number of nonzero entries is order ε to the minus one times |A| times log squared N. Finally, the running time satisfies a recurrence in which each level costs, up to subpolynomial and logarithmic factors, order (r times ε to the minus one times |A| plus |B|) times a subpolynomial factor in N — using that the candidate set has size controlled by the sparsity bound — plus the cost of the single recursive call on universe N over r. Setting r equal to two to the power of the square root of log N solves this recurrence to the claimed bound of (ε to the minus one times |A| plus |B|) times a subpolynomial factor in N, and all constants and the subpolynomial overhead are uniform in the instance.
nl_theorem: There exists a deterministic popular-sums algorithm (a Post–Turing machine with binary tape alphabet and a finite nonempty state set) satisfying the following specification. There are a subpolynomial overhead function g and positive real constants C_time and C_sparsity such that for every natural number N > 0, all multisets A, B ⊆ {0,…,N−1} whose cardinalities counted with multiplicity are at most N, and every real ε > 0, there exist a finitely supported vector f : ℕ →₀ ℕ, a halting configuration c, and a step bound t with: the machine, started on the canonical little-endian binary encoding of (N, A, B, max(1, ⌈ε⁻¹⌉)), reaches c within t steps and c has no successor transition; the tape of c encodes f as a sparse list of support pairs; the step bound satisfies t ≤ C_time · (ε⁻¹·|A| + |B|) · g(N); the support cardinality satisfies |support f| ≤ C_sparsity · ε⁻¹ · |A| · (log(N+2))²; and for every k ∈ ℕ, the distance between f(k) and the convolution coefficient (1_A ∗ 1_B)(k) = Σ_{i≤k} mult_A(i)·mult_B(k−i) is at most ε·|B|.

core_claim: A universal positive constant makes the worst-oracle minimax error for smooth quasar-convex objectives with quadratic growth at least the stated variance over curvature, quasar-parameter squared, log factor, and query count.

metainfo.paper: New Lower Bounds for Non-Convex Stochastic Optimization through Divergence Decomposition

nl_proof:
The paper proves the bound by reducing minimization to a function-identification problem and applying a divergence-decomposition argument. Fix the parameters and set the effective dimension to the smallest integer at least twice the base-5/4 logarithm of 2/τ. All constructed objectives depend only on the first that-many coordinates; a lifting lemma shows that L-smoothness, τ-quasar-convexity and μ-quadratic growth of a function on the reduced space are inherited by its extension to the full space, whose minimizer set is the convex slab over the reduced minimizer.

Step one is the hard family. A parameter a is chosen as the positive root of a quadratic so that 1−a ≤ τ; this is the largest value keeping the pieces both quasar-convex and quadratic-growth. One picks m distinct centers inside a ball of radius 5Δ and, for each, builds an objective vanishing at that center whose gradient is radial and piecewise defined: it equals 169μ times the displacement near the center (strong local curvature), then bends over a transition annulus, becomes a constant-magnitude radial field of size 169μ(1−a)Δ farther out, and finally grows again outside a large ball. An explicit case analysis verifies each objective is μ-quadratic-growth, τ-quasar-convex, and, because the relevant Lipschitz constant of the gradient never exceeds 202μ ≤ L, also L-smooth; hence each lifted objective lies in the admissible class and has the corresponding center as unique minimizer.

Step two fixes the oracle: the response is the true gradient plus an independent Gaussian vector on the active coordinates with zero mean and covariance (σ²/d₀) times the identity, whose total variance is σ², so it belongs to the allowed oracle family.

Step three reduces to identification against a reference objective G whose gradient is zero inside a large ball and matches the common outer field beyond it. For each center define the "good event" that the algorithm's output lands in the ball of radius 2Δ about that center. Since inside such a ball an objective is at least (169/2)μΔ² away from its minimum whenever the output misses it, the expected suboptimality under objective i is at least (1−probability of good event) times (169/2)μΔ².

Step four bounds identification error. The centers are chosen so that the m balls of radius 2Δ are disjoint, which forces the query counts across balls to sum to at most T and the reference-measure good-event probabilities to sum to at most one; a packing-number estimate lets m be of order (5/4) raised to the effective dimension, hence at least 2/τ². Averaging Pinsker's inequality over the family bounds the average good-event probability by 1/m plus the square root of the averaged relative entropy. The relative entropy between the reference experiment and objective i is controlled by the divergence-decomposition (chain-rule) lemma: because the feedback is Gaussian with fixed covariance, each round contributes (d₀/2σ²) times the squared gradient gap, split into rounds spent inside the center's ball, where the gap is at most 169μΔ, and rounds spent outside, where it is at most 169μτΔ. This yields an averaged relative entropy of order (169²d₀μ²Δ²/σ²)(τ² + 1/m)T. Choosing the effective dimension of order log(2/τ) makes the 1/m term negligible against τ², which is precisely why the dimension threshold is needed.

Step five combines these estimates: the averaged expected suboptimality is at least (169/2)μΔ² times (1/2 minus a multiple of Δ times the square root of μ²τ²log(2/τ)T/σ²). Optimizing over Δ balances the two effects and produces a lower bound of order σ²/(μτ²log(2/τ)T) on the average expected error over the family. Since the maximum over the admissible class dominates this average and the chosen oracle is one admissible oracle, the infimum over algorithms and supremum over oracles inherit the same lower bound, giving the claimed universal constant c > 0.
nl_theorem: There exists a numerical constant c > 0, independent of every problem parameter, such that for all real numbers μ, L, τ, σ and all natural numbers d, T satisfying μ > 0, L > 0, 0 < τ ≤ 1, T > 0, d ≥ 3·log_{5/4}(2/τ), and L/μ ≥ 202, the worst-oracle minimax optimization error after T queries — the supremum over all first-order stochastic oracles of variance at most σ² of the infimum over measurable adaptive first-order algorithms of the supremum over differentiable L-smooth, τ-quasar-convex objectives on ℝ^d obeying μ-quadratic growth of the expected suboptimality of the algorithm's output — is at least ofReal(c·σ²/(μ·τ²·log(2/τ)·T)), the inequality being taken in the extended nonnegative reals.

core_claim: For correlated sparse random graphs, the optimally coupled overlap of uniform shortest-path trees converges in probability to an explicit piecewise limit determined by the three parameter limits.

metainfo.paper: Overlap Analysis of the Shortest Path Problem: Local Search, Landscapes, and Franz-Parisi Potential

nl_proof:
The argument first reduces the random tree overlap to a vertex average of local parent overlaps. Under the optimal coupling of the two uniform shortest-path-tree measures, the conditional expectation of the overlap equals the normalized sum, over reachable non-root vertices, of the ratio of the size of the common parent set to the larger of the two parent-set sizes. So it suffices to show this deterministic-given-the-graphs quantity concentrates at the stated limit.

Step 1 (localization to two depths). One introduces, for each depth d and vertex v, a variable that equals the local parent overlap when v lies in both graphs at distance d and is joined to the common depth-(d−1) frontier, and is zero otherwise. Two observations are established. First, conditioned on the explored frontiers through depth d−1, these variables over the fresh vertices are independent and identically distributed, because whether such a variable is nonzero and its value depend only on the edges from v to the depth-(d−1) frontiers. Second, the full overlap differs negligibly from the sum restricted to the critical depth d* and the next depth d*+1: single-graph distance concentration shows all other depth classes have vanishing vertex proportion, and a separate estimate shows the vertices whose two distances disagree (one at d*, one at d*+1) contribute negligibly, since such vertices typically have many parents at the deeper layer but only boundedly many at the shallower one, forcing their local ratio to zero.

Step 2 (exact parent law). Conditioned on the frontiers, the joint law of the two parent counts and their common part is obtained from an inclusion–exclusion decomposition of the neighborhoods of a fresh vertex: independent binomial contributions from the parts of each depth-(d−1) frontier outside the intersection, plus a multinomial contribution from the common frontier that splits edges into those present in both graphs, only the first, or only the second. Writing the counts this way, the local overlap becomes the common count divided by the maximum of the two total parent counts, restricted to the event that the common count is positive.

Step 3 (concentration to conditional means). Let the conditional expectation of this local overlap at depth d be denoted a proxy random variable. Because each local overlap lies in the unit interval, its conditional variance across the identically distributed fresh vertices is at most one quarter divided by the number of fresh vertices, so Chebyshev's inequality shows the empirical average concentrates at its conditional mean. Combining the critical and next-depth contributions with the frontier proportions (the proportion of vertices past depth d*−1 tends to one, and the proportion past d* tends to the intersection proportion of the postcritical layer), the overlap is shown to differ negligibly from the critical-depth proxy plus the postcritical proxy weighted by that layer proportion.

Step 4 (evaluating the limits). One then computes the limits of the two proxies using the single-graph and correlated frontier asymptotics. When lambda equals one, the common count at depth d* is positive with vanishing probability, so only the postcritical term survives; parent-count concentration and Poisson limits, together with the fact that a positive correlation limit forces the resampling parameter to one, yield the value gamma (and zero when gamma vanishes, giving gamma again). The case lambda equals zero is symmetric with the roles of the two depths exchanged, again giving gamma. When lambda lies strictly between zero and one, the shallower parent counts converge to independent Poisson variables of rate (1−gamma)·log(1/lambda), the common count converges to a Poisson variable of rate gamma·log(1/lambda), the graph-specific extra parents vanish because the correlation tends to one, and the event that the common count is positive has limiting probability 1−lambda^gamma; this makes the critical proxy converge to the conditional Poisson overlap function evaluated at those rates times (1−lambda^gamma). For the postcritical proxy, the frontier proportions give total parent mass proportional to (1−lambda) and common mass proportional to the intersection proportion 1−2·lambda+lambda^{2−gamma}, while the common-edge probability divided by the edge probability tends to the correlation limit, so the proxy converges to ((1−2·lambda+lambda^{2−gamma})/(1−lambda))·rho, which after multiplication by the postcritical layer proportion lambda^{2−gamma} yields the first summand of the interior formula. Adding the two contributions produces the interior limit, and the three cases together give the piecewise limit claimed.
nl_theorem: Consider a correlated sparse Erdős–Rényi shortest-path-tree model on a probability space, in which for every n two graphs on n+1 vertices are drawn from the correlated Erdős–Rényi edge law with edge probability q_n = α_n·log(n+1)/(n+1), where α_n is eventually bounded above and away from zero, together with the associated critical depth d_n* and proxy sequences λ_n (defined through log(1/λ_n) = ((n+1)q_n)^{d_n*}/(n+1)) and γ_n = ρ_n^{d_n*}, ρ_n being the correlation. Suppose λ_n → λ, γ_n → γ, and ρ_n → ρ with λ, γ ∈ [0,1]. Then the model's random optimal shortest-path-tree overlap, the vertex-averaged optimally coupled parent overlap rooted at vertex 0, converges in probability to the piecewise limit L(λ,γ,ρ): for 0 < λ < 1 it equals ((1 − 2λ + λ^{2−γ})/(1 − λ))·λ^{2−γ}·ρ + g((1−γ)log(1/λ), γ·log(1/λ))·(1 − λ^{γ}), where g(a,b) is the conditional Poisson overlap function; and for λ ∈ {0,1} it equals γ.

core_claim: Under combined global and strong local corruption, a stability-based mean estimator run with an inflated stability parameter achieves, with high probability, error proportional to the stability level plus corruption radius.

metainfo.paper: Optimal Robust Estimation under Local and Global Corruptions: Stronger Adversary and Smaller Error

nl_proof:
The argument reduces the combined corruption model to a plain global corruption of a stable set, so that the black-box guarantee of any stability-based algorithm applies. Fix the sufficiently small constant governing the outlier rate and the sufficiently large multiplier used to set the stability parameter. Write the corrupted data as the result of first applying strong local perturbations to the stable inliers and then inserting an epsilon-fraction of global outliers; denote by Δ_i the local displacement of each inlier point.

The heart of the proof is to show that even though local perturbations can blow up the covariance of the whole set, a large subset of the perturbed inliers remains stable, with the stability parameter degrading only by an additive term of order the local radius. This rests on three ingredients.

First, a deterministic existence result: for vectors whose average length is controlled in every direction (that is, whose first directional moment is at most the local radius), there is a subset containing all but an epsilon-fraction of the indices on which the average squared length in every direction is at most of order (radius squared)/epsilon. The paper obtains this by relaxing the discrete choice of subset to a fractional weighting over a capped simplex, rewriting the objective through the convex hull of rank-one (more generally rank-k) projections, and invoking min-max duality for the resulting bilinear program over convex compact sets. Duality swaps the order of the minimization over weights and the maximization over directions, which permits a direction-dependent truncation: for each fixed direction, discarding the epsilon-fraction of points with the largest projected length and applying Markov's inequality bounds the truncated second moment. A rounding step then converts the fractional solution back into an honest large subset.

Second, to make the truncation argument valid for the relaxed (convex-hull) directions and not only for genuine projections, the paper proves via a Gaussian rounding scheme that the average Mahalanobis length over the relaxed matrices is bounded by a constant times the average projected length over genuine projections. Sampling Gaussian vectors with the given covariance, forming an empirical second-moment matrix, and using fourth-moment control of quadratic Gaussian forms together with concentration of the sampled covariance yields this comparison. Consequently the selected subset of displacements has both bounded average length and bounded average squared length in every relaxed direction.

Third, a stability-preservation lemma shows that adding displacements with these two bounded-moment properties to a stable set produces a stable set with parameter increased only by an additive amount of order the local radius. Its proof verifies the mean condition, an upper bound on the covariance, and a matching lower bound over all large subsets, each by expanding the perturbed second moment into the original moment, the displacement moment, and a cross term; the cross term is handled by splitting indices according to whether the inlier is far in the relevant direction and applying Cauchy-Schwarz together with the stability of the original points.

Combining these, apply the existence result and the Gaussian-rounding comparison in the rank-one case to the displacements, restricted to a large subset of the inliers, which is itself stable as a large subset of a stable set. The stability-preservation lemma then certifies that the locally perturbed subset is stable with parameter of order the sum of the original stability parameter and the local radius. Finally, the global outliers only shrink the overlap slightly, so the fully corrupted data is an epsilon-order global corruption of this stable set (using that large subsets of stable sets remain stable up to constant factors). Feeding this into the black-box guarantee of the stability-based algorithm, run with the inflated stability parameter equal to the multiplier times the sum of the original parameter and the radius, yields an estimate whose distance to the true mean is at most the accuracy constant times that inflated parameter, hence of order the stability parameter plus the local radius with high probability.
nl_theorem: There exist absolute constants c₀, C₀ > 0 with the following property. Fix natural numbers n and d, a randomness type Ω, an event functional highProbability sending predicates on Ω to propositions, a proposition asserting polynomial-time execution, a stability estimator A, and a real accuracy constant K. Fix indexed datasets S₀ and T of cardinality n in the Euclidean space ℝ^d, a point μ in ℝ^d, and real numbers c, C, ε, δ, ρ. Assume: A is stability-based relative to highProbability, the polynomial-time proposition, and accuracy constant K; 0 < c and c ≤ c₀; C₀ ≤ C; 0 < ε and ε < c; 0 < ρ; ε < δ; S₀ is (ε, δ)-stable with respect to μ; and T is obtained from S₀ by a combined (ε, ρ)-corruption. Then highProbability holds of the event that, running the estimator on T with contamination rate ε and stability parameter C·(δ + ρ), the output satisfies ‖A T ε (C·(δ + ρ)) ω − μ‖ ≤ K·(C·(δ + ρ)).

core_claim: A universal positive constant exists making gradient descent on the residual optimum a scalable algorithm for weighted integral flow time whenever the integral residual optimum is discrete-supermodular.

metainfo.paper: Online Scheduling via Gradient Descent for Weighted Flow Time Minimization

nl_proof:
The argument is a potential-function analysis that compares the gradient-descent schedule to an arbitrary offline optimum running at unit speed, with the algorithm granted speed one plus epsilon. Fix the instance. Write A for the gradient-descent schedule and O for the fixed optimum, and treat each arriving job as producing two independent copies, one belonging to A and one to O, so the two alive-job sets are always disjoint. Let the remaining-size vectors of the alive jobs under A and O be denoted by their concatenation. The proof studies the potential defined as two over epsilon times the residual optimum on A's remaining sizes minus one half of the residual optimum on the concatenation of A's and O's remaining sizes.

The analysis rests on three ingredients. First, one shows that following an optimal residual schedule decreases the residual optimum at a rate exactly equal to the total weight of the currently alive jobs. The reason is that the optimal residual schedule, restricted to what remains after an infinitesimal step, is still optimal for the reduced sizes; since every alive job's projected completion time in the shifted schedule drops by exactly the elapsed time, the minimum weighted completion objective falls at a rate equal to the sum of the weights of the jobs with positive remaining size. Comparing the shifted schedule against the true optimum in both directions pins this rate down to an equality. A companion observation is that running speed s scales this decrease rate by s, and that gradient descent can be realized by simply following the optimal residual schedule until a new job arrives. Because gradient descent by definition achieves the largest possible decrease of the residual optimum, this rate is also the maximum any schedule can attain.

Second, the discrete changes of the potential caused by arrivals and completions are shown to be nonpositive. Completions have no effect, because a job of zero remaining size does not enter the residual problem. For an arrival, the increase of the second (concatenated) residual term is bounded below using discrete supermodularity of the residual optimum viewed as a set function of the jobs with their sizes fixed: adding both the A-copy and the O-copy, each of the same freshly arrived size, raises the concatenated residual optimum by at least twice the amount by which adding the single A-copy raises the residual optimum on A alone. This is obtained from the supermodular inequality applied to the sets of A-jobs, O-jobs, and the two new copies, using that the two copies have equal size at arrival. With the coefficient one half in front of the concatenated term, the two contributions cancel and the potential does not increase.

Third, between events the continuous change is controlled. The decrease of the first term is exactly speed times the total weight of A's alive jobs. For the concatenated term, viewing A's processing at speed one plus epsilon together with O's processing at speed one as a single feasible schedule of speed two plus epsilon, the maximal-decrease property bounds its rate of decrease by two plus epsilon times the combined total weight of the alive jobs in A and O. Combining these with speed one plus epsilon yields that the time derivative of the potential is at most minus the total weight of A's alive jobs plus a factor of order one over epsilon times the total weight of O's alive jobs.

Finally, since the potential is zero before any arrival and zero after all completions, and it never increases at events, the integral of its time derivative is nonnegative. Integrating the continuous bound therefore gives that the time integral of the total alive weight under A is at most a factor of order one over epsilon times the corresponding integral for O. These two integrals are precisely the total weighted integral flow times of the gradient-descent schedule and of the optimum. Hence gradient descent is one-plus-epsilon-speed and order one over epsilon-competitive, with the competitive constant absolute and independent of the job set, its size, the polytope, and the implementation.
nl_theorem: There is a universal constant C greater than zero such that the following holds. For every finite job type, every polytope scheduling problem P on it (a compact convex downward-closed set of nonnegative feasible rate vectors containing the zero vector), and every gradient-descent algorithm for P (an online, causal scheduling algorithm whose normalized current rate lies in the active feasible-rate set of the remaining-size vector and, among all such active feasible directions, minimizes the processing-direction right derivative of the integral residual optimum), if for every strictly positive job-weight vector w the integral residual optimum f_w is discrete-supermodular, then for every ε greater than zero the algorithm is (1+ε)-speed (C/ε)-competitive for total weighted integral flow time; that is, at speed 1+ε its weighted integral flow time on any instance is at most (C/ε) times the unit-speed offline optimum. Here the residual optimum f_w(x) is the infimum over residual schedules for remaining-size vector x of the sum of w_j times each first-completion time, and discrete supermodularity means that for every nonnegative x the set function sending Z to f_w restricted by the indicator of Z is supermodular.

core_claim: Thompson sampling with growing variance inflation splits pulls uniformly among optimal arms, gives sharp logarithmic suboptimal pull counts, and is stable relative to the stated deterministic centering sequences.

metainfo.paper: Optimism Stabilizes Thompson Sampling for Adaptive Inference

nl_proof:
The result is established through a long, detailed argument that first fixes two high-probability events and then treats the optimal and suboptimal arms separately.

Two controlling events. The first event is a time-uniform concentration statement: with probability tending to one, every arm's empirical mean stays within a slowly growing multiple of its own inverse pull count of the true mean, simultaneously over all rounds and all arms. This is obtained from a time-uniform sub-Gaussian maximal bound for the running sums of the noise, applied arm by arm with a union bound. The second event says the total number of suboptimal pulls is small. It follows from a preliminary bound on the expected number of pulls of any fixed suboptimal arm, which shows this expectation grows like the inflation factor times a logarithmic term; Markov's inequality then makes the total suboptimal count of that order with high probability. This expected-pull bound is itself proved by decomposing each suboptimal selection into three regimes — empirical mean atypically high, index atypically high given a typical mean, and a comparison regime — and bounding each by sub-Gaussian tail estimates, a Gaussian index tail with rate governed by the squared gap over the inflation factor, and a Mills-ratio comparison against a fixed optimal arm.

Uniform allocation among optimal arms. The goal here is that each optimal arm's pull count divided by the horizon converges in probability to one over the number of optimal arms. Because the suboptimal pulls are asymptotically negligible, the optimal arms together occupy essentially the whole horizon, so it suffices to balance the optimal arms among themselves. The balancing is first understood in a simplified world where all arms share a common mean. There the next arm chosen is essentially the maximizer of a standard Gaussian divided by the square root of its current proportion, which defines a pure-noise winner map on the simplex. Two structural facts about this map drive everything: a monotonicity property showing that an arm sampled more often wins less often, proved by differentiating the winning probability in each scale and using symmetrization of the Gaussian integrand; and a dot-product inequality showing that the proportion-weighted winning probabilities sum to at most the uniform value, with strict deficit away from the uniform point, obtained from a reversed Chebyshev (rearrangement) inequality applied to the oppositely ordered proportions and winning probabilities. This is the negative-feedback mechanism: over-sampled arms are penalized and under-sampled arms rewarded.

To turn this geometric tendency into convergence, the argument controls the empirical-mean perturbations that separate the real algorithm from the idealized winner map. A uniform exponential-tightness estimate shows the standardized empirical means have uniformly bounded exponential moments; it is proved by coupling two Lyapunov estimates — a weighted exponential-moment recursion for the proportion times an exponential of the squared standardized mean, and an inverse-proportion recursion resting on an anti-starvation lower bound for the one-step selection probability — and closing them through Hölder's inequality. A weighted perturbation bound then shows that replacing the true selection probabilities by the pure-noise winner probabilities costs at most a constant over the square root of the inflation factor times the summed standardized fluctuations. Feeding the negative-feedback inequality and this perturbation bound into a quadratic Lyapunov function measuring squared distance of the proportion vector from uniform yields a drift recursion; solving it gives an expected Lyapunov value of order one over the horizon plus one over the square root of the inflation factor, which vanishes because the inflation factor diverges, forcing the proportions to the uniform point.

The full bandit is handled by adapting this scheme to the within-optimal proportions. Suboptimal arms need not have controlled inverse proportions, so only their positive standardized overshoot above the optimal mean is controlled, via exponential tail bounds; combined with the weighted exponential-moment recursion this yields exponential tightness for the optimal arms' standardized means. The winner map and negative-feedback inequality are then applied restricted to the optimal set, the extra probability of leaking to a suboptimal arm is absorbed as a small error, and a Lyapunov drift for the within-optimal balance is run in calendar time. A stopping-time localization ensures the optimal count stays proportional to the elapsed time, and summing the drift shows the within-optimal balance converges to uniform. Multiplying by the optimal share of the horizon, which tends to one, gives the claimed limit for each optimal arm.

Sharp suboptimal asymptotics. For a fixed suboptimal arm the target is that its pull count divided by the inflation factor times the logarithm of the horizon over the inflation factor converges in probability to twice the reciprocal squared gap. First, a lower-tail estimate shows that after a burn-in some optimal arm is well sampled, so the maximum optimal index rarely dips far below the optimal mean. Then one-step selection probabilities for the suboptimal arm are bracketed above and below by expressions of the form a constant times the square root of the inflation-factor-over-count times an exponential whose rate is essentially the squared gap over twice the inflation factor; the upper bound uses that beating the optimal maximum requires an unlikely large index draw, and the lower bound uses independence of the fresh Gaussian draws together with Mills-ratio estimates. Because the index variance of the suboptimal arm stays fixed between its own pulls, the waiting time for its next pull is coupled, on an enlarged space using shared uniforms, between two geometric variables built from these one-step brackets. The time to reach a negligible cutoff count is shown to be a vanishing fraction of the horizon. Summing the geometric waiting times and invoking a logarithmic growth law for such geometric sums pins the count at which the accumulated waiting time first exceeds the horizon: a lower target count is reached with probability tending to one, and an upper target count is not, giving matching lower and upper brackets. Letting the bracket tolerance and the concentration slack shrink squeezes both brackets to twice the reciprocal squared gap. A finite union bound extends the conclusion simultaneously to all suboptimal arms.

Conclusion. Combining the uniform optimal allocation and the sharp suboptimal asymptotics shows the realized pull counts concentrate around the stated deterministic sequences — the horizon split evenly among optimal arms, and the gap-dependent inflated-logarithmic scale for each suboptimal arm — and these deterministic sequences diverge, yielding the stated stability.
nl_theorem: Consider a stochastic bandit with at least two arms whose reward noises are measurable, mutually independent, identically distributed, non-degenerate, centered, and 1-sub-Gaussian, run by Thompson sampling with empirical-mean centers and Gaussian index variance equal to the inflation schedule divided by the current pull count. Assume every arm is pulled once during initialization; that at every round, including initialization, each contemporaneous arm noise is conditionally centered and 1-sub-Gaussian given the pre-round interaction history together with the selected arm; that after initialization the conditional index vector has the prescribed independent Gaussian coordinate laws and is conditionally independent of all contemporaneous and future reward noises; and that the selected arm maximizes the indices. Suppose the inflation schedule always exceeds one, tends to infinity, and its product with the squared logarithm of the horizon divided by the horizon tends to zero. Then every optimal arm's terminal pull count divided by the horizon converges in probability to one over the number of optimal arms; every suboptimal arm's terminal pull count divided by the inflation schedule times the logarithm of the horizon-to-inflation ratio converges in probability to twice the reciprocal squared gap; and the algorithm is stable with respect to the deterministic centering sequences equal to the horizon over the optimal-arm count on optimal arms and twice the inflation schedule times that logarithm over the squared gap on suboptimal arms, meaning each pull-count ratio converges in probability to one and each center diverges.

core_claim: In preferential attachment networks, when the changepoint occurs late enough, the observable final unlabeled graph cannot statistically distinguish the changepoint law from the no-changepoint law asymptotically.

metainfo.paper: A Proof of The Changepoint Detection Threshold Conjecture in Preferential Attachment Models

nl_proof:
The argument bounds the total variation distance between the no-change law and the late-change law by a chain of reductions, each shrinking the problem until a second-moment estimate can be carried out.

Step 1 (interpolation and data processing). Writing the change size as the gap between the final time and the changepoint, one interpolates the changepoint from the final step down to the true changepoint, obtaining a sequence of laws whose consecutive pairs differ by moving the changepoint one step. The triangle inequality bounds the target distance by the sum of these consecutive distances. A data-processing argument (continuing to grow the graph with the post-change parameter cannot increase total variation, since observing a later snapshot is a further processing of an earlier one) shows each consecutive distance is at most the distance between the no-change law and the one-step-before-the-end change law on a smaller network. Hence it suffices to prove that, when the change occurs exactly one step before the last vertex, this distance is smaller in order than the reciprocal of the change size.

Step 2 (revealing early history). Fix an auxiliary scale strictly between the square of the change size and the network size, and set an earlier time by subtracting this scale from the final time. One reveals the entire network history up to that earlier time. By data processing and the convexity of total variation (Jensen's inequality), the distance is bounded by the expected total variation, over realizations of the revealed history, between the two conditional laws of the final snapshot given that history.

Step 3 (second moment). The conditional total variation is controlled by the chi-squared divergence via Cauchy-Schwarz: it is at most half the square root of the variance, under the null conditional law, of the likelihood ratio between the two conditional laws. It therefore suffices to show this variance is of order the reciprocal of the auxiliary scale, which, being larger than the square of the change size, yields the required bound after summing over the interpolation steps.

Step 4 (explicit likelihood ratio). Because only one vertex arrives after the changepoint and the connected components formed by the vertices arriving after the revealed time can appear in any relative arrival order, one derives a closed form for the conditional likelihood ratio. Counting admissible arrival orders within each component (via multinomial coefficients) collapses the average over hidden arrival times into a single weighted sum over the late-arriving vertices, each term being the size of the vertex's component times the probability that the vertex is the last arrival within its component times a bounded attachment-probability ratio comparing the two shift parameters. A bounded prefactor multiplies this normalized sum. Both the last-arrival weight and the attachment ratio are bounded above and below by absolute constants, so the variance is driven by the fluctuation of component sizes.

Step 5 (Efron-Stein with a tailored encoding). To bound the variance of this normalized sum, the conditional law is generated from independent random variables, one triple per post-history attachment, using an encoding that mixes a uniform choice of vertex with a uniform choice among directed edges (adjusted by a shift-dependent integer so the rule reproduces the affine attachment probabilities for any admissible shift). Applying the Efron-Stein inequality bounds the variance by a sum over these variables of the expected squared change caused by resampling one of them. The crucial combinatorial observation, enforced by the structured encoding, is that resampling a single variable only alters the component containing the corresponding arriving vertex; a careful component-containment analysis then shows the resulting change in the statistic is of order the sum of the sizes of the affected components divided by the auxiliary scale.

Step 6 (component sizes via subcritical branching). It remains to prove that the second moment of a component's size is bounded uniformly. A breadth-first exploration of the component is coupled so that its spanning tree is dominated by a branching tree whose offspring law is the independent sum of a binomial and a geometric variable, both with small parameters because the auxiliary scale is small relative to the network size. This branching process is subcritical, and a generating-function fixed-point argument shows its total size has an exponential tail, so the size has a bounded second moment.

Combining the steps, the variance of the likelihood ratio is of order the reciprocal of the auxiliary scale, the conditional total variation is of order the reciprocal of its square root, and summing over the interpolation steps and using that the scale exceeds the square of the change size yields that the total variation between the no-change and late-change snapshot laws tends to zero.
nl_theorem: Fix a preferential-attachment snapshot model over a measurable space of finite multigraph isomorphism classes, with a fixed number m > 0 of edges added by each arriving vertex and fixed distinct attachment shifts δ ≠ δ', both greater than −m. For each network size n and changepoint τ, let Q(n, τ) be the law of the isomorphism class of the final multigraph, generated by the preferential-attachment history weights with shift δ before time τ and δ' after, and with vertex arrival labels unobserved. Let τ : ℕ → ℕ be a changepoint sequence satisfying τ_n ≤ n for every n, and suppose that n − τ_n = o(√n) as n → ∞. Then the total variation distance between the no-changepoint law Q(n, n) and the changepoint law Q(n, τ_n), defined as half the total variation measure of the difference of the associated signed measures evaluated on the whole space, tends to 0 as n → ∞, i.e. it is o(1).

core_claim: Every finite planar metric admits a polynomial-time constructor producing furthest-neighbor coresets whose size is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the inverse accuracy parameter, with universal constants.

metainfo.paper: A Polynomial Coreset for Furthest Neighbor in Planar Metrics

nl_proof:
The argument combines two ingredients: an algorithmic reduction that turns a bound on a purely combinatorial invariant into a coreset construction, and a polynomial bound on that invariant for planar metrics. Throughout, one may assume the accuracy parameter is below one and the point set has more than one element, since otherwise a single point works.

Ingredient one is the reduction from coresets to comatchings. Here a comatching at scale δ is a family of distinct points with associated query points such that each query is at distance more than a threshold R from its own point but within (1−δ)R of every other point; the comatching index is the largest possible size of such a family. Fix the point set P and let Δ be its diameter and set δ equal to a quarter of εΔ. First, query points extremely far from P (farther than Δ/ε from a fixed reference point) are automatically (1−ε)-approximated by any point, so one fixed point takes care of them. The remaining queries are grouped, according to the distance to their furthest point of P, into only O(1/ε) buckets. Within one bucket, associate to each query the set of points of P lying at least (a bucket-dependent multiple of) δ away; this set is the complement of a metric ball, and any point common to the associated set is a valid approximate furthest neighbor. Thus building a coreset for the bucket amounts to solving a hitting-set problem whose ranges are complements of balls, hence a set system of the same bounded VC dimension as the ball system. Applying the classical linear-programming rounding theorem for hitting set in bounded-VC set systems produces, in polynomial time, a hitting set whose size is controlled by the fractional optimum times the VC dimension and a logarithmic factor. The fractional optimum is in turn bounded by the comatching index: from an optimal dual solution one samples queries according to the normalized dual weights, uses the dual feasibility constraints to show that in expectation few sampled queries "threaten" one another, and after discarding one endpoint of each threatening pair one is left with a genuine comatching at scale ε²/4 whose size is a constant fraction of the fractional optimum. Combining these estimates over all O(1/ε) buckets yields, in polynomial time, a furthest-neighbor ε-coreset whose size is polynomial in 1/ε times the VC dimension times the comatching index at scale ε²/4 (with a logarithmic factor).

Ingredient two supplies the two facts that make the reduction effective for planar metrics: the closed-ball set system of a planar metric has VC dimension at most four, and the comatching index of any planar metric is bounded by a fixed polynomial in 1/ε.

The VC-dimension bound is proved by contradiction: if five points were shattered by balls, then choosing for each pair a ball whose trace is exactly that pair and taking shortest paths from its center to the two points, then contracting shared initial segments and resolving intersections, produces five pairwise-disjoint connected branch sets mutually joined by edges, i.e. a five-clique minor, contradicting planarity.

The polynomial comatching bound is the technical heart and proceeds through successive reductions on a plane realization of the comatching. One fixes a consistent family of shortest paths between the relevant point pairs and passes to a clean instance in which terminals have degree one and every edge lies on some path. Setting δ to a small multiple of the threshold R, one shows the diameter is O(R), so rounded distance profiles to a set of paths take only O(1/ε) values, and the VC-dimension-four property bounds the number of distinct profiles polynomially. A separation lemma follows: if three pairs share a rounded distance profile relative to a family of short paths, none of them is separated by those paths, because otherwise a concatenation of shortest paths would have to cross the separating set and yield a contradictory chain of triangle inequalities. Consequently any union of few short paths separates only polynomially many pairs. A charging argument then reduces to a local instance, in which each pair's two terminals can be joined by a link avoiding every other pair's shortest paths. Next, using a spanning tree whose upward paths are each covered by O(log ℓ) of the comatching paths, one obtains a tree decomposition whose bags are unions of three such paths and separates the instance in a balanced recursive fashion; this extracts a large subfamily whose links are pairwise disjoint, a linked noncrossing instance. Finally, a detailed topological case analysis of a linked noncrossing instance—exploiting that crossing shortest paths would violate the comatching distance inequalities—shows that only O(1/ε) pairs can coexist. Tracking the polynomial losses through the three phases gives a polynomial bound on the comatching index.

Putting the pieces together, a planar metric has VC dimension at most four and comatching index polynomial in 1/ε, so the reduction constructs in polynomial time a furthest-neighbor ε-coreset whose size is polynomial in 1/ε. This provides the universal constants and the polynomial-time constructor asserted in the statement.
nl_theorem: There exist natural-number constants C and k with the following property. For every finite type V equipped with a metric space structure whose distance is a planar shortest-path metric (that is, realized by a connected straight-line planar simple graph on V for which each distance equals the minimum, actually attained, of the metric lengths of graph walks between the two points), there exists a function F assigning to each finite point set and each real number a finite subset of V such that: (1) the uncurried function (P, ε) ↦ F(P, ε) is polynomial-time computable; and (2) for every nonempty finite point set P ⊆ V and every real ε with 0 < ε < 1, the set F(P, ε) is contained in P and is a furthest-neighbor ε-coreset for P, meaning that for every v ∈ V some q ∈ F(P, ε) satisfies (1 − ε) · max_{p ∈ P} dist(v, p) ≤ dist(v, q), and moreover the cardinality of F(P, ε) is at most C · ⌈ε⁻¹⌉^k.

core_claim: A universal constant guarantees that, under bounded f-divergence and eventual subquadraticity, enough independent samples yield a measurable estimator achieving multiplicative accuracy of the normalizing constant with high probability.

metainfo.paper: Partition Function Estimation under Bounded $f$-Divergence

nl_proof:
The paper proves the guarantee by reducing the f-divergence bound to a coverage-based analysis of a median-of-means estimator, so the argument proceeds through several intermediate results.

Choice of estimator. The estimator does not depend on the unknown scale: the samples are split into a number of groups proportional to the logarithm of the inverse failure probability, the average of the observed unnormalized ratios is formed within each group, and the estimate is the median of these group averages. A standard median-of-means fact converts a per-group guarantee that holds with a fixed constant probability into a high-probability guarantee: if each group average lands in a target interval with probability at least one half plus a constant, then their median lands there except with probability decaying exponentially in the number of groups. Because the estimator is scale invariant and the accuracy is multiplicative, it suffices to analyze the normalized case where the true constant equals one, i.e. where the group averages are empirical means of the density ratio.

Concentration of a single group average via integrated coverage. The density ratio may be heavy-tailed, so its variance can be infinite; the paper therefore analyzes truncated copies of the ratio purely as an analytic device. Truncating at a level M, the truncated summands are bounded by M, have expectation at least one minus the coverage at M, and, by a tail-integration identity, have second moment at most the integrated coverage at M. Applying Bernstein's inequality to these bounded, controlled-variance summands and splitting into a lower tail and an upper tail (the discarded tail mass being handled by Markov's inequality through the definition of coverage) shows that, once M is chosen so that the integrated coverage at M is at most a constant multiple of the accuracy times M, and once the number of samples per group is at least of order M times the log of the inverse failure probability divided by the accuracy, the empirical mean lies within the multiplicative window with the required probability. The key improvement over a naive bounded-difference bound comes from bounding the truncated variance by the integrated coverage itself, a self-normalizing relationship between truncation bias and variance.

Passing from integrated coverage to f-divergence. To express the required level M through the f-divergence, the paper establishes two comparison inequalities. First, a convexity lemma shows that for an admissible generator any point beyond M is bounded by one plus a factor times the value of the generator there, which combined with Markov's inequality yields that the coverage at M is at most M times the f-divergence divided by the value of the generator at M. Second, and crucially for controlling the integrated coverage, the eventual subquadraticity assumption, that the generator divided by the square of its argument is non-increasing past the threshold, gives the pointwise inequality that any argument squared is at most the square of M times the generator ratio; integrating this against the base measure bounds the truncated second moment, and hence the integrated coverage at M divided by M, by the square of the threshold divided by M plus M times the f-divergence divided by the value of the generator at M.

Choosing the level and assembling the bound. By the definition of the inverse growth profile, taking M equal to that profile evaluated at the f-divergence divided by the product of accuracy and failure parameter forces M times the f-divergence divided by the generator value at M to be small. Choosing M to be the larger of this value and the squared threshold over the same product makes both terms of the previous bound small, so the integrated-coverage requirement is met. Substituting this choice into the single-group concentration result gives that averages over groups of the stated size concentrate multiplicatively around the true constant with constant probability, in a number of samples governed by the inverse growth profile term maximized against the squared-threshold-over-accuracy-squared term. Feeding this per-group guarantee into the median-of-means fact upgrades it to hold with probability at least one minus the failure parameter, which is exactly the claimed guarantee for the fixed pair of measures, uniformly over every positive finite value of the normalizing constant.
nl_theorem: There exists a positive finite universal constant C with the following property. For every measurable space X, generator f : ℝ → ℝ, threshold c, accuracy and failure parameters ε, δ, sample size n, and probability measures μ, ν on X with ν absolutely continuous with respect to μ, suppose that f is convex and nonnegative on [0, ∞), that f(1) = 0, that f is differentiable at 1 with derivative 0, that 1 ≤ c, that t ↦ f(t)/t² is antitone on [c, ∞), and that 0 < ε < 1 and 0 < δ < 1. If C times the sample-complexity scale (the maximum of γ_f(6·D_f(ν‖μ)/ε)·log(1/δ)/ε and c²/ε²) is at most n, then there exists a measurable estimator Ẑ, depending only on the sample vector and the observed unnormalized density ratios, such that for every finite Z > 0 the law of n i.i.d. samples from μ assigns probability at least 1 − δ to the event that (1 − ε)Z ≤ Ẑ ≤ (1 + ε)Z. Here D_f is the f-divergence and γ_f is the generalized inverse of t ↦ f(t)/t on [1, ∞).

core_claim: Falsity of the Primal Pathwidth SETH is equivalent to a fixed-width list-coloring speedup, which is itself equivalent to a uniform large-pathwidth list-coloring speedup, giving two chained equivalences among these three complexity statements.

metainfo.paper: The Primal Pathwidth SETH

nl_proof:
The paper establishes the two equivalences by proving a cycle of three implications among the statements, where statement one is "the Primal Pathwidth SETH is false," statement two is the fixed-width list-coloring speedup (an algorithm running in time about the vertex count raised to p minus four minus epsilon for some fixed width p greater than four), and statement three is the uniform speedup (one algorithm running in time about the vertex count raised to (1 minus epsilon) times p, for every width p above a threshold). Since these form a cycle, all three are equivalent, which yields both conjoined equivalences.

Implication "three implies two" is immediate. Given the uniform algorithm with its epsilon and threshold, choose a single fixed integer width p exceeding the threshold, exceeding four, and exceeding four divided by epsilon. Setting delta equal to epsilon times p minus four, which is positive, one has (1 minus epsilon) times p equal to p minus four minus delta, so the uniform algorithm restricted to width-p inputs already meets the fixed-width bound.

Implication "two implies one" is the reduction from three-CNF satisfiability to List Coloring. Fix the width p and speedup exponent, and set k equal to p minus four. Given a formula and a path decomposition of its primal graph, one first makes the decomposition nice, obtaining a linear number of bags (polynomial, of order n to the fourth) together with an injective assignment of each clause to a bag containing all its variables; this uses the auxiliary result that any path decomposition can be made nice, with at most a fixed number of intermediate bags per transition, without increasing width. A second auxiliary result partitions the variables into k groups so that every bag meets every group in at most the ceiling of (width plus one) divided by k variables. For each bag and each group one creates a vertex whose list has one fresh color per partial assignment of the group's variables in that bag, giving roughly two to the power (width over k) colors per vertex, with disjoint color sets. Consistency across neighboring bags is enforced by contracting vertices that carry the same group, and by a carefully designed consistency gadget built from two parallel paths joined by control vertices, engineered specifically to avoid the quadratic blow-up in list sizes that a naive forbidden-pair construction would incur; clause satisfaction is enforced by a triangle gadget with a shared three-color list plus auxiliary vertices that forbid exactly the partial assignments falsifying each literal. The resulting graph has vertex count of order two to the power (width over k) times n to the fourth, is built in linear time, and admits a path decomposition of width exactly p obtained by lifting the nice decomposition and inserting short bag sequences for the gadgets. A valid list coloring corresponds to a consistent satisfying assignment and vice versa. Running the assumed fixed-width algorithm therefore decides satisfiability in time about two to the power ((width over (p minus four)) times (p minus four minus epsilon)) times n to the power four p; choosing epsilon prime so that two minus epsilon prime equals two to the power ((p minus four minus epsilon) over (p minus four)) and a polynomial exponent equal to four p gives a running time of the form (two minus epsilon prime) to the power width times a polynomial in n, with epsilon prime strictly between zero and two, contradicting the Primal Pathwidth SETH.

Implication "one implies three" is the reduction from List Coloring to satisfiability. Assuming the Primal Pathwidth SETH is false, fix a satisfiability algorithm running in time about (two minus epsilon) to the power pathwidth times a polynomial in the formula size. Given a List Coloring instance with n vertices and a path decomposition of width p, one may assume n is a power of two and every list has size at most n (larger lists always allow a color, so such vertices are removed). For each vertex one introduces log n Boolean variables encoding the index of the chosen color in that vertex's sorted list. Clauses of the first kind forbid index values that exceed the list length; clauses of the second kind, added for each edge, forbid every pair of indices whose selected colors coincide. This produces a formula of size of order n cubed, constructible in linear time. Replacing each vertex in the given decomposition by its block of log n index variables yields a valid path decomposition of the primal graph of width (p plus one) times log n, since every added clause involves the index blocks of two adjacent vertices. Satisfying assignments correspond exactly to proper list colorings. Running the satisfiability algorithm then takes time about (two minus epsilon) to the power (p times log n) times a polynomial in n, which equals n to the power ((1 minus delta) p) times a polynomial, where delta equals one minus the base-two logarithm of (two minus epsilon), a positive constant. Choosing the threshold to be twice the polynomial slack divided by delta makes the polynomial factor negligible for all larger p, so with epsilon prime equal to delta over two one obtains an algorithm meeting the uniform bound for every width above the threshold.

Closing the cycle of these three implications gives that all three statements are equivalent, and in particular both stated equivalences hold.
nl_theorem: Consider the following three statements about deterministic timed decision procedures acting on fixed binary encodings. (1) The Primal Pathwidth SETH holds: for every real ε with 0 < ε < 2 and every natural exponent c, no timed decision procedure both correctly decides satisfiability of every valid encoded decomposed 3-CNF input and runs in time bounded by a constant times (2 − ε) raised to the recorded decomposition width times the variable count raised to c. (2) The fixed-width list-coloring speedup holds: there exist a real ε > 0, a natural number p > 4, and a timed decision procedure that correctly decides colorability of every valid encoded decomposed list-coloring input of recorded width p and runs on such inputs in time bounded by a constant times the vertex count raised to (p − 4 − ε). (3) The uniform pathwidth list-coloring speedup holds: there exist a real ε > 0, a positive natural number p₀, and one timed decision procedure that correctly decides colorability of every valid encoded decomposed list-coloring input and, for every natural p > p₀, runs on the valid inputs of recorded width exactly p in time bounded by a constant times the vertex count raised to (1 − ε)·p. The theorem asserts the conjunction of two equivalences: the negation of statement (1) is equivalent to statement (2), and statement (2) is equivalent to statement (3).

core_claim: No bounded-degree polynomial threshold test can reliably distinguish the non-Gaussian hidden-direction distribution from standard Gaussian samples within the stated sample and degree regime.

metainfo.paper: PTF Testing Lower Bounds for Non-Gaussian Component Analysis

nl_proof:
The argument fixes the free constant and several auxiliary parameters and then bounds the averaged acceptance-probability difference by combining a random-direction derivative-decay estimate, a mollification-plus-sandwiching reduction, and a one-sample-at-a-time hybrid replacement argument.

Setup. Choose the absolute constant large enough, and set the auxiliary parameters so that the smoothing scale is 2(1/4 − c*/2), the moment-truncation parameter is c*/2, and the failure tolerance is 0.05. The hypotheses max(k,m) < d^(c*/C*) and n < d^((1/4−c*)m) are exactly what make each quantitative estimate below go through.

Step 1: Derivative decay along a random direction. For a fixed degree-k polynomial and a uniformly random unit direction v, one shows that, with probability at least 0.99 over v, a standard Gaussian sample array satisfies, simultaneously for every order t up to k and with probability at least 1 − 0.05 over the samples, that the Frobenius norm of the t-th directional derivative tensor of p projected onto v is at most (k/0.05)^(4t) d^(−t/4) times |p|. The key inputs are: a strong anti-concentration ("slow growth of derivatives") fact stating that the size of the full t-th derivative tensor of a degree-k polynomial exceeds (k^3/ε)^t |p| only with probability O(ε); the identity expressing the projected tensor as the contraction of the full derivative tensor with v^{⊗t}; a bound on the averaged direction matrix E_v[(v^{⊗t})(v^{⊗t})^T], obtained by comparing the sphere and Gaussian laws and applying Isserlis' theorem, yielding a factor (2t/e)^t d^(−t/2); and finally Jensen's and Markov's inequalities together with a union bound over t.

Step 2: Mollification and sandwiching. Because the sign test is discontinuous, one replaces it by a smooth mollified test h = sign(p)·g, where g is a product over orders t of a fixed smooth bump function applied to d^(Θ(t)) ‖p^{[t]}‖_F² / p². By construction g equals one whenever the derivative-decay bound holds and forces h to vanish when any projected derivative is too large relative to |p|. Since g lies in [0,1], h is pointwise below the sign test, and by Step 1 it agrees with the sign test under the Gaussian up to error 0.05. A sandwiching argument (using this together with the same construction applied to −p) shows that if the hidden-direction product law fools h relative to the Gaussian product law with error δ, then it fools the original sign test with error at most δ + 0.05.

Step 3: Single replacement step. The core estimate is that replacing one Gaussian coordinate sample by one hidden-direction sample changes the expectation of h by at most d^(−c_g m/2 + cm). Writing a hidden sample as an orthogonal Gaussian part plus a scalar multiple of v, one conditions on all other coordinates and reduces to a one-dimensional comparison of the scalar law A against N(0,1). First A and the Gaussian are truncated to [−d^{c_t}, d^{c_t}]; a higher-moment Chebyshev bound and Hölder's inequality show the truncation costs little and preserves approximate moment matching up to order m. If the fixed coordinates are not "well-behaved" (no point in the interval satisfies the derivative-decay inequalities), the mollifier annihilates h throughout the interval and the difference is zero. Otherwise a Taylor-type stability lemma shows the derivative-decay bounds propagate from one good point to the whole truncated interval. One then Taylor-expands h in the scalar variable along v to order m: exact matching of the first m moments cancels the low-order terms, and the remainder is controlled by a mollified-derivative bound stating that the t-th directional derivative of h is at most (k+t)^{O(t)} d^(−c_g t/2). This last bound follows from an explicit unfolding of the derivatives of the mollifier into a sum of k^{O(t)} products of ratios of directional derivative tensors, each estimated via Cauchy–Schwarz and the propagated derivative-decay inequalities.

Step 4: Assembling the bound. Summing the n single-replacement errors by the triangle inequality gives, for a fixed good direction v, that the hidden product law fools h relative to the Gaussian with error at most n·d^(−(1/4−c*)m), which is at most 0.05 by the sample-size hypothesis. The sandwiching lemma then yields, for every good v, a conditional distinguishing gap at most 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.1. Finally, by Jensen's inequality the averaged gap over v is bounded by the average of the conditional gaps. Splitting this average over the set of good directions (probability at least 0.99, gap at most 0.1) and its complement (probability at most 0.01, gap trivially at most 1) gives at most 0.1·0.99 + 1·0.01 ≤ 0.11, which is the claimed bound.
nl_theorem: There exists an absolute real constant C* greater than 8 with the following property. For every real number c* with 0 < c* < 1/4, all positive integers d, k, n, m with m even, every multivariate polynomial p over the reals in variables indexed by pairs from Fin n and Fin d, and every probability measure A on the reals, suppose that max(k, m) < d^(c*/C*), that n < d^((1/4 − c*)·m), that the total degree of p is at most k, and that A matches the first m moments of the standard Gaussian N(0,1) (its j-th moment equals that of N(0,1) for every j ≤ m). Then the absolute difference between the acceptance probability of the sign test sgn(p) — where sgn(t) = 1 if t ≥ 0 and 0 otherwise — computed under a uniformly random hidden direction on the unit sphere followed by n independent hidden-direction samples, and the acceptance probability under n independent standard Gaussian samples, is at most 0.11.

core_claim: Two vanishing sequences exist so that, for a logarithmic target size, a stopped empty-start Glauber chain on a random half-density graph approximates the uniform independent-set law in normalized Wasserstein distance with high probability.

metainfo.paper: Polynomial-time sampling despite disorder chaos

nl_proof:
The paper proves this high-probability closeness in normalized Wasserstein distance by relating the stopped Glauber chain to a simpler greedy procedure and then chaining several concentration and coupling estimates. Throughout, logarithms are base two, and the target size is on the order of the logarithm of the number of vertices minus a logarithmic-of-logarithmic correction.

Step 1 (up-degree concentration). For a set S, the up-degree is the number of vertices outside S that are non-adjacent to all of S; its mean over the random graph is (n minus size of S) times two to the minus size of S. A Chernoff-plus-union-bound argument shows that, with probability tending to one over the random graph, every set of size up to the logarithm of n minus a large constant times its double logarithm has up-degree within a small relative error of this mean. This uniform control is the engine of the whole argument.

Step 2 (coupling Glauber dynamics with randomized greedy). The randomized greedy algorithm starts from the empty set and repeatedly adds a uniformly random still-available vertex. Glauber dynamics instead picks a uniform vertex each step and stochastically adds or removes it. Because, while the current independent set stays below the target size, there are far more addable vertices than removable ones, dropping a vertex before adding one is very unlikely; moreover each new vertex is added quickly. Conditioning on the up-degree concentration event, the paper builds an explicit coupling in which, with probability tending to one, the empty-started Glauber chain reaches a set of the target size within the allotted time budget on the order of a constant times the logarithm of n times two to the target size, and its output coincides with the greedy output. This justifies replacing the stopped Glauber output law by the greedy output law.

Step 3 (greedy samples nearly uniformly in total variation). Fixing an independent set of the target size, greedy outputs it exactly when its vertices are added in some order, and the probability of any particular order is a product of reciprocals of up-degrees along the way. Using the uniform up-degree concentration, this product is shown to be the same, up to a factor tending to one, across all target-size independent sets. Summing over orderings and over sets shows that the greedy output distribution is within total variation o(1) of the uniform distribution over independent sets of that size.

Step 4 (from a slightly smaller size to the hardcore-typical sizes). Separate concentration analysis of the number of independent sets of each size shows the hardcore measure places almost all mass on sizes in a window of width on the order of the double logarithm of n around a value slightly larger than the greedy target size. Conditioning on such a size k, the paper couples the uniform law on the smaller target-size sets with the uniform law on size-k sets by drawing a smaller set from greedy and then extending it by a uniformly chosen collection of additional vertices that keep it independent. To show this extension induces the near-uniform law on size-k sets, it controls the multi-vertex up-degree (the number of ways to complete a set by a fixed number of vertices). Concentration of this multi-vertex up-degree is obtained by bounding a poly-logarithmic moment of its deviation using combinatorial counting lemmas (bounding vertex overlaps, internal edges, and configuration counts) together with the correlation inequality for increasing events. A union bound then makes every smaller set's completion count concentrate.

Step 5 (assembling the Wasserstein bound).
