Viewing the containment relation between smaller sets and size-k sets as a bipartite graph, the stationary measure of the natural random walk is proportional to degree; the concentration of completion counts makes the induced marginal on smaller sets close in total variation to uniform, and the marginal on size-k sets is exactly uniform. Applying the data-processing inequality, the total-variation coupling characterization, and the time-reversal of the walk produces a coupling of the greedy law and the size-k uniform law whose paired sets share all but a lower-order number of vertices. Because the normalized second moments are close to the logarithm of n, this large overlap makes the normalized squared Wasserstein cost o(1) for each size in the window. Convexity of the Wasserstein distance over the size mixture, together with a final triangle-inequality comparison between the size-restricted hardcore law and the full hardcore law (whose sizes concentrate and whose largest independent set is of logarithmic order), yields that the normalized Wasserstein distance between the hardcore law and the greedy law is o(1). Combining with the Glauber-greedy coupling of Step 2, the normalized Wasserstein distance between the hardcore law and the stopped Glauber output law is at most an error term tending to zero, on an event of probability at least one minus a failure term tending to zero, which is the claimed statement.
nl_theorem: There exist functions failureBound, errorBound : ℕ → ℝ, both tending to 0 at infinity, such that for every n, if we set the target size kₙ = max{0, ⌊log₂ n − 30·log₂(log₂ n)⌋} (negative floor values truncated to zero), then the Erdős–Rényi measure G(n,1/2) assigns to the event that the normalized 2-Wasserstein distance between the fugacity-one hardcore (uniform independent-set) measure of the sampled graph and the empty-start Glauber output law stopped at min{100(log n)2^{kₙ}, τ_{kₙ}} is at most errorBound n, a probability (as a real number) at least 1 − failureBound n.

core_claim: There exists one dimension-indexed family of randomized adaptive matrix-vector algorithms that simultaneously meets a uniform soft query bound and, in every dimension, the high-probability finite-family Frobenius approximation guarantee.

metainfo.paper: Query Efficient Structured Matrix Learning

nl_proof:
The paper builds the required family of algorithms in three layers, all resting on a single Frobenius-norm sketching fact: if a random sign matrix has on the order of log(1/failure)/accuracy-squared columns, then right-multiplying any fixed matrix by it preserves its Frobenius norm up to a multiplicative factor close to one with the stated confidence. This follows from a Hanson-Wright type concentration bound.

First, the paper describes a one-sided baseline that only uses right products with the target. It maintains a candidate set initialized to the whole family and, over a number of rounds, draws a small sign sketch, forms the sketched product of the target, and discards every candidate whose sketched distance to the target exceeds a threshold tied to the assumed error bound. A union bound over rounds shows the true best candidate always survives, while every candidate that is far from the target is eliminated with high probability, so after enough rounds only near-optimal candidates remain. This uses on the order of log of the family size right products.

Second, and this is the key step, the paper simulates the one-sided method using both the target and its transpose while spending only about the square root of the logarithm of the family size queries. It precomputes one left sketch of the transpose. In each round it draws several right sketches and, for each, tries to find a sampled representative candidate whose left-sketched distance to the target is small; the reusable left sketch lets it compare these distances without ever forming the right product of the target. A dichotomy governs each right sketch: either no good representative exists, in which case that sketch is highly productive and issuing it cuts the candidate set by a factor exponential in the square root of the log family size; or good representatives are found for all the right sketches, in which case the algorithm uses those representatives as proxies for the target and filters down to a final answer in a single shot with no further right queries. To keep the left sketch reusable across rounds despite the candidate sets depending on it, the paper draws several right sketches per round and unions over the limited number of candidate sets that could arise, so the left sketch remains accurate for all of them. A triangle-inequality argument then shows the returned matrix is within a factor of three plus the accuracy times the assumed error bound, that the optimal candidate always survives, and that the candidate set shrinks fast enough that termination occurs within about the square root of the log family size productive rounds; the total query cost is the soft envelope claimed.

Third, since this simulation assumes a known upper bound on the optimal error, the paper removes that assumption. A simple Gaussian sketch of constant width with a median-of-independent-trials estimator produces, with high probability, a coarse bound sandwiching the optimal error between itself and roughly the family size times the optimal error; this uses only a logarithmic number of queries and relies on a Markov upper tail and a chi-square lower tail for the Gaussian sketch. Starting from that coarse bound, the paper runs a binary search over a geometric grid of candidate error bounds, one of which is guaranteed to lie within a factor close to one of the true optimum. At each search step it runs the two-sided simulation with the current median bound, cheaply estimates the resulting approximation error with one shared right sketch, and moves the search interval accordingly, keeping the best solution seen. After a doubly logarithmic number of steps it certifies a solution whose Frobenius distance to the target is at most three plus the accuracy times the true optimal family error, with the failure probability controlled by union bounds over all steps. Assembling these pieces yields, for every dimension, a single randomized adaptive two-sided algorithm meeting both the uniform soft query bound and the high-probability approximation guarantee, which is exactly the asserted existence statement.
nl_theorem: There exists a family of randomized adaptive two-sided matrix-vector algorithms, one for each dimension n, that solves finite-family approximation. This means two things hold together. First, there is a single positive constant C and two fixed nonnegative integer polylogarithmic powers such that, in every dimension n, for every nonempty finite family F of real n-by-n matrices, every target matrix A, all real numbers epsilon and delta strictly between 0 and 1, and every seed in the support of the algorithm's seed distribution, the pathwise number of matrix-vector queries the algorithm makes against A equals at most C times the soft query envelope, where that envelope is (sqrt(log |F|) / epsilon^2) times (log(2+|F|) + log(2 + 1/epsilon)) raised to the input power times (log(2 + 1/delta)) raised to the failure power. Second, in every dimension n, for every nonempty finite family F, every target A, and all epsilon, delta strictly between 0 and 1, the probability (under the push-forward of the seed distribution through executing the program against A) that the returned matrix lies in F and has Frobenius distance to A at most (3 + epsilon) times the minimum over B in F of the Frobenius distance from A to B is at least 1 - delta.

core_claim: For two-part-code MDL classification, the worst-case limiting population error equals a specific closed-form curve, matching both the supremum of pointwise limits and the limit of finite-sample worst-case suprema.

metainfo.paper: Quantifying Overfitting along the Regularization Path for Two-Part-Code MDL in Supervised Classification

nl_proof:
The paper obtains this tight characterization by combining a uniform upper bound with a matching family of lower-bound constructions, so that the worst-case limiting error equals the specified curve both when the sample-size limit is taken inside the supremum over problems and when it is taken outside.

Upper bound direction. The paper first proves a single generalization guarantee that holds simultaneously for every predictor. Starting from a concentration inequality that controls, with high probability, the Bernoulli relative entropy between the empirical and population error of each predictor (obtained by a union bound over a sharp two-sided binomial tail estimate, weighted by the prior mass of each predictor), it specializes to the predictor actually selected by the rule. Multiplying that inequality by the penalty parameter and adding the empirical entropy of the selected predictor, then invoking the fact that the selected predictor minimizes the two-part-code objective and that the empirical entropy of the fixed reference concentrates around its mean (via a bounded-difference argument), yields an inequality of the form: an auxiliary function of the selected predictor's population error is at most the binary entropy of the reference error plus terms that vanish as the sample grows. The auxiliary function is the pointwise minimum over admissible empirical errors of the penalized relative entropy plus entropy. The paper evaluates this minimum explicitly: when the penalty is at most one the minimizer sits at zero, producing the closed form whose inverse is one minus two to the power of minus the reference entropy over the penalty; when the penalty exceeds one the minimizer is interior, producing the tilted-error function whose low-error inverse defines the second branch. Inverting the guarantee, and controlling the derivative of the inverse through the mean value theorem (which introduces the factors depending on how far the reference error is from one half), gives a finite-sample bound on the expected error of the rule. Crucially, the vanishing remainder depends only on the penalty, the reference error, and the reference's description length, but not otherwise on the prior or source. This uniformity means the bound controls both each individual configuration's limit and the supremum over configurations taken before the limit, so both quantities are at most the curve.

Lower bound direction. To show the curve is actually approached, the paper constructs explicit hard problems. Fix any target value strictly below the curve and at least the reference error. Take instances that are infinite binary strings with a balanced label, where each coordinate is conditionally independent given the label; the zeroth coordinate agrees with the label up to Bernoulli noise at the reference level and serves as the good reference predictor with prior mass bounded below, while every other coordinate agrees up to noise at the higher target level and serves as a bad predictor, all under a universal prior with slowly decaying mass. The argument shows that, with probability tending to one, the two-part-code objective is smaller on some bad predictor than on the good reference, so the selected predictor has population error equal to the target and the expected error converges to it. For penalty at most one, one shows that among sufficiently many bad predictors some interpolates the sample, giving an objective dominated by its description length, which is below the reference objective exactly when the target is below the first branch. For penalty above one, one takes the empirical-error minimizer among an exponentially large block of bad predictors; the minimum of independent binomials concentrates, so this predictor's empirical error tends to the tilted error and its objective tends to the second-branch function evaluated at the target, again below the reference objective exactly when the target is below the second branch. Hence configurations exist whose limiting expected error is arbitrarily close to the curve from below.

Combination. The lower-bound constructions show the supremum, over configurations, of the pointwise limiting expected error is at least the curve, while the uniform upper bound shows it is at most the curve, so this supremum equals the curve. The same uniform upper bound, applied to the supremum taken at each fixed sample size, shows those worst finite-sample expected errors converge, and their limit equals the curve as well. Finally, since each configuration's expected error at a given sample size never exceeds the worst finite-sample value, taking limits shows the supremum of pointwise limits is bounded by the limit of the finite-sample suprema, which closes the chain and yields the stated equalities.
nl_theorem: Fix real parameters lambda and Lstar with 0 < lambda and 0 < Lstar < 1/2. Consider the two-part-code MDL learning setting, where an admissible configuration specifies an instance space, a predictor class, a measurable structure on instance-label pairs, a binary prediction map, a valid description prior (nonnegative, summable, total mass at most one), a probability source, a reference predictor of positive prior mass whose population error equals Lstar, and, for each sample size, a selected predictor of positive prior mass with empirical error at most one half that minimizes the objective lambda times description length plus the base-2 logarithm of the binomial coefficient of sample size choose number of sample errors, together with the required measurability conditions. Let the expected MDL error at sample size m be the integral, over the i.i.d. product law of the source, of the population error of the selected predictor. Then there exists a real number b such that the finite-sample worst-case supremum (over all such configurations) of the expected MDL error tends to b as the sample size grows, and moreover the worst-case limiting error curve at (lambda, Lstar) equals the supremum of all real numbers r arising as sample-size limits of some configuration's expected MDL error, this supremum is at most b, and b again equals the worst-case limiting error curve. Here the curve is defined to be 1 minus 2 raised to the power minus binary entropy of Lstar (in bits) divided by lambda when lambda is at most one, and otherwise the low-error inverse, restricted to [0,1/2], of the function q ↦ lambda times the Bernoulli KL (in bits) between the tilted error and q plus the binary entropy (in bits) of the tilted error, evaluated at the binary entropy of Lstar.

core_claim: For every positive integers with the first at least the second, a specific nontrivial constraint relation exists whose non-redundancy exponent equals their ratio and whose non-redundancy grows exactly like that power.

metainfo.paper: The Richness of CSP Non-redundancy

nl_proof:
The paper produces the required relation explicitly and analyzes its non-redundancy from both sides.

Construction. Fix positive integers p ≥ q. The domain has the two Boolean values together with one extra symbol for each Boolean string of length q. A tuple of length p + p^q lies in the OR-direct-product relation exactly when its first p entries form a Boolean vector that is not identically zero, and each of the remaining p^q entries is the length-q Boolean string obtained by reading off the first-block entries at the q positions encoded (through the fixed base-p indexing bijection) by that entry's index. This last condition is a rigid "direct product" constraint: the first p Boolean values determine all remaining entries. The paper also introduces a companion relation, called the scaffolding, obtained by dropping the requirement that the Boolean vector be nonzero, so the scaffolding adds exactly the all-zero-driven tuple.

Nontriviality. Choosing any single coordinate equal to one and completing it with its forced direct-product entries yields a tuple in the relation, so it is nonempty; the tuple built from the all-zero Boolean vector violates the OR condition and hence is omitted, so the relation is a proper subset of the ambient power.

Lower bound. Start from the complete OR instance on n variables whose clauses are all p-subsets; it is non-redundant because setting the p chosen variables to zero and all others to one falsifies exactly that clause, giving n-choose-p clauses. This instance is lifted to the OR-direct-product relation by adjoining a fresh padding variable for every q-tuple of original variables (at most n^q of them) and placing, in each clause, the padding variable that the direct-product coordinates demand. A witness for deleting a lifted clause is obtained by extending the original witness so that each q-tuple of variables receives the corresponding q-tuple of Boolean values; this satisfies all direct-product coordinates and leaves the OR coordinate false only for the deleted clause. Hence the lifted instance stays non-redundant, so the non-redundancy at n + n^q variables is at least n-choose-p. Since n-choose-p grows like n^p and n + n^q grows like n^q, this yields a lower bound of order n^{p/q}.

Upper bound. Using the triangle inequality for conditional non-redundancy with the scaffolding relation, and the reduction that lets one restrict to multipartite instances up to constant factors, it suffices to bound the conditional non-redundancy of the relation given its scaffolding, plus the non-redundancy of the scaffolding itself. The scaffolding is shown to have only linear non-redundancy because it embeds into a coset of an Abelian group (its coordinates are affine projection constraints), and Mal'tsev/affine embeddings force linear non-redundancy. For the conditional part, one argues by induction on the number of variables. If two clauses share a padding variable but differ on a governed first-block position, the rigid direct-product structure of the scaffolding forces those two first-block variables to receive equal values in any scaffolding-satisfying assignment; identifying them removes a variable without changing the number of clauses and preserves conditional non-redundancy, so induction applies. Otherwise the instance is "reduced," and then distinct clauses have distinct first-block variable sets, yielding a p-uniform set family whose size equals the clause count, while the padding variables injectively cover its q-shadow. The Kruskal-Katona theorem bounds the size of a p-uniform family by (roughly) the (p/q)-power of its q-shadow, and the shadow is at most the number of padding variables, giving a bound of order n^{p/q} on the clause count. Combining the linear scaffolding bound with this conditional bound produces an overall upper bound of order n^{p/q}.

Conclusion. The matching lower and upper bounds give two-sided asymptotic control of the non-redundancy function by n^{p/q}. Because q ≤ q ≤ p and q is positive, the target exponent p/q is at least one; a function that is bounded above and below by constant multiples of n^{p/q} is big-O of n^{p/q + ε} for every positive ε yet fails to be big-O of any smaller power, so the least admissible exponent, i.e. the non-redundancy exponent, equals p/q. This establishes existence of the nontrivial relation with the stated exponent and the stated two-sided asymptotic growth.
nl_theorem: For all positive integers p and q with q at most p, there exists a relation R over the domain that is the disjoint union of a Boolean sort and a sort of Boolean q-tuples, of arity p + p^q, such that: R equals the OR-direct-product relation ORDP_{p,q}; R is nontrivial (it contains at least one tuple and omits at least one tuple of the ambient Cartesian power); the non-redundancy exponent of R (the infimum of the admissible exponents a ≥ 1 for which, for every ε > 0, the real-valued non-redundancy function n ↦ NRD(R, n) is big-O of n ↦ n^{a+ε} as n → ∞) equals p/q; and the real-valued non-redundancy function of R is Θ(n^{p/q}) as n → ∞, meaning it and n ↦ n^{p/q} mutually bound one another in the big-O sense along the at-infinity filter. Here NRD(R, n) is the largest number of clauses in a non-redundant instance for R on n variables, where a clause is an r-tuple of variables in [n], an instance is a finite set of clauses, an assignment satisfies a clause when the induced tuple lies in R, the solution set collects assignments satisfying every clause, and an instance is non-redundant when erasing any single clause strictly enlarges the solution set.

core_claim: Every admissible approachability instance with neutral actions admits an improper phi-regret minimization instance together with a tight reduction preserving worst-case value at every horizon.

metainfo.paper: Rate-Preserving Reductions for Blackwell Approachability

nl_proof:
The argument rests on a single idea: augment the learner's action so that it also records which constraint the learner is being measured against, and then read the approachability loss directly as a phi-regret on this augmented space.

Step 1 (encode the affine constraints as an inner product). Each constraint index carries a linear form on the tensor product of the action and loss spaces together with a real constant; evaluated at a pure tensor of an action and a loss, the constraint produces the affine value obtained by applying the linear form to that tensor and adding the constant. Negating these values gives a bilinear pairing that sends a constraint index tensored with an action, paired against a loss, to the negative of the corresponding constraint value. To also capture the constant term of each affine constraint, one works on the space obtained by taking the tensor product of the constraint space with the action space and adjoining a further copy of the constraint space; the augmented action associated with a constraint index and an action is the pair consisting of the constraint-index tensor action in the first summand and the constraint index itself in the second summand, the latter recording the constant coefficient. Because all spaces are finite dimensional, this bilinear data is realized by an affine map from the loss space into the augmented space such that the inner product of an augmented action against the image of a loss reproduces the negative of the affine constraint value evaluated at that action and loss. This is simply the matrix (Riesz) representation of the bilinear pairing.

Step 2 (build the improper phi-regret instance). Take the target action set to be the image of the original action set under the augmentation embedding, the target loss set to be the image of the original loss set under this representing affine map, and the benchmark set to consist of one affine self-map for each constraint index. The benchmark associated with a constraint index shifts the recorded constraint by that index while leaving the action coordinate untouched; concretely, on augmented actions built from a constraint index and an action, it replaces that constraint index by its sum with the fixed index. This shift is exactly the operation that converts the maximization over constraints into a comparison between the played augmented action and its transform. Such shift maps generally send augmented actions outside the target action set, so the resulting instance is genuinely improper.

Step 3 (fixed points and validity). To confirm that the constructed instance is a legitimate improper phi-regret instance, each benchmark map must fix some point of the target action set. This is where the hypothesis of neutral actions enters: for every constraint index there is an action on which the corresponding affine constraint vanishes for every loss, and the augmented image of such an action is left invariant by the associated shift map, giving the required fixed point. Since the target action and loss sets are affine images of convex, bounded, and nonempty sets, they remain convex, bounded, and nonempty, and the benchmark set is nonempty because the constraint set is nonempty. Hence the instance meets the definition of an improper phi-regret instance.

Step 4 (the exact loss identity). By the representing identity of Step 1 and the definition of the shift maps, for every constraint index, action, and loss, the inner product of the played augmented action minus its benchmark transform against the represented loss equals the original affine constraint value at that action and loss. Summing over the horizon and maximizing over constraint indices, the phi-regret of the augmented play against the represented losses equals, term by term, the approachability loss of the original play against the original losses.

Step 5 (tightness in both directions). The augmentation embedding returns the original action in its first coordinate, and the representing map returns the original loss in its loss coordinate, so both embeddings are injective and admit explicit coordinate projections on their images. Given any approachability algorithm, one embeds each of its actions through the augmentation map and reconstructs each source loss from a target loss history via the loss-coordinate projection, producing a deterministic nonanticipating regret algorithm whose plays lie in the target action set. Conversely, given any regret algorithm, one feeds it the embedded loss histories and projects each of its outputs back to an action, producing a deterministic nonanticipating approachability algorithm whose plays lie in the source action set. The exact identity of Step 4, together with the bijection between admissible loss histories induced by the representing map, shows that in each direction the transferred algorithm attains the same worst-case value at every horizon. This is precisely the definition of a tight reduction, completing the argument.
nl_theorem: Let the ambient spaces be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces. Consider an approachability instance consisting of an action set, a loss set, a constraint set, and a linear coefficient map assigning to each constraint index a pair made of a linear functional on the tensor product of the action and loss spaces together with a real constant, so that the constraint indexed by u sends a pure tensor p⊗ℓ to the affine value Lu(p⊗ℓ)+cu. Suppose this instance is admissible, meaning its action, loss, and constraint sets are each convex, bounded, and nonempty, and suppose it has neutral actions, meaning that for every constraint u in the constraint set there is an action p in the action set with Lu(p⊗ℓ)+cu = 0 for every loss ℓ in the loss set. Then, on the L2 product space of the action space with the L2 product of the loss space and the L2 direct sum of the tensor product of the constraint and action spaces with the constraint space, there exists a phi-regret minimization instance—given by an action set, a loss set, and a set of affine self-maps—that is improper (its action and loss sets are convex, bounded, and nonempty, its benchmark set is nonempty, and every benchmark map has a fixed point in its action set) and that admits a tight reduction from the approachability instance: every approachability algorithm is matched by a regret algorithm with the same worst-case value at every horizon, and conversely every regret algorithm is matched by an approachability algorithm with the same worst-case value at every horizon.

core_claim: A universal constant makes likelihood peeling along fixed onion decompositions exactly recover the hidden dense planted subgraph whenever its minimal maximum density eventually exceeds the stated logarithmic divergence threshold.

metainfo.paper: Recovery of Planted Subgraphs

nl_proof:
The paper analyzes the likelihood peeling estimator, which reconstructs the hidden copy layer by layer along the onion decomposition of the template. The argument bounds the worst-case probability that the final output differs from the planted copy and shows it vanishes under the stated density condition, giving a universal constant (the paper obtains 4 when the inner edge probability is one and 16 otherwise).

Step 1 (reduction to per-layer errors). The overall failure event is the union, over the layers, of the events that the estimate at some layer is wrong. Using the elementary inequality that the probability of a union of nested increasing events is at most the sum of the conditional probabilities of each event given the complement of the previous one, the total error is bounded by the sum, over layers, of the probability that a given layer is estimated incorrectly conditioned on all preceding layers being correct.

Step 2 (first-moment control of a single layer). Fix a layer and condition on the preceding layer having been identified correctly. The peeling estimate at this layer chooses, among all copies of the next onion layer that extend the previously fixed estimate, one maximizing the number of observed edges added beyond the fixed part. This estimate is wrong only if some competing copy other than the planted one attains at least the planted score, so by Markov's inequality the conditional error is at most the expected number of competing extensions present in the observed graph.

Step 3 (probability that a competing copy appears). For each candidate extension, the edges it adds that do not coincide with the planted layer are non-planted and hence present independently with the background probability. Thus the probability that a candidate appears decays geometrically in the number of its edges that fall outside the planted layer. The defining maximality of the onion layer, namely that it maximizes relative density over the previous layer among all subgraphs of the template, lower bounds this edge count: for a candidate sharing all but a certain number of newly added vertices with the planted layer, the number of missed edges is at least the layer's relative density times the number of unshared added vertices. This ties the decay rate to the layer's relative density.

Step 4 (counting competing copies by overlap). Candidates are grouped by how many of their newly added vertices coincide with those of the planted layer. The number of candidates with a given overlap is bounded crudely by choosing which added vertices are shared and mapping the remaining fresh vertices into the ambient set, giving a bound polynomial in the number of vertices raised to the number of unshared vertices.

Step 5 (rigidity at full overlap). A delicate point is the case where a distinct candidate shares its entire added vertex set with the planted layer; such a term would not decay and would break the bound. The paper rules this out through a uniqueness property: any copy of the layer that extends the same previous layer and adds exactly the same vertices must have the same edges, hence must equal the planted layer. This is proved from the edge-maximality of the onion layer, since a distinct full-overlap copy would furnish a subgraph on the same vertices with strictly more edges, contradicting maximality. Consequently the full-overlap term is absent and the summation over overlaps runs only up to one less than the full count. (The paper stresses that this rigidity holds for onion layers but not for the whole template, which is why peeling along layers, rather than a global search, is needed.)

Step 6 (summation and threshold). Combining the geometric per-candidate decay with the counting bound yields, for each layer, a geometric series in the number of unshared vertices whose ratio is the number of added vertices times the ambient size times the background probability raised to the layer's relative density. This series is small once that ratio is below a small target divided by the number of layers. Because the number of layers is at most quadratic in the number of vertices and the added-vertex count is at most the ambient size, the requirement reduces to the relative density of each layer exceeding a constant multiple of the logarithm of the ambient size divided by the Bernoulli Kullback–Leibler divergence. Since the minimal maximum subgraph density equals the smallest layer relative density, the hypothesized lower bound on it enforces this for every layer simultaneously.

Step 7 (conclusion). Summing the per-layer bounds over the layers keeps the total below any prescribed level for all sufficiently large ambient sizes, uniformly over the hidden copy. Hence the worst-case error tends to zero, establishing exact recovery. The case where the inner probability is strictly below one is handled by the same scheme with a more careful moment computation of the appearance probabilities, again exploiting the layer maximality, yielding the larger universal constant.
nl_theorem: There exists a universal constant C > 0 such that the following holds. For each n let Γ_n be a finite undirected simple graph on the ambient vertex set {0,…,n−1}, whose planted-template vertex set is its support (so the template has no isolated vertices, may omit ambient labels, and has at most n vertices). Let p, q : ℕ → ℝ be edge-probability sequences with 0 < q_n < p_n ≤ 1 for every n, both of which are dense probability sequences (each eventually bounded below by a strictly positive constant). Let estimate be any graph estimator that implements likelihood peeling: for every n there is one onion decomposition of Γ_n, chosen independently of the observation, along which, starting from the empty graph, each stage's estimate is a copy of the next onion layer that contains the previous estimate and maximizes the peeling score among all such extensions. Assume Γ_n is onion-full-overlap rigid for all sufficiently large n. Then for every ε > 0, if for all sufficiently large n the minimal maximum subgraph density of Γ_n is at least C · (1 + ε) · log n / d_KL(p_n ‖ q_n), where d_KL is the Bernoulli Kullback–Leibler divergence, then estimate achieves exact recovery of the hidden copy of Γ_n in the planted-subgraph model, meaning its worst-case recovery error tends to zero as n → ∞.

core_claim: For a smooth convex finite-sum objective minimized by random reshuffling with small stepsizes, the expected suboptimality of the weighted average iterate satisfies an explicit convergence bound combining an initial-distance term and a variance term.

metainfo.paper: Random Reshuffling Dominates Stochastic Gradient Descent

nl_proof:
The paper obtains the stated bound by proving two separate convergence estimates for the weighted average iterate and then taking, term by term, whichever is stronger; each estimate holds under the stepsize restriction that every stepsize is at most one sixth of the reciprocal of the maximum smoothness, so both apply simultaneously.

First estimate (never worse than plain stochastic gradient descent). This part shows that the expected suboptimality is at most a distance term of the form (initial squared distance)/(2·n·H_K) plus a variance term equal to 51 times (sum of squared stepsizes)/(H_K) times the gradient variance at the minimizer, where H_K is the cumulative stepsize. It rests on two core lemmas. The first core lemma exploits the exchangeability of a uniformly random permutation: by decomposing the average objective at an inner iterate into its per-component pieces and using that, conditioned on the earlier draws, the component processed at position i is exchangeable with any later one, the expected gap between the full objective and the currently sampled component objective is rewritten as an average, over earlier positions j, of expected differences between the component objective evaluated at a coupled "virtual" trajectory (the one obtained by swapping positions i and j in the permutation) and at the true trajectory. The second core lemma bounds the distance between this virtual trajectory and the true one: because the two runs coincide before the swap and thereafter apply the same component gradients, co-coercivity (equivalently nonexpansiveness of a smooth convex gradient step under stepsize at most twice the reciprocal of the maximum smoothness) makes each subsequent step nonexpansive, so the whole discrepancy is controlled by a single stepsize times the difference of the two swapped gradients at the shared point. Combining these, together with smoothness and elementary inequalities, yields an intermediate inequality bounding the expected full objective at an inner iterate by the expected sampled component objective plus a stepsize times the squared gradient at that iterate plus a coefficient of order stepsize over n times the sum of earlier squared gradients; the crucial factor 1/n keeps the accumulated within-epoch error controlled. A standard per-iterate descent identity, obtained by expanding the squared distance to the minimizer along the update, expresses each sampled component gap as a telescoping squared-distance difference plus a stepsize-weighted squared gradient minus a Bregman divergence. Summing the descent identity over an epoch and taking expectations, summing the intermediate inequality over the epoch, and adding the two, one arranges that the squared-gradient contributions are converted, via co-coercivity, into Bregman divergences (absorbed by the negative Bregman terms because the stepsize is small enough) plus a residual proportional to the gradient variance at the minimizer. Multiplying by the epoch stepsize, summing over epochs so that the distance terms telescope, dividing by n·H_K, and finally applying convexity of the objective through Jensen's inequality to pass from the average of iterates to the objective at the weighted average iterate, produces the first estimate.

Second estimate (strictly better under small stepsize). This part shows the expected suboptimality is at most 6·(initial squared distance)/(n·H_K) plus a variance term of the form 8·(sum of cubed stepsizes)·n·(average smoothness)/(H_K) times the gradient variance at the minimizer. Its strategy treats an entire epoch as a single step and compares it with a gradient-descent-like reference. A second virtual sequence is introduced whose updates use the component gradients evaluated at the minimizer; since the full gradient vanishes at the minimizer, this sequence returns exactly to the minimizer at the end of every epoch. A per-epoch descent lemma, proved again through co-coercivity under the stepsize condition, bounds the stepsize-weighted sum over the epoch of the sampled Bregman divergences of the true iterates by a telescoping squared-distance difference plus twice the stepsize-weighted sum of the sampled Bregman divergences of this reference sequence. A second lemma lower-bounds the true progress: using the same exchangeable-permutation identity and virtual-swap stability from the core lemmas, together with co-coercivity and the exact first- and second-moment identities for sampling component gradients without replacement (which produce average-smoothness rather than maximum-smoothness constants), it controls the expected full Bregman divergence at each inner iterate by a constant multiple of the expected sampled Bregman divergence, an averaged sum of earlier such terms, and a term of order (squared stepsize)·(average smoothness)·(gradient variance). A residual lemma bounds the expected sum of the reference sequence's sampled Bregman divergences by a quantity of order (squared stepsize)·n²·(average smoothness)·(gradient variance), using smoothness and a bound on the sums of partial gradient prefixes that benefits from the gradient summing to zero at the minimizer. Combining the descent lemma with the residual bound, then combining with the summed second lemma to replace sampled Bregman divergences by true objective gaps, telescoping over epochs, dividing by n·H_K, and applying convexity through Jensen's inequality, gives the second estimate.

Conclusion. Both estimates bound the same expected suboptimality of the weighted average iterate. Bounding the smaller distance coefficient of the first estimate by the coefficient six and the smaller variance coefficient of the second estimate by fifty-one, the two right-hand sides are each dominated by the common expression consisting of six times the initial squared distance divided by n·H_K plus fifty-one times, respectively, the two variance structures times the gradient variance at the minimizer. Since both are valid upper bounds, so is their minimum, which is exactly the claimed inequality with the minimum taken over the two variance terms.
nl_theorem: Let d, n, K be positive natural numbers and work in the Euclidean space of dimension d. Let f_1,...,f_n be real-valued functions on this space, each differentiable and convex, with the gradient of each f_j being L_j-Lipschitz for a constant L_j ≥ 0. Let f be the finite-sum objective f(x) = (1/n) Σ_j f_j(x), let the average smoothness be (1/n) Σ_j L_j, the maximum smoothness be the supremum of the L_j, and the gradient variance at a point be (1/n) Σ_j ‖∇f_j(that point)‖². Let x_⋆ be a global minimizer of f and let x_0 be a fixed point. On a probability space, suppose the permutations (π_k) for k < K form an independent uniform random reshuffling of the index set, that the epoch starts and current permutations satisfy the epoch-conditioning contract (each epoch's starting iterate depends only on the earlier permutations, and each current permutation is conditionally uniform on every atom of the prior-permutation history), that the stepsizes satisfy 0 < η_k ≤ 1/(6·(maximum smoothness)) for every k < K, and that the iterates (x_k^i) are generated from x_0 by the Shuffling-SGD recursion. Let H_K = Σ_{k<K} η_k be the cumulative stepsize and let the weighted average iterate be x̄_K = ((n·H_K)^{-1}) Σ_{k<K} Σ_{i<n} η_k · x_k^i. Then the expectation of f(x̄_K) − f(x_⋆) is at most 6‖x_0 − x_⋆‖² / (n·H_K) plus 51 times the minimum of (Σ_{k<K} η_k²)/H_K and (Σ_{k<K} η_k³)·n·(average smoothness)/H_K, times the gradient variance at x_⋆.

core_claim: A binary linear relaxed locally correctable code with perfect completeness and soundness below a query-dependent threshold is a genuine locally correctable code with the same number of queries.

metainfo.paper: Relaxed vs. Full Local Decodability with Few Queries: Equivalence and Separations for Linear Codes

nl_proof:
The argument follows the paper's soundness-threshold route, treating the relaxed locally correctable case by running the relaxed locally decodable analysis separately for each codeword coordinate.

Reduction to a smooth corrector. The paper first recalls the classical observation that it suffices to build, for each queried codeword coordinate, a corrector that makes at most q queries, is perfectly correct on genuine codewords, and is smooth, meaning no fixed coordinate is queried with probability more than 1/(ηn). Any η-smooth corrector is automatically a locally correctable code with radius ηε and error ε: if fewer than ηεn coordinates are corrupted, a union bound over the smoothness bound shows that with probability at least 1−ε none of the queries hits a corrupted coordinate, and then perfect completeness forces the correct output. So the task reduces to extracting a smooth corrector of smoothness parameter η = αδ/q, which yields exactly the claimed radius αδε/q.

Handling adaptivity and canonical form. Because the relaxed corrector may be adaptive but has perfect completeness, one may first put it into a canonical nonadaptive form: an adaptive perfectly complete linear relaxed corrector can be converted, without loss in soundness, into a nonadaptive one that behaves canonically. Canonically, when the corrector queries a set Q of size at most q and reads the values there, it checks whether these values are consistent with some codeword; if not it may safely output the abort symbol, and if so perfect completeness and linearity force it to output the value of the target coordinate determined by the local view. By linearity, consistency with a codeword and the value of the target coordinate are governed by the rows of the generator matrix indexed by Q and by the target functional.

Per-coordinate structure. Fix a codeword coordinate u and its induced linear functional on messages. If this functional is zero, the coordinate is identically zero on all codewords, so the trivial corrector that always outputs zero is perfectly complete and has error zero, hence trivially meets the requirement. Otherwise, the functional is nonzero and one analyzes the canonical corrector as a query distribution over sets of size at most q.

Heavy/light split and smooth/nonsmooth decomposition. Partition the coordinates into a heavy set H, those queried with probability more than q/(δn), and the rest. Summing query probabilities shows the heavy set has size at most δn. Call a query set smoothable if the target functional already lies in the span of the generator rows indexed by its light coordinates, so the target value can be recovered from light coordinates alone. Conditioning the query distribution on being smoothable, and querying only the light part, defines a smooth corrector; conditioning on the complementary event defines the nonsmooth corrector. The original corrector runs the smooth branch with some probability p and the nonsmooth branch with probability 1−p.

The fooling lemma. The heart of the proof is a lemma showing the nonsmooth corrector has relaxed soundness error at least s(q) = 2^{−⌊q/2⌋}. Fix any codeword and any query set that is not smoothable, so the target functional is not spanned by the light rows. Build a corrupted word that agrees with the codeword off the heavy set and, on the heavy coordinates, takes the values of a uniformly random codeword whose target value is flipped. Since only heavy coordinates are altered, the word lies within relative Hamming radius δ. Using linearity, whether such a word fools a fixed query set into looking like a codeword with the wrong target value is governed by two nested spaces of local parity checks V ⊆ W, whose quotient dimension is at most the smaller of the number of heavy and of light queries in that set, and hence at most ⌊q/2⌋. The random construction satisfies the required constraints with probability at least 2^{−dim(W/V)} ≥ 2^{−⌊q/2⌋} = s(q). Averaging over the query distribution produces a single corrupted word on which the nonsmooth corrector outputs a wrong, non-abort value with probability at least s(q).

Lower bounding the smooth mass. Combining this with the code's assumed relaxed soundness gives (1−α)s(q) ≥ s ≥ (1−p)·s(q), so p ≥ α: the smooth branch carries at least an α fraction of the mass. Consequently, conditioning on smoothability increases each light coordinate's query probability by a factor at most 1/p ≤ 1/α, so the smooth corrector queries any coordinate with probability at most q/(αδn); it is (αδ/q)-smooth and perfectly complete.

Assembling the correctable code. Applying the smooth-corrector-to-LCC reduction to each coordinate's smooth corrector, and combining the per-coordinate correctors (trivial ones for zero coordinates and smooth ones otherwise), yields a q-query corrector with perfect completeness and error at most ε on all words within relative Hamming distance αδε/q of a codeword, which is exactly a locally correctable code with the stated parameters.
nl_theorem: Let q, k, n be natural numbers and let delta, s, alpha be real numbers with 0 ≤ delta ≤ 1, 0 ≤ s ≤ 1, and 0 ≤ alpha ≤ 1. Let C be a binary linear code from messages of length k to codewords of length n. Define the binary soundness threshold s(q) = 1 / 2^(q/2), using natural-number division in the exponent. Suppose C is a (q, delta, 1, s)-relaxed locally correctable code with a possibly adaptive decoder (perfect completeness, and for every received word within relative Hamming distance delta of a codeword the decoder returns neither the requested codeword symbol nor the abort symbol with probability at most s), and suppose s ≤ (1 - alpha)·s(q). Then for every real epsilon > 0, the code C is a (q, alpha·delta·epsilon/q, 1, epsilon)-locally correctable code: there is a possibly adaptive q-query decoder with perfect completeness whose decoding error is at most epsilon on every word within relative Hamming distance alpha·delta·epsilon/q of a codeword.

core_claim: A single two-stream learner, fixed before seeing the target and distributions, achieves the desired accuracy with high probability using a sample size obeying a polylogarithmic bound at the stated principal scale.

metainfo.paper: Smoothed Analysis of Learning from Positive Samples

nl_proof:
The argument exhibits one explicit learner, depending only on the class, its VC dimension, the smoothness parameters, and the accuracy and confidence targets, and shows it meets the required guarantee uniformly over all admissible targets and measures. The universal polylogarithmic constant and exponent come from the concentration bound used below, and the promised principal scale is exactly the non-logarithmic part of the chosen sample size.

The building block is a constrained empirical program, called pessimistic empirical risk minimization: given a batch of positive covariates and a batch of reference covariates, select the hypothesis in the class covering the fewest reference points subject to covering all the positive points (tolerance zero). The learner runs this program a bounded number of times in an iterative, nested fashion. Set the number of rounds to the reciprocal of (sigma·epsilon) raised to the power q. In round one the reference batch is the full batch; in each later round one discards every reference point not lying in the intersection of the previously selected hypotheses, and re-solves the program on the surviving reference points while still requiring all positive points to be covered. The output is the intersection of all the hypotheses produced across rounds; this is an improper hypothesis, which is necessary because proper learning is impossible here. The sample size for both batches is chosen as the VC dimension plus the logarithm of the inverse confidence, divided by (epsilon·sigma) to the power 2q, up to polylogarithmic factors.

Correctness splits into controlling false negatives and false positives.

For false negatives, each selected hypothesis covers all positive points, so by feasibility its complement contains no positive sample. Applying a second-order (small-error) uniform convergence bound to the class together with its complements, and using that the chosen sample size makes the deviation term of order (sigma·epsilon) to the power 2q, one concludes that the positive-conditional mass of the complement of each selected hypothesis is at most (sigma·epsilon) to the power 2q. Because the positive-conditional law is the target law restricted and renormalized to the positive region, the target mass of the positive region missed by any single hypothesis is bounded by that same quantity. Summing over the rounds, whose number is the reciprocal of (sigma·epsilon) to the power q, the target mass of the positive region missed by the final intersection is at most order (sigma·epsilon) to the power q, hence at most order epsilon.

For false positives, consider, for each round, the set of surviving reference points that lie in all earlier hypotheses but are excluded by the current one. Optimality of each solved program forces the sizes of these successive sets to be non-increasing, and the sets are pairwise disjoint because a discarded reference point never returns; therefore their total size is at most the batch size, and the last one has size at most the batch size divided by the number of rounds, i.e. at most (sigma·epsilon) to the power q times the batch size. Since the true positive region is itself feasible in the final round, optimality shows the empirical reference mass of the final intersection outside the positive region is likewise at most (sigma·epsilon) to the power q. A second-order uniform convergence bound applied to the class of bounded intersections (whose VC dimension grows by a factor of order the number of rounds, up to logarithms) transfers this to the reference measure: the reference mass of the intersection outside the positive region is of order (sigma·epsilon) to the power q. The generalized smoothness hypothesis, which bounds target mass by the inverse of sigma times the q-th root of reference mass, then yields target mass at most order epsilon for the false-positive region.

Combining the two parts by additivity, the total target misclassification error of the output is at most order epsilon; rescaling epsilon by a constant and taking a union bound over the two failure events (each of confidence half the budget) gives error at most epsilon with probability at least one minus the confidence budget. Independence of the two batches identifies their joint law with the product of the two product measures, and the finite, data-measurable construction makes the output hypotheses and the success event measurable, which is exactly the stated guarantee. Choosing the universal constant and exponent from the uniform convergence bound completes the proof.
nl_theorem: Let X be a standard Borel space and let H be a class of measurable Boolean hypotheses whose numerical VC dimension equals d and which admits a jointly measurable empirical-risk selector. Fix smoothness parameters with 0 < sigma ≤ 1 and q ≥ 1. Then there exist a constant C > 0 and a natural number k, not depending on the accuracy, confidence, target, or data-generating measures, such that for every epsilon, delta in the open interval (0, 1/2) there are a sample size n and a single two-stream learner A (a map taking an ordered batch of n positive covariates and an ordered batch of n reference covariates to a Boolean hypothesis) for which n satisfies the polylogarithmic sample bound n ≤ C · scale · (log(e + scale))^k at the principal scale scale = (d + log(1/delta)) / (epsilon·sigma)^(2q), and, uniformly over every target hstar in H and every triple of probability measures Dtrue, Ptrue, Dref on X such that Ptrue is the positive conditional law of Dtrue given hstar = 1 and Dtrue is (sigma, q)-smooth with respect to Dref, the learner A meets the (epsilon, delta) two-stream guarantee: its output hypotheses are measurable, the associated success event is measurable, and with probability at least 1 - delta (under the product of the n-fold products of Ptrue and Dref) the output hypothesis has Dtrue-misclassification error at most epsilon.

core_claim: There is a universal constant such that, under conditionally sub-Gaussian noise and bounded-density smooth predictable covariates, the self-normalized energy of the cumulative score obeys the stated high-probability bound at every confidence level.

metainfo.paper: Self-Normalized Martingales and Uniform Regret Bounds for Linear Regression

nl_proof:
The paper obtains the high-probability bound by combining a deterministic regret decomposition with two probabilistic estimates, one for the noise term and one for the covariate term, and then taking a union bound.

The starting point is an exact algebraic identity. For any sequence of predictions produced online, completing the square shows that the self-normalized energy of the cumulative score equals the square-loss regret of those predictions against the best linear comparator plus a residual sum of the form: the sum over rounds of twice the prediction times the outcome minus the squared prediction. The paper applies this identity with no regularization matrix, so the left side is exactly the self-normalized energy against the pseudoinverse of the Gram matrix. The predictions are supplied by the unregularized Vovk–Azoury–Warmuth forecaster.

The residual sum is controlled stochastically using conditional sub-Gaussianity. The key observation is that the exponential of one over twice the noise variance times the running residual sum is a nonnegative supermartingale with expectation at most one: at each round, since the current prediction is measurable with respect to the past, plugging the sub-Gaussian moment-generating bound with the appropriately scaled parameter makes the one-step conditional expectation at most one. Ville's maximal inequality for nonnegative supermartingales then shows that, with probability at least one minus half the confidence parameter, the residual sum is bounded by twice the noise variance times the logarithm of two over that parameter.

The regret term is controlled by a smoothed-analysis argument for the forecaster. First, a deterministic potential-style analysis reduces the regret to the sum over rounds of the leverage scores, each score being the covariate quadratic form against the pseudoinverse of the current prefix Gram matrix; the reduction uses a rank-one update inequality for pseudoinverses (valid because the score vector lies in the range of the Gram matrix) applied recursively and telescoped, and its sub-Gaussian variant introduces the noise scale together with a logarithmic confidence term via a further exponential-moment argument and Markov's inequality.

It then remains to bound the sum of leverage scores, which without further assumptions can be linear in the horizon. The paper does this in three combinatorial steps. Since each leverage score lies between zero and one, a layer-cake identity bounds the leverage sum by one plus a dyadic sum over thresholds of the form two to the negative power, each weighted by the length of the longest subsequence whose successive prefix leverages all exceed that threshold. Next, the smoothness assumption is used through a coupling result: because each conditional covariate law has density bounded by the smoothness constant relative to the fixed base measure, rejection sampling couples the covariate process, with high probability, to an order-preserving subsequence of a bank of independent base-measure samples of total size the horizon times a per-round budget of order the smoothness constant times a logarithmic factor. On the coupling success event the relevant subsequence lengths for the actual covariates are dominated by those of the independent sample. Finally, the paper shows high-leverage subsequences are rare for independent samples: revealing a selected block in reverse order, the conditional average leverage of the remaining vectors is the normalized trace of a Gram matrix times its pseudoinverse, which is at most the dimension divided by the number of remaining vectors; Markov's inequality at each reverse step, multiplied along the block and summed over all index subsets using standard binomial and factorial estimates, shows that with high probability the longest bad subsequence at threshold r has length of order the square root of (sample size times dimension over r) plus a logarithmic term. Substituting these length bounds into the dyadic sum, summing the resulting geometric series, and using that the horizon times two to the negative number of levels is bounded, yields that with probability at least one minus half the confidence parameter the leverage sum is at most an absolute constant times the square root of (dimension times smoothness constant times horizon times the logarithm of twice the horizon over the parameter) plus the logarithm of two over the parameter.

Combining the deterministic identity with the two high-probability estimates and applying a union bound over their two failure events, both hold simultaneously with probability at least one minus the confidence parameter. On that event the self-normalized energy is bounded by the regret plus the residual term, hence by an absolute constant times the noise variance multiplied by the square root of (dimension times smoothness constant times horizon times the logarithm of twice the horizon over the parameter) plus the logarithm of two over the parameter, which is the claimed rate; adjusting the various numerical constants inside the logarithms into the single universal constant, using that the horizon, dimension, and smoothness constant are at least one and the confidence parameter is in the open unit interval, gives the stated conclusion for one absolute constant valid across all admissible instances.
nl_theorem: There exists an absolute constant C greater than zero with the following property. For every positive horizon T and dimension d, every probability space with a round filtration and an auxiliary filtration, every predictable covariate process X taking values in R^d that is measurable at each round, every real response process Y, every family of probability kernels P representing the conditional laws, every base probability measure on R^d, every choice of matrix-valued map V-dagger, and all real parameters sigma, Ccov, delta with T,d positive, sigma positive, Ccov at least 1, and delta in (0,1): if the auxiliary filtration is generated by the earlier covariates and is contained in the round filtration, X is predictable, Y is conditionally sub-Gaussian with parameter sigma, P is the conditional law of X, the kernels are Ccov-smooth relative to the base measure, and V-dagger is pointwise a Moore–Penrose inverse of the empirical Gram matrix, then the probability that the self-normalized energy of the cumulative score S_T with respect to V-dagger is at most C times sigma squared multiplied by the sum of the square root of d·Ccov·T·log(2T/delta) and log(2/delta) is at least 1 − delta.

core_claim: Every randomized static retrieval scheme within the polynomial parameter regime, with expected query cost at most a given bound, must use at least an explicit number of memory bits.

metainfo.paper: Static Retrieval Revisited: To Optimality and Beyond

nl_proof:
The paper proves this space lower bound by contradiction, through the analysis of a one-way communication game; the constant C plays the role of a sufficiently large fixed constant depending only on the polynomial exponents.

First, the argument reduces to the interesting parameter range. Writing v for log₂ V, if the quantity wt/v is either below 1 or above a small constant times ln n, then the exponential term n·exp(−C·wt/v) drops below 1, its floor is 0, and the claimed bound collapses to the classical information-theoretic requirement of nv bits, which every retrieval structure satisfies. So one only needs the regime where wt/v lies between 1 and a small multiple of ln n.

Next comes the communication setup. Suppose for contradiction that a scheme stores n key-value pairs using only m words of w bits with mw strictly below nv + ⌊n·exp(−C·wt/v)⌋; write the space as nv + R with R at most n·exp(−C·wt/v). Alice holds a key set X of size n together with the associated values A, and wants to transmit both to Bob; the two parties share the public random tape. A standard counting bound shows that any correct protocol must transmit at least log C(U,n) + nv bits in expectation. The goal is to use the hypothesized space-efficient structure to build a protocol beating this bound, which is the contradiction.

The protocol is organized around a probe-count control property. By Markov's inequality, with probability at least 4/5 over the random tape the encoded structure has average query time at most ten times t both over the stored keys and over the whole universe. Alice first sends one bit stating whether this property holds; if it fails she simply sends X and A outright and stops, an event that is rare enough to be harmless in expectation.

Several notions are introduced for the good case. A query is called slow if it probes at least a threshold number t_slow = t·exp((C/2)·wt/v) of cells, and fast otherwise; truncated queries run each query only until this many probes, returning a symbol for slow queries so that worst-case time guarantees hold. For a set S of keys, Probe(S) is the set of cells touched by the truncated queries on S, and f(S) its size. The footprint Foot(S) lists, in increasing key order, the contents of the newly probed cells; given S and Foot(S), Bob can replay every truncated query and recover its answer, and this encoding is prefix-free. The number of cells is M = (nv + R)/w. A threshold T = (nv − (10t/t_slow)·nv − 100)/w is chosen to represent roughly the number of cells needed to encode the fast-query answers. Alice then sends one further bit indicating whether f(X) is below T.

In the first case, f(X) < T, Alice compresses the values by transmitting X with about log C(U,n) bits, then the footprint Foot(X) using f(X)·w bits, and finally the answers to the few slow queries, of which the property guarantees at most (10t/t_slow)·n. Bob reconstructs the fast-query answers from the footprint and receives the slow answers explicitly. Summing these costs and using the definition of T shows the whole message is below log C(U,n) + nv − 10 bits.

In the second case, f(X) ≥ T, the key set itself is compressed. Consider a random set S in which each universe element is kept independently with probability n/U. The function f is a coverage function, hence monotone and submodular, with marginal increments bounded by t_slow. Its expectation is bounded by M·(1 − exp(−20wt/v)) using that each cell is probed by a limited total number of queries together with Jensen's inequality, while the choice of T together with R ≤ n·exp(−C·wt/v) gives T at least M·(1 − exp(−(C/3)·wt/v)). This gap lets a concentration inequality for monotone submodular functions of independent inputs bound the probability that f(S) ≥ T by exp(−n·exp(−(2C/3)·wt/v)). Consequently Alice can send the memory configuration D using nv + R bits and then describe X by an entropy encoding conditioned on the rare event f(S) ≥ T. Since a Stirling estimate gives −log Pr[S = X] equal to log C(U,n) up to O(log n), conditioning on this rare event saves more than n·exp(−(3C/4)·wt/v) bits, again pushing the total below log C(U,n) + nv − 10. After receiving D and X, Bob simulates the untruncated queries to recover the values A.

Finally the expected cost is tallied. When the control property fails, which happens with probability at most 1/5, Alice pays a little more than log C(U,n) + nv bits; when it holds she saves at least ten bits. Weighting these outcomes, the overall expected communication is strictly less than log C(U,n) + nv bits, contradicting the counting lower bound. Hence no scheme in the stated parameter regime can use fewer than nv + ⌊n·exp(−C·wt/v)⌋ bits, which is exactly the asserted inequality.
nl_theorem: Fix natural number exponents a and b. Then there exists a positive real constant C such that for all natural numbers n, U, V, w, t, m and every randomized static retrieval scheme storing n key-value pairs with keys from Fin U and values in Fin V using m cells of w bits, the following holds: if the parameters satisfy 2n ≤ U, U ≤ n^a, V ≤ n^b, 1 < V, and log₂ V ≤ w, and if for every stored instance and every query key belonging to it the probe-count function over the fair random tape is integrable with expectation at most t, then n·log₂ V + ⌊n·exp(−C·(w·t / log₂ V))⌋ ≤ m·w.

core_claim: For every fixed positive number of identical machines, precedence-constrained unit-job makespan scheduling admits a uniform optimal algorithm whose certified running time obeys the stated subexponential bound.

metainfo.paper: A Subexponential Time Algorithm for Makespan Scheduling of Unit Jobs with Precedence Constraints

nl_proof:
The paper establishes the claim by exhibiting one concrete recursive procedure, fixing the number of machines m, and proving both that the procedure always returns a schedule of minimum makespan and that its number of elementary operations obeys the stated envelope for all sufficiently large numbers of jobs.

The argument rests on a structural decomposition of optimal schedules. Working with the precedence relation as a directed acyclic graph that equals its transitive closure, the authors introduce the notion of a proper separator: a distinguished sequence of individual timeslots that carves an optimal schedule into blocks, arranged so that the sinks of the graph appear only inside these separator slots and the final block, and so that the block of jobs sitting between two consecutive separator slots is completely determined by those two slots (each of size at most m). They prove that for any precedence graph with at most m sources, some minimum-makespan schedule admits such a proper separator. This is shown by starting from any optimal schedule and running a conflict-resolution process that repeatedly moves a non-sink job earlier whenever its predecessors are already finished and its target timeslot has spare non-sink capacity, swapping out a sink if necessary. Each move pushes a non-sink earlier and only sinks later, so the process terminates without increasing the makespan, and the resulting conflict-free schedule is verified to satisfy the three separator conditions.

Next the authors give a reconstruction routine that, given the optimal makespans of all the intermediate blocks (the subschedules, indexed by pairs of small antichains related by the successor relation), computes the minimum makespan of the whole graph. This routine uses dynamic programming over a table indexed by a candidate separator slot together with the number of sinks scheduled so far; the key point, proved from the separator properties, is that the set of non-sink jobs already placed is fully determined by the current separator slot, while sinks—being interchangeable because they have no successors—need only be tracked by their count. A recurrence links a table entry to an earlier separator slot plus one intermediate block plus one timeslot, and its correctness is proved by a two-sided induction over consecutive separator slots and the number of sinks. This routine runs in time polynomial times a binomial factor counting slot pairs of combined size at most 2m.

These two ingredients drive the actual algorithm, which is organized around intervals of the graph delimited by two antichains. The main subroutine computes the minimum makespan of an interval by iterating over all admissible pairs of small antichains that could serve as consecutive separator slots, recursively solving the associated smaller interval subproblem (whose new sinks are defined explicitly), and then combining the recursive answers with the reconstruction routine. Correctness follows because the recursion collects exactly the subschedules required by the reconstruction routine, a fact proved by an interval identity showing that the recursive subproblem's job set matches the intended intermediate block.

Finally the running time is bounded by analyzing the tree of recursive calls, using a lookup table so that each distinct subproblem is expanded only once. Choosing the threshold parameter equal to the floor of the square root of n times m, the calls are split at subproblems whose sink-boundary is small: the number of such distinguished subproblems is controlled by a binomial coefficient because a slot pair is recovered from its union, while every subtree between them has bounded branching and height at most on the order of n divided by the threshold, since each recursive step removes at least a threshold's worth of jobs. Multiplying these bounds, invoking the cost of the reconstruction routine per node, and estimating the resulting binomial coefficients through the inequality relating them to powers yields a total bound of the form one plus n over m raised to a constant times the square root of n times m. Bundling this uniform procedure, its returned optimal schedule, and its certified operation count produces the required algorithm together with the subexponential running-time guarantee.
nl_theorem: Fix a positive natural number m of identical machines. A precedence instance on n jobs is an irreflexive, transitive decidable relation on the n jobs. A unit-job schedule on m machines assigns each job to one of makespan-many time slots so that every slot receives at most m jobs; it respects a precedence instance when every precedence pair maps to a strictly earlier slot, and it is optimal when it respects the instance and its makespan is at most that of every other precedence-respecting schedule on m machines. A makespan scheduling algorithm bundles, uniformly in n and in each precedence instance, a returned schedule together with a certified running-time count, subject to the returned schedule always being optimal. Then there exists such an algorithm A whose running time is subexponential in the sense that there is a real constant C greater than 0 with the property that, for all sufficiently large n and every precedence instance on n jobs, the certified operation count is at most (1 + n/m) raised to the power C·√(n·m).

core_claim: For any full-feedback constrained bandit run of the described mirror-descent algorithm and any failure probability below one, the cumulative regret stays within the stated logarithmic bound with probability at least one minus three times that probability.

metainfo.paper: Truly Adapting to Adversarial Constraints in Constrained MABs

nl_proof:
The paper proves the bound in several linked steps, working with the expected loss and constraint vectors and only afterwards transferring to the realized quantities.

First, it establishes that the optimistic per-round decision set — the set of simplex points whose estimated constraint value, shifted down by the known confidence width, is nonpositive — is nonempty at every round. This follows from the Slater-type feasibility assumption (positivity of the feasibility parameter): any strategy that is feasible on average survives the optimistic lower-shift with high probability, by an Azuma-type concentration estimate for the empirical constraint means.

Second, it locates two reference strategies inside or near these sets. Using the concentration bound that controls the distance between the empirical constraint estimate and the average of the mean constraint vectors (whose slack term splits into a computable statistical width and an unknown corruption part of order C over the elapsed rounds), the paper shows that the offline optimal solution satisfies the optimistic constraint up to roughly 2C over the elapsed round count, while a strictly feasible strategy attains a margin of at least the feasibility parameter below zero. Consequently the convex combination that assigns weight equal to the feasibility parameter divided by that parameter plus twice C over the elapsed rounds to the optimum, and the remaining weight to the strictly feasible strategy, is exactly feasible for the optimistic set and hence belongs to it at that round. Because these mixing weights are nondecreasing in time, each such combination remains admissible in all later sets.

Third, the paper controls the tracking cost of the mirror-descent iterates against a benchmark that may change across rounds. It proves a switching-regret guarantee for entropic online mirror descent with the fixed-share update: partitioning the horizon into a small number of phases and holding the benchmark fixed within each phase, the regret is bounded by a term proportional to the number of phases times the reciprocal learning rate plus the log of the state count over the rate, plus the rate times the horizon. This is obtained by telescoping the Bregman (relative-entropy) divergences within each phase, using that the projected iterate only decreases the divergence to any point of the set, the fixed-share mixing to bound the phase-boundary divergence jump by the logarithm of the horizon and arm count, and the elementary inequality that the exponential of a nonpositive argument is at most one minus it plus its square to control the stability term.

Fourth, the phases are chosen by a doubling schedule: the benchmark is refreshed only when the round index doubles, giving on the order of the base-two logarithm of the horizon phases, and inside each phase the fixed benchmark is the admissible convex combination described above. Decomposing the regret of the iterates against the true offline optimum by inserting and subtracting the phase benchmark, the switching-regret term supplies the first contribution, while the residual measures the loss gap between each phase benchmark and the optimum. Since losses lie in the unit interval, that residual is at most the sum over rounds of one minus the mixing weight; summing the geometric doubling contributions of the corruption-dependent weights telescopes to at most twice C divided by the feasibility parameter, times the base-two logarithm of the horizon.

Setting the learning rate to the square root of the log of the arm-round product divided by the horizon balances the two switching-regret terms, yielding, with probability at least one minus the failure parameter, that the gap between the iterates' cumulative expected loss and the optimum is at most four times the log-of-horizon factor times the square root of the horizon times the log of the arm-round product, plus twice C over the feasibility parameter times that log factor.

Finally, the paper converts this bound on expected quantities into a bound on the actually incurred regret. Two more Azuma–Hoeffding concentration inequalities control the deviation between the cumulative realized loss of the played arms and the cumulative expected loss of the strategies, and between the cumulative sampled and mean losses evaluated at the optimum; each contributes a term of the form the square root of the horizon times the log of the arm-round count over the failure parameter. A union bound over these two events and the earlier high-probability event gives overall probability at least one minus three times the failure parameter, and adding the statistical terms produces the final bound consisting of the mirror-descent term, the corruption term scaled by the feasibility parameter, and the concentration term.
nl_theorem: Consider a run of the full-feedback constrained multi-armed bandit algorithm (Constrained Online Mirror Descent with Fixed Share), packaged with horizon T > 0, K > 0 arms, m > 0 constraints, a probability space carrying loss and constraint processes with values in [0,1] and [-1,1], their conditional means with respect to a history filtration recording all strictly earlier realized losses, constraints, and plays, played actions sampled from simplex strategies produced by the prescribed entropic update with learning rates η = ζ = √(ln(KT)/T) and mixing coefficient γ = 1/T, nonnegative dual iterates bounded in [0,1], an offline optimal feasible benchmark defining OPT, the regret random variable R(ω) = (Σ_{t<T} ℓ_t(ω)(a_t(ω))) − OPT, a corruption level C ≥ 0, and a Slater feasibility parameter ρ with 0 < ρ ≤ 1. Then for every real δ with 0 < δ < 1, the probability of the set of outcomes ω for which R(ω) ≤ 4 log₂(T) √(T ln(KT)) + (2C/ρ) log₂(T) + 4 √(T ln(TK/δ)) is at least 1 − 3δ.

core_claim: Under two-sided conversation calibration in the one-dimensional agreement setting, when the effective gain is positive, most days reach agreement within a bounded number of rounds while squared error improves linearly each round.

metainfo.paper: Tractable Agreement Protocols

nl_proof:
The paper proves the two conclusions together by tracking, for each conversation round, the squared error of the (bucketed) prediction sequence made at that round over all days whose conversation reaches it, and using that squared error as a potential function.

Intuition and case structure. For any round, either most conversations that reach it already satisfy the closeness condition (so they stop, shrinking the population of surviving days), or most predictions at that round differ from the previous round's prediction by at least the tolerance. The argument handles both possibilities uniformly, without splitting into cases, by showing that surviving disagreement forces a quantitative drop in squared error.
