Workhorse decrease for perfect calibration. The core lemma assumes a party's round-k predictions are perfectly conversation-calibrated with respect to the bucketing of the other party's previous-round prediction, and shows the squared error at round k is at most the squared error of the other party's round-(k-1) predictions, decreased by (tolerance minus bucket width) squared times the number of days that go on to the next round, plus a small additive term proportional to the bucket width times the horizon. The proof partitions days by the pair (previous-round bucket, current prediction value). On each such block it adds and subtracts the squared deviation from the block's true label mean, so the difference of squared errors becomes a difference of "bias" terms measured against that mean. Perfect calibration makes the current prediction equal to the block mean, collapsing one bias term. A geometric observation then shows that whenever two adjacent-round predictions disagree by at least the tolerance, the discretized previous prediction and the current prediction differ by at least tolerance minus bucket width; summing over exactly the days that proceed to the next round yields the claimed decrease.

From perfect to approximate calibration. Because parties are only close (in aggregate absolute distance) to being perfectly calibrated rather than exactly calibrated, the paper bounds the total distance-to-calibration of a round's predictions by summing the per-bucket calibration-error guarantees; concavity of the error function turns this sum into a single term of the form error(bucket-width times horizon) divided by the bucket width. Since squared error is Lipschitz on the bounded prediction range, small aggregate movement in predictions changes squared error by a controlled amount. This upgrades the perfect-calibration decrease into a decrease that carries an extra additive slack proportional to that calibration-error term, giving a one-round improvement bound for both the human (even rounds) and the model (odd rounds).

Composition and recursion. Chaining the human and model one-round bounds across two consecutive rounds shows the human's round-k squared error is below its round-(k-2) squared error by roughly the disagreement mass times tolerance squared minus the accumulated per-round error. Collecting the bucket-width and calibration terms of both parties into the single quantity denoted here as the accumulated error yields, per two rounds, an improvement of order tolerance-squared times the surviving fraction minus that accumulated error times the horizon. Applying this recursively down to the initial human round, and using that every earlier round with population at least the prescribed fraction of the horizon contributes at least that fraction, gives that the normalized round-r squared error is at most the normalized round-2 squared error minus r times the effective gain (tolerance squared times the fraction minus the accumulated error). A final single application of the one-round bound relates the round-2 human error to the round-1 model error, so the round-r error is also below the model's initial (round-1) error by the same linear-in-r amount; taking the smaller of the two initial baselines yields the stated minimum. This establishes the per-round accuracy-improvement conclusion.

Round bound. For the bound on the number of rounds, the paper uses that squared error is nonnegative and, since labels and predictions lie in the unit range, never exceeds the horizon. Plugging these bounds into the recursive squared-error inequality forces the round index times the effective gain to be at most one; rearranging shows that agreement is reached within a number of rounds bounded by the reciprocal of the effective gain on all but the prescribed fraction of days. Together these two derivations give the round-count guarantee and the accuracy-improvement guarantee stated in the theorem.
nl_theorem: Consider a canonical conversation over a positive number of days, with calibration-error functions for the Human and the Model, bucketing-width functions for each, and tolerances epsilon and delta both in the closed interval from 0 to 1. Assume the Human is conversation-calibrated with its error and width functions, the Model is conversation-calibrated with its error and width functions, and the conversation is an epsilon-agreement run. Let the effective gain be epsilon squared times delta minus the accumulated calibration-and-bucketing error term beta. Then two conclusions hold simultaneously. First, if the effective gain is strictly positive, then there exists a real number K, at most the reciprocal of the effective gain, such that agreement is reached by round K on at least a (1 minus delta) fraction of the days. Second, for every even round k at least 2 whose round subsequence has cardinality at least delta times the horizon, the Human's bucketed round-k squared error divided by the horizon is at most the minimum of the Model's bucketed round-1 squared error divided by the horizon and the Human's bucketed round-2 squared error divided by the horizon, minus k times the effective gain.

core_claim: For separable two-dimensional data with identical labels, large-stepsize gradient descent on logistic loss reaches a stable loss threshold within a bounded transition time, after which the loss decays reciprocally.

metainfo.paper: Tight Bounds for Logistic Regression with Large Stepsize Gradient Descent in Low Dimension

nl_proof:
The paper proves the two conclusions separately: a bound on the transition time τ (which in particular shows that the defining threshold F(w_τ) ≤ 1/(8η) is attained) and a reciprocal decay of the loss after τ. Throughout, the analysis is carried out in the fixed orthonormal frame given by the unit maximum-margin direction w* and an orthogonal unit vector v*, and one tracks the two coordinates ŵ_t = ⟨w_t, w*⟩ and w̃_t = ⟨w_t, v*⟩ of the iterate. Since every datum satisfies ⟨w*, x_i⟩ ≥ γ, the alignment ⟨w_t, x_i⟩ is at least γŵ_t + w̃_t⟨v*, x_i⟩.

Bounding the transition time. The first ingredient is a growth estimate for the margin coordinate: taking the inner product of the gradient-descent update with w* and using ⟨w*, x_i⟩ ≥ γ shows ŵ_t is strictly increasing and that ŵ_{t+1} − ŵ_t ≥ ηγ·G(w_t), where G is the average logistic weight (gradient potential). Evaluating the first step gives ŵ_1 ≥ ηγ/2, and combining with a potential lower bound (if F(w) ≥ 1/(8η) then G(w) ≥ 1/(16η)) yields a linear lower bound on ŵ_t before τ; the stepsize condition η ≥ η_0 guarantees ŵ_t is large enough that a certain threshold λ̃ is dominated.

The core of the argument is a fine-grained study of the oscillations of the orthogonal coordinate. An auxiliary lemma shows that if |w̃_t| ≤ γŵ_t/2 then every alignment is at least γŵ_t/2, which is large enough (again because η ≥ η_0 controls λ̃) to force F(w_t) ≤ 1/(8η). Contrapositively, before transition one has |w̃_t| > γŵ_t/2. Calling an index t an oscillation when the loss exceeds 1/(8η) at t and t+1 and w̃_t changes sign, the paper proves two facts. First, at an oscillation ŵ_{t+1} ≥ (1+γ²)ŵ_t: because the margin-coordinate increment dominates the step length, ŵ_{t+1} − ŵ_t ≥ γ‖w_{t+1} − w_t‖ (equivalently the step length is at most (ŵ_{t+1} − ŵ_t)/γ); the step length in turn is at least the change in the orthogonal coordinate, ‖w_{t+1} − w_t‖ ≥ |w̃_{t+1} − w̃_t|, and since w̃_t and w̃_{t+1} have opposite signs this equals |w̃_{t+1}| + |w̃_t|, which is at least γ(ŵ_{t+1} + ŵ_t)/2 ≥ γŵ_t by the pre-transition bound on the orthogonal coordinate; chaining these gives ŵ_{t+1} − ŵ_t ≥ γ²ŵ_t. Second, since the update size is η·‖∇F‖ ≤ η by 1-Lipschitzness, the same opposite-sign chain forces γŵ_t ≤ η, so an oscillation can only occur while ŵ_t ≤ η/γ.

To control how often oscillations happen, the trajectory between two oscillations is analyzed by splitting the data into those aligned and anti-aligned with the current orthogonal coordinate. A recursion shows that anti-aligned points, whose contributions all have positive pairwise inner product and dominate the aligned points' negligible contributions, have strictly increasing alignment, with quantitative per-step increments. Together with a global bound |w̃_t| ≤ η before τ, this yields that starting from any pre-transition index, within roughly 4n/γ + 192/γ² further steps either transition occurs or a new oscillation happens: first all points become correctly classified within O(n/γ) steps, and then the potential G obeys a contracting recursion driving it below 1/(16η) within O(1/γ²) steps unless an oscillation intervenes. A further lemma extends the multiplicative growth of ŵ_t to every step preceding an oscillation, giving ŵ_{t+1} ≥ (1+γ²/2)ŵ_t there.

Combining these, if oscillations occur at times t_0 < t_1 < …, then ŵ at an oscillation is at least (1+γ²/2)^{t_k−1}·ηγ/2 (repeated multiplicative growth from ŵ_1) and at most η/γ (the oscillation bound), forcing t_k ≤ 1 + 3log(2/γ²)/γ². Hence only finitely many oscillations occur and the last one, t_N, is at most 1 + 3log(2/γ²)/γ². Applying the frequency lemma one step past t_N, no further oscillation is possible, so the process must reach the threshold: τ ≤ t_N + 1 + 4n/γ + 192/γ², which is O(n/γ + log(1/γ)/γ²). This also establishes F(w_τ) ≤ 1/(8η).

Post-transition decay. Once F(w_τ) ≤ 1/(8η), the paper shows by induction that F(w_t) ≤ 1/(8η) persists for all t ≥ τ. The step size ‖w_{t+1}−w_t‖ = η‖∇F(w_t)‖ ≤ ηF(w_t) ≤ 1/8 is small enough to apply a modified descent inequality valid for this objective, F(w') ≤ F(w) + ⟨∇F(w), w'−w⟩ + 4F(w)‖w'−w‖². Substituting the update gives F(w_{t+1}) − F(w_t) ≤ −η(1 − 4ηF(w_t))‖∇F(w_t)‖² ≤ −(η/2)‖∇F(w_t)‖². Because the loss is small, all points are correctly classified, so a lower bound ‖∇F(w)‖ ≥ (γ/2)F(w) applies, yielding the quadratic one-step decrease F(w_{t+1}) − F(w_t) ≤ −(ηγ²/8)F(w_t)². Rewriting this in terms of reciprocals telescopes to 1/F(w_t) ≥ 1/F(w_τ) + (ηγ²/8)(t−τ), whence F(w_t) ≤ 8/(ηγ²(t−τ)) for every t > τ. This gives the stated bound with universal constant C_loss = 8, completing the proof.
nl_theorem: There exist positive universal constants C_tr and C_loss such that the following holds. Let n be a natural number and let x be a family of n points in the two-dimensional Euclidean space that is admissible with maximum margin γ, meaning n > 0, 0 < γ < 1, every point has norm at most one, there is a unit vector w* with ⟨w*, x_i⟩ ≥ γ for all i, and every unit vector w satisfies ⟨w, x_i⟩ ≤ γ for at least one i. Suppose the stepsize satisfies η ≥ max(n, (32/γ²)·log(256/γ²)), and let w be the zero-initialized full-batch gradient-descent orbit for the empirical logistic loss F with stepsize η. Let τ be the transition time, defined as the least natural number t with F(w_t) ≤ 1/(8η). Then F(w_τ) ≤ 1/(8η), and τ ≤ C_tr·(n/γ + log(1/γ)/γ²), and for every integer t > τ, F(w_t) ≤ C_loss / (η·γ²·(t − τ)).

core_claim: A finite connected regular graph whose every edge lies in a triangle keeps strong expansion under any suitably Lipschitz reweighting, giving explicit lower bounds on the even-power walk conductance and the spectral gap.

metainfo.paper: Time-Biased Random Walks and Robustness of Expanders

nl_proof:
The argument proves the two bounds in turn, first controlling the conductance of the combined chain that fuses 2K single steps of the weighted walk, and then transferring this to the spectral gap of the one-step walk. Throughout, the stationary distribution of the combined chain is the same as that of the weighted walk, and the choice K = ⌈2/log(1+ψ)⌉ with σ = exp(1/(2K)) is exactly what makes the local weight comparisons below tie together.

Step 1 (boosting the geometric expansion). Because the graph has vertex expansion at least ψ, any set of at most half the vertices grows by a factor at least 1+ψ when one adds its external neighbours, so iterating shows that the k-ball around any set has size at least the minimum of (1+ψ)^k times the set size and half the vertex count. For k ≥ K this growth factor exceeds e², so balls of radius K essentially multiply small sets by e². A separate two-sided estimate extends the expansion inequality to sets of arbitrary size: every set has external boundary at least (ψ/3) times the smaller of the set and its complement; this is obtained by partitioning the vertices into the set, its boundary, and the rest, applying expansion to whichever of the two sides is small, and using that ψ ≤ 2.

Step 2 (level partition and locality). Vertices are sorted into blocks on which the stationary mass lies in consecutive intervals (1/e^i, 1/e^{i-1}]. The Lipschitz control on adjacent weights, together with the calibrated K and σ, forces the stationary mass to change by at most a factor e across any two vertices within graph distance K. Consequently the K-ball of a level block meets only the neighbouring blocks, so mass in one level can only leak to the immediately adjacent levels.

Step 3 (selecting representative levels). For a fixed target set S of at most half the vertices, one records the levels S occupies and, scanning through them, extracts a family of blocks R_ℓ (unions of consecutive levels) on which the set sizes are genuinely growing; a level is kept while its successor is at least half of e² times the accumulated mass, and a new block begins when sizes start increasing again. The remaining, discarded levels carry geometrically decaying mass. Two accounting lemmas result: the selected part R carries at least a 1/22 fraction of the stationary mass of S, and within each block the top level S_{b_ℓ} carries at least a 1/11 fraction of that block's mass. Both follow from the exponential spacing of stationary values across levels together with the growth conditions defining the blocks.

Step 4 (outflow from each block). For each selected block, one shows its 2K-neighbourhood contains, outside S, at least a third of the block's size. When e² times the block is below half the vertex count this comes from the boosted ball growth minus the two neighbouring levels that could lie inside S; otherwise the neighbourhood already reaches half the graph, and one either iterates the two-sided expansion estimate to push it past a fixed fraction of the graph or observes the neighbourhood is already so large that removing S leaves the required proportion. Since the smallest nonzero one-step transition probability is at least 1/(dσ), the fused chain assigns any vertex reachable within 2K steps a transition probability at least (dσ)^{-2K} = e^{-1} d^{-2K}; here the assumption that every edge lies in a triangle guarantees such length-2K connecting walks exist. Multiplying the neighbourhood count, this smallest positive 2K-step probability, and the minimal stationary mass on the block, and then using the two mass-fraction lemmas, yields that the flow out of each block is at least (1/90) d^{-2K} times the block's stationary mass.

Step 5 (conductance bound). Summing the per-block flow estimates and invoking that the selected part holds a 1/22 fraction of the mass of S, the flow from S to its complement divided by the stationary mass of S is at least (1/2000) d^{-2K} for every set of at most half the vertices. Symmetry of the flow across a cut lets one handle sets larger than half by passing to the complement, at the cost of a factor two, giving that the conductance of the fused chain is at least (1/4000) d^{-2K}, which is the first claimed inequality.

Step 6 (spectral gap transfer). Cheeger's inequality converts this conductance bound into a lower bound on the spectral gap of the fused chain of order the square of the conductance. Finally, since the eigenvalues of the fused chain are the 2K-th powers of the eigenvalues of the weighted walk, one relates 1 minus the second eigenvalue of the fused chain to 2K times the spectral gap of the weighted walk. Dividing the fused-chain gap by 2K therefore yields a lower bound on the weighted-walk spectral gap of order (1/K) d^{-4K}, and tracking the constants gives the stated bound of (1/10^8)(1/K) d^{-4K}.
nl_theorem: Let G be a finite simple graph on a finite vertex type V that is locally finite, connected, and regular of degree d. Let ψ be a real number with 0 < ψ that is at most the vertex expansion of G, where the vertex expansion is the infimum, over nonempty vertex sets S with 2|S| ≤ |V|, of the ratio of the external vertex boundary size to |S|. Set K = ⌈2 / log(1+ψ)⌉ (natural-number ceiling, log the natural logarithm) and σ = exp(1/(2K)). Assume every edge of G lies in a triangle: whenever x and y are adjacent, some vertex z is adjacent to both x and y. Let w be a positive symmetric edge-weighting (strictly positive on adjacent pairs, zero otherwise) that is σ-Lipschitz, meaning σ⁻¹ ≤ w(x,y)/w(x,z) ≤ σ for all x, y, z with y adjacent to x adjacent to z. Let P_w be the weighted random walk with P_w(x,y) = w(x,y)/w(x) for x ≠ y and 0 otherwise, where w(x) is the total incident weight, and let π_w(x) = w(x)/W be its stationary distribution. Then both of the following hold: the conductance of the 2K-step chain (P_w)^{2K} is at least (1/4000)·d^{-2K}, and the spectral gap of P_w, defined by the Poincaré variational formula as the infimum of the Dirichlet-form to variance ratio over functions of positive variance, is at least (1/10^8)·(1/K)·d^{-4K}.

core_claim: Under small noise and a sufficiently large learning rate, every stable interior local minimum of the denoising score-matching risk keeps its excess risk strictly above an explicit positive threshold, preventing memorization.

metainfo.paper: Taking a Big Step: Large Learning Rates in Denoising Score Matching Prevent Memorization

nl_proof:
The argument proceeds by contraposition: one assumes that the excess risk is at most π n⁵ μ³ Δ³ / (2³⁶ e^{1/2} A⁴ σ⁴) and shows this forces the learning rate to satisfy η ≤ 2¹² σ² / (μ n² Δ), which is the negation of the stated lower bound on η. Here n is the number of ordered training points, Δ their minimum spacing, μ the signal scale, σ the noise level, and A the outer-weight bound, chosen to grow only polynomially in 1/σ.

Step 1 (control of the optimal-score risk). A regularity bound on the empirical optimal score shows that, once σ is small enough relative to μΔ, the risk of the optimal score itself is at most 4 μ² (x_n − x_1)² σ⁻⁴ · exp(−μ²Δ² / (32 σ²)). This follows from a local linearization of the optimal score near each data point together with Gaussian tail control away from the points, and it converges to zero as σ → 0.

Step 2 (from excess risk to network risk). Adding the optimal-score risk bound to the assumed excess-risk bound yields an upper bound on the network risk R_n(θ*) itself. Because A grows only polynomially in 1/σ while the optimal-score risk decays exponentially in 1/σ², the exponential term is negligible for small σ, so one obtains R_n(θ*) ≤ π n⁵ μ³ Δ³ / (2³⁵ e^{1/2} A⁴ σ⁴). For σ small this in particular gives R_n(θ*) ≤ 1/(16 n σ²), the smallness threshold needed later.

Step 3 (total-variation lower bound for low-risk networks). Since R_n(θ*) is below the threshold 1/(16 n σ²), a sign-change argument applies: were the network score to keep a fixed sign or too small a derivative on a half-spacing interval around any data point, the risk would exceed the threshold, a contradiction obtained through Gaussian moment estimates. Consequently the score's derivative must fluctuate, giving the weighted total variation of the derivative of the network score the lower bound μ n² Δ / (2¹¹ σ²). This transfers the irregularity known for the optimal score to every sufficiently low-risk network.

Step 4 (total-variation upper bound via stability). The risk is twice differentiable everywhere, and its Hessian can be written explicitly as a neural-tangent-kernel term plus lower-order pieces. The top eigenvalue of the kernel term is bounded below by a multiple of the same weighted total variation, while the remaining Hessian pieces are controlled using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, a Lipschitz estimate on the residual, and Gaussian integrals. Since θ* is a linearly stable minimum, the largest Hessian eigenvalue is at most 2/(mη). Combining these gives an upper bound on the total variation of the form 1/(2η) plus a term proportional to √R_n(θ*) and a term that is the larger of a square-root and a cube-root expression in the risk.

Step 5 (combining the bounds). For σ small the risk bound of Step 2 makes the cube-root branch the dominant one among the maximum, so the upper bound reads 1/(2η) + (√R_n(θ*))/2 + (a cube-root term). Using the Step 2 risk bound and A ≥ C_n/σ⁶, the square-root term is bounded by a quarter of the base quantity μ n² Δ / (2¹¹ σ²), namely by μ n² Δ / (2¹³ σ²), and the cube-root term by a half of the base, namely by μ n² Δ / (2¹² σ²). Subtracting these from the Step 3 lower bound leaves 1/(2η) ≥ μ n² Δ / (2¹³ σ²), that is, η ≤ 2¹² σ² / (μ n² Δ). This contradicts the hypothesized lower bound on η, completing the contraposition; the threshold σ₀ is the smallest of the finitely many thresholds required along the way.
nl_theorem: Fix a natural number k, a sample x indexed by Fin (k+2), and a signal scale μ, and write n = k+2. Then there exists a threshold σ₀ > 0, depending only on x and μ, with the following property. For every hidden width m and every width-m denoising problem p whose sample equals x and whose signal scale equals μ and which is valid (meaning m > 0, 0 < μ < 1, the outer-weight bound A satisfies A ≥ 1, the sample is strictly increasing, and each fixed inner weight is 1 or −1), and for all real σ and η with 0 < σ < 1, σ ≤ σ₀, the scale-compatibility condition C_n(x)/σ⁶ ≤ A (where C_n(x) = (1 + n + Σ_i |x_i|)⁶), and η > 2¹² σ² / (μ n² Δ), where Δ is the minimum consecutive spacing of the sample, the following holds: for every parameter vector θ* whose outer weights all lie strictly inside (−A, A) and which is a linearly stable local minimum of the empirical denoising score-matching risk Rₙ at noise scale σ and learning rate η, the excess risk Rₙ(θ*) − Rₙ(s*), where s* is the empirical optimal score, is strictly greater than π n⁵ μ³ Δ³ / (2³⁶ · e^{1/2} · A⁴ · σ⁴).

core_claim: A universal nonnegative constant exists so that every finite planar point set admits a cover by two spanning trees whose induced distances approximate Euclidean distances up to that constant.

metainfo.paper: Tree covers of size 2 for the Euclidean plane

nl_proof:
The paper proves the statement with the explicit universal constant forty, which is nonnegative and independent of the point set and its cardinality. The argument has three layers: a combinatorial grid construction, a scaling-and-approximation reduction, and a final passage to a limit.

Grid construction. For each n the authors build two non-crossing planar trees, one "red" and one "blue", on an integer triangular grid. They start from a single right isosceles triangle and recursively refine it: at each step, in every current triangle they drop the height from the right angle to the hypotenuse and add the short segment near the right-angle vertex to the tree whose color matches the hypotenuse, then split the triangle along the height. Colors of catheti and hypotenuses alternate with the parity of the step. Refinement stops at atomic triangles with no interior grid points. This yields a red tree with unit edges and a blue tree with edges of length √2 that together cover all grid points.

Metric analysis of the trees. Two geometric lemmas bound tree distances by Euclidean ones. The first shows that from an interior point of a triangle to a same-color vertex on its hypotenuse the tree distance is at most 2√2 times the Euclidean distance, proved by induction on the nested triangles along the height. The second shows that from a point to a same-color point lying on a cathetus the tree distance is at most 5 times the Euclidean distance; here one follows the shortest path to its first turning vertex, uses that the turning angle is at least π/4, and combines the law of sines with the first lemma, optimizing the resulting expression to the constant 5.

Auxiliary grid theorem. From these one obtains, for the leaf set L of the red tree, two properties: every grid point lies within Euclidean distance 3 of a point of L (from the covering structure of atomic triangles), and any two leaves have combined tree distance at most 5‖x−y‖₂+12. For the latter one locates the lowest-order height separating the two leaves; if it is red, the intersection point with the segment joining them is charged twice by the second lemma to give the bound 5‖x−y‖₂; if it is blue, one first attaches each red leaf to a nearby blue vertex at distance 1 (forming a modified blue tree), applies the same estimate to those blue vertices, and adds the additive slack 12 via the triangle inequality.

Reduction for an arbitrary finite set. Given a finite planar set P, scale it so its minimum interpoint distance is at least a large D, translate it into a grid box, and apply the grid theorem. Connect each point of P by an edge (added to both trees) to its nearest point of L, which lies within a bounded distance by the covering property; this creates two Steiner trees whose extra vertices are grid points. Using the triangle inequality together with the leaf route bound, and letting D grow, the resulting Steiner two-tree cover has terminal stretch at most 5+ε for any ε>0.

Removing Steiner points. Applying Gupta's Steiner-point-removal result to each of the two Steiner trees produces genuine spanning trees whose vertex set is exactly P, at the cost of multiplying distances by at most a factor of 8 (Euclidean edge lengths only help). Hence one gets a two-tree cover on P of stretch at most 8(5+ε)=40+ε.

Passage to the limit. Since P is finite there are only finitely many possible pairs of spanning trees on it, so among covers achieving stretch 40+ε for a sequence of ε tending to zero one pair recurs infinitely often; that pair has stretch at most 40. Taking C=40, which works uniformly for every finite P, establishes the claimed existence of a size-two tree cover with universal constant stretch.
nl_theorem: There exists a constant C, with C at least zero, such that for every finite set P of points in the Euclidean plane (real Euclidean space of dimension two with its standard ℓ₂ metric) there is a tree cover of size two of P, meaning an ordered pair of Euclidean spanning trees on exactly the vertex set P (each a simple graph on P that is preconnected and acyclic, with every edge weighted by the Euclidean distance between its endpoints), such that for all x, y in P the minimum over the two trees of the shortest-path distance between x and y is at most C times the Euclidean distance between x and y. The constant C is independent of both P and the size of P.

core_claim: There exist universal positive constants making the truthful forecaster's expected subsampled step calibration error at most a square-root-log factor times expected root variance plus a polylogarithmic term, uniformly over horizon, smoothness parameter, and smoothed setting.

metainfo.paper: Truthfulness of Decision-Theoretic Calibration Measures

nl_proof:
The paper obtains the asymptotic bound as a direct simplification of an explicit inequality it proves for the same quantity. That explicit inequality states that, for every horizon at least two, every smoothness parameter in the open-closed unit interval, and every smoothed setting, the truthful forecaster's expected subsampled step calibration error is at most (547·√(ln(1/c))+1161)·E[√Var_T] plus (log₂T+3)·(16·log₂T·log₂(T/c)+15) plus 8·√(2·ln(1/c)) plus 17·√2. The asymptotic form with two universal constants follows because, when c is at most e^(−1), ln(1/c) is at least 1, so the constant 1161 can be folded into the √(ln(1/c)) coefficient, and the remaining additive terms (whose base-2 logarithms differ from natural logarithms only by fixed factors, since log₂x=ln x/ln 2) are all dominated by a single term proportional to (ln T)²·ln(T/c). Thus proving the explicit inequality is the whole task.

The explicit inequality is proved as follows.

First, the quantity of interest is rewritten in martingale form. For a threshold α and a subsampling mask y, define the partial sums that accumulate y_s·1{p*_s ≤ α}·(x_s − p*_s) over the first t steps. Because the true conditional probability is revealed before the outcome and the outcome is Bernoulli with that probability, each increment has zero conditional expectation given the past, so these partial sums form a martingale adapted to the filtration generated by drawing each conditional probability and then each outcome. The truthful forecaster's expected subsampled step calibration error equals the expectation, over the outcomes, the conditional probabilities, and a uniformly random mask, of the supremum over α of the absolute value of the full-horizon martingale.

Second, the time steps are partitioned into adaptive epochs, adapting a doubling scheme from prior work. The k-th epoch is the shortest continuation of the previous epochs whose realized variance, augmented by c times its length, reaches 2^(k−1). Several structural facts are recorded: the realized variance accumulated within epoch k is at most 2^k; an epoch can be completed only if Var_T+cT is at least 2^(k−1), which forces every epoch beyond index ⌈log₂T⌉+2 to be incomplete; the event of lying in a given epoch is measurable with respect to the past; and each epoch lasts at most ⌈2^(k−1)/c⌉ steps.

Third, a variance floor is established: in any smoothed setting, E[√Var_T] is at least √(7cT)/(16√2). This holds because the density bound of 1/c makes each conditional probability lie in [c/8, 1−c/8] with probability at least 3/4, and on that event the per-step variance p*(1−p*) is at least 7c/64; a counting argument then shows that with probability at least one half, at least half of the steps contribute this much variance. Using this floor, the exponentially weighted sum over epochs of √(2^k) times the probability that the epoch is reached is bounded by a constant multiple of E[√Var_T]; the key steps are that reaching epoch k requires Var_T+cT to be at least 2^(k−2), and that E[√(Var_T+cT)] is at most a constant times E[√Var_T] by subadditivity of the square root together with the floor.

Fourth, the calibration error contributed by a single reached epoch is bounded. Fixing a threshold α, the indicator 1{p ≤ α} is decomposed telescopically over nested dyadic grids: a coarse rounding of α onto a grid of resolution ε*, followed by successive refinements at resolutions 2^(−i)·ε*, plus one final residual sub-interval. This splits the epoch's martingale supremum into three parts, each controlled by a separate lemma. The prefix part, a maximum over the coarse grid, is bounded using Freedman's inequality (the epoch's realized variance is at most 2^k), a union bound over the grid points, and a layer-cake integration of the resulting tail. The segment parts, one per refinement level, restrict the martingale to a short interval; smoothness bounds the probability that a conditional probability lands in an interval of length ℓ by ℓ/c, so combined with the epoch length bound the restricted quadratic variation is at most ε*·2^(k−i)/c², and Freedman's inequality with a union bound and layer-cake integration again applies. The suffix part counts how many conditional probabilities fall into the finest residual interval; this count is stochastically dominated by a binomial variable, and a multiplicative Chernoff bound with a union bound and tail integration controls its expectation. Choosing ε*=c² and m=⌊log₂T⌋ and summing the three contributions (the segment sums are handled with convergent geometric and arithmetic series) yields a per-epoch bound of the form 8·√(2^k·ln(1/c)) + 17·√(2^k) + 16·log₂T·log₂(T/c) + 15, conditioned on the epoch being reached.

Finally, summing the per-epoch bound over epochs 1 through ⌈log₂T⌉+2, weighted by the probability each epoch is reached, and applying the exponentially weighted-sum estimate to the √(2^k) terms produces the coefficient in front of E[√Var_T], while the additive polylogarithmic term is multiplied by the number of epochs, ⌈log₂T⌉+2. Collecting these gives exactly the explicit inequality, and hence the asymptotic bound with universal constants.
nl_theorem: There exist real constants C₁ > 0 and C₂ > 0 such that for every natural number T with T ≥ 2, every real number c with 0 < c ≤ e^(−1), and every c-smoothed setting P of horizon T, the expected subsampled step calibration error of the truthful forecaster satisfies err ≤ C₁ · √(ln(1/c)) · E_P[√Var_T] + C₂ · (ln T)² · ln(T/c), where E_P[√Var_T] is the expected square root of the realized variance and err denotes the truthful forecaster's expected subsampled step calibration error. Here a c-smoothed setting assigns to every binary history of length below T a probability measure on the unit interval given by a Lebesgue density bounded above by 1/c, and the truthful forecaster reports the drawn conditional probability.

core_claim: Any finite open cover of a sphere by sets each contained in an open hemisphere must have some collection whose size exceeds the dimension sharing a common point.

metainfo.paper: Tight list replicability bounds via a novel sphere covering theorem

nl_proof:
The paper proves this by combining a partition of unity with the Borsuk–Ulam theorem and a dimension-counting (measure) argument. Throughout, the cover consists of sets Aᵢ, each contained in the open hemisphere of points whose inner product with a fixed unit pole uᵢ is positive.

Step 1 (Building a self-map of the sphere). Because the sphere is a compact Hausdorff space, there is a partition of unity subordinate to the cover: continuous functions fᵢ from the sphere into the unit interval, each supported inside Aᵢ, summing identically to one. Form the continuous map g(x) = Σᵢ fᵢ(x)·uᵢ. For each point x on the sphere, only indices i with x in the support of fᵢ contribute, and for those x lies in Aᵢ, hence ⟨x, uᵢ⟩ > 0; since the weights are nonnegative and sum to one, at least one is positive, so ⟨x, g(x)⟩ > 0. In particular g(x) is never zero. Normalizing, h(x) = g(x)/‖g(x)‖ is a continuous map from the sphere to itself, and it inherits the strict positivity property ⟨x, h(x)⟩ > 0 for every x.

Step 2 (Surjectivity of h via Borsuk–Ulam). Suppose h were not surjective and pick a point p on the sphere missed by h. Stereographic projection through p is a homeomorphism from the sphere minus p onto d-dimensional Euclidean space, so the composite of that projection with h is a continuous map from the sphere into d-dimensional space. By the Borsuk–Ulam theorem, this composite takes equal values on some antipodal pair w and −w. Injectivity of stereographic projection forces h(w) = h(−w). But then the positivity property gives both ⟨w, h(w)⟩ > 0 and ⟨−w, h(w)⟩ = ⟨−w, h(−w)⟩ > 0, which are contradictory. Hence h is surjective onto the sphere.

Step 3 (Overlap forced by surjectivity). Consider the set T that is the union, over all index subsets S whose corresponding sets Aᵢ have a common point, of the convex hulls σ_S of the poles {uᵢ : i ∈ S}. The image of g lies in T. For each such S there is a point making all inner products ⟨·, uᵢ⟩ positive, so σ_S avoids the origin, and the radial projection of σ_S onto the sphere is contained in the sphere intersected with the linear span of {uᵢ : i ∈ S}, a subspace of dimension at most |S|. Consequently the image of h lies in the union of the radial projections of these hulls. Now suppose, for contradiction, that no d+1 of the sets share a common point. Then every contributing S has at most d indices, so each associated span has dimension at most d, strictly less than d+1, and its intersection with the sphere has measure zero. The image of h would then be contained in a finite union of measure-zero subsets of the sphere, hence itself of measure zero, contradicting the surjectivity established in Step 2. Therefore some d+1 of the sets must have a common nonempty intersection, which is exactly the existence of an injection from a (d+1)-element index set with nonempty common intersection.
nl_theorem: Let d be a natural number and let C be a finite open hemisphere cover of the d-dimensional unit sphere in real (d+1)-space: that is, C consists of a number m, sets A₁,…,A_m of the sphere's ambient space, and unit pole vectors u₁,…,u_m, such that each Aᵢ is the intersection of an open set with the unit sphere, each Aᵢ lies inside the unit sphere, the sphere is covered by the union of the Aᵢ, and each Aᵢ is contained in the open hemisphere of points x with ⟨x, uᵢ⟩ > 0. Then there exists an injection S from {1,…,d+1} into {1,…,m} such that the intersection of the sets A_{S(1)},…,A_{S(d+1)} is nonempty.

core_claim: For an average-case binary classification problem satisfying two approximate strong data processing inequalities, the minimal memorization required by any algorithm achieving error below one half is bounded below by an explicit information-theoretic quantity.

metainfo.paper: Trade-offs in Data Memorization via Strong Data Processing Inequalities

nl_proof:
The paper obtains this bound by first proving a pointwise excess-memorization inequality valid for every algorithm, then combining it with a testing (Fano-type) lower bound and taking an infimum over admissible algorithms.

Preliminary tool. The central quantitative device is a post-processing consequence of approximate strong data processing. If a pair of variables satisfies the coupling-based approximate inequality with constants (rho, delta), then for any randomized map A of the second coordinate into the model space, the information about the first coordinate is bounded by rho times the information about the second coordinate plus an additive penalty of the form eight times delta times the logarithm of the model-space size divided by delta. This is proved by working with the coupled variable that satisfies the exact inequality: two auxiliary continuity facts show that variables close in total variation have nearly equal entropy (up to a term of order delta log of the alphabet size over delta), and hence that a fixed randomized channel extracts nearly equal information from two total-variation-close sources. Applying the exact strong data processing inequality to the coupled variable and transferring the estimate back through these total-variation bounds yields the stated additive-penalty inequality. When delta is zero the penalty vanishes, and when the model space is infinite with positive delta the penalty is infinite and the inequality is vacuous.

Step 1 (data-generation direction). Applying the post-processing tool to the pair formed by the parameter and the training sample, with the algorithm as the map, gives that the information the output carries about the parameter is at most tau times the information it carries about the training sample, plus the penalty at epsilon.

Step 2 (test/train direction). Applying the same tool to the pair formed by the fresh test point and the training sample, and rearranging using that rho is strictly positive, gives that the information the output carries about the training sample is at least the information it carries about the test point divided by rho, minus the penalty at delta divided by rho.

Step 3 (chain rule for excess memorization). The average-case excess memorization equals the conditional information of the training sample and the output given the parameter. Expanding by the chain rule and using that the output is conditionally independent of the parameter given the training sample, this conditional information equals the information between output and training sample minus the information between output and parameter. Substituting the Step 1 estimate bounds the excess memorization below by (one minus tau) times the information between output and training sample, minus the penalty at epsilon. Since tau lies between zero and one, the coefficient is nonnegative, so substituting the Step 2 estimate and distributing yields the pointwise bound: the excess memorization is at least (one minus tau) over rho times the information between output and the test point, minus the combined correction term equal to (one minus tau) over rho times the penalty at delta plus the penalty at epsilon.

Step 4 (accuracy forces test information). For any algorithm whose balanced average classification error is at most alpha with alpha below one half, the information between output and test point is at least the binary capacity constant. This is a testing argument: because the null distribution equals the marginal of the test point, the information equals the divergence between the joint law of output and test point and the product of their marginals. Post-processing by the prediction map does not increase this divergence, so it is at least the divergence between two Bernoulli laws whose parameters are the true-positive and false-positive rates. The error hypothesis forces the gap between these rates to be at least one minus two alpha, and optimizing the Bernoulli divergence subject to this constraint (as in the standard Fano optimization) gives at least (one minus two alpha) times the logarithm of (one minus alpha) over alpha, which is the capacity constant.

Step 5 (infimum). For each algorithm meeting the error constraint, Steps 3 and 4 together give that its excess memorization is at least the target quantity, namely (one minus tau) over rho times the capacity constant minus the correction term; the nonnegativity of the coefficient lets the capacity lower bound be substituted directly. Algorithms failing the error constraint contribute the value plus infinity, which also exceeds the target. Hence every term of the infimum defining the minimal necessary memorization is bounded below by the target quantity, and taking the infimum establishes the claimed bound.
nl_theorem: Fix a sample size n, a parameter law Ψ, and a Markov kernel P sending each parameter to an example distribution. Assume the parameter space Θ and example space X are Hausdorff, second countable, Borel spaces, that X is nonempty, and that the n-fold product space of X is standard Borel; let the model-output space M be a countably generated measurable space whose singletons are measurable. Suppose the random variables (parameter, training sample, test point) obey the learning-problem sampling law: the parameter has law Ψ, and conditionally on the parameter the n training coordinates and the test point are independent draws from that parameter's example distribution. Assume the pair (parameter, training) satisfies the coupling-based (τ, ε)-approximate strong data processing inequality, and the pair (test, training) satisfies the coupling-based (ρ, δ)-approximate strong data processing inequality with ρ strictly positive. Fix a measurable prediction map on M × X and use the balanced labeled test distribution. Then for every α strictly below one half, the minimal necessary memorization, defined as the infimum of the excess memorization over all randomized algorithms whose balanced average classification error is at most α, is at least ((1 − τ)/ρ) times the binary classification capacity constant C_α minus the excess-memorization correction term, where C_α equals +∞ when α ≤ 0 and equals (1 − 2α)·log((1 − α)/α) when 0 < α < 1/2, and the correction term equals ((1 − τ)/ρ) times the information-error penalty at δ plus the information-error penalty at ε. This inequality holds in the extended reals.

core_claim: A measurable event family over a finite product space has finite linear VC dimension exactly when it is uniformly estimable against every uniformly box-continuous family of probability measures.

metainfo.paper: Uniform Laws of Large Numbers in Product Spaces

nl_proof:
The paper establishes the equivalence by proving the two implications separately.

Sufficiency (finite linear VC dimension forces uniform estimability against every uniformly box-continuous family). Fix such a family and an accuracy and confidence pair. The estimator constructed splits the sample into two independent halves. In the first phase it forms a product grid by projecting the first half onto each coordinate and taking the Cartesian product of the resulting coordinate sets. The crucial property established is a hitting guarantee: with high probability the grid meets the symmetric difference of any two events whose probability difference under the target distribution is large; equivalently the grid is a net for the family of pairwise symmetric differences under the target pseudo-metric. This is proved first for the product of marginals and then transferred to the target distribution using uniform box-continuity, which converts a lower bound on the target measure of a symmetric difference into a lower bound on its product-of-marginals measure. The hitting bound for the product-of-marginals case rests on controlling the empirical product estimator: the linear VC dimension of the symmetric-difference class is at most a constant times that of the original class (via a bound on the VC dimension of symmetric differences obtained from an aggregation-rule VC bound), the expected uniform deviation of the empirical product estimator is bounded coordinate by coordinate using the classical one-dimensional VC inequality on axis-parallel sections, and this expectation bound is upgraded to a high-probability statement through a bounded-differences (McDiarmid) argument. The grid then induces an equivalence relation on the class, where two events are equivalent when they agree on the grid, and one representative is chosen from each class. On the hitting event, agreement on the grid forces the two events to have close probabilities, so every event can be rounded to its representative at small cost. In the second phase the empirical mean over the second half estimates the probabilities of the finitely many representatives; a Hoeffding bound with a union bound over representatives controls all of them simultaneously. The number of representatives, that is the number of distinct traces of the class on the grid, is bounded by a grid version of the Sauer-Shelah-Perles lemma expressed through the linear VC dimension: partitioning the grid into axis-parallel lines and applying the classical Sauer-Shelah-Perles bound line by line gives the trace count, so its logarithm is controlled and the finite-class estimation succeeds. Combining the rounding error from the first phase with the estimation error from the second yields uniform accuracy for all events with the prescribed confidence, establishing uniform estimability with explicit sample size.

Necessity (uniform estimability against every uniformly box-continuous family forces finite linear VC dimension). This is proved by contraposition. The family of all product distributions is uniformly box-continuous (each product distribution equals the product of its own marginals, so the modulus can be taken to be the identity). Assuming the linear VC dimension is infinite, there is a coordinate and a fixing of the remaining coordinates whose induced section class has arbitrarily large classical VC dimension, hence shatters a large finite set on that axis-parallel line. Placing point masses on the fixed coordinates and the uniform distribution over the shattered points on the varying coordinate yields a product distribution under which estimating the probabilities of the events reduces exactly to a one-dimensional uniform estimation problem for a class of large VC dimension. The classical no-free-lunch VC lower bound then shows that no fixed sample size can achieve the required accuracy and confidence, so the pair consisting of the class and the product distributions fails to be uniformly estimable. Therefore uniform estimability against every uniformly box-continuous family cannot hold, which is the contrapositive of the desired implication.

Combining the two implications gives the stated equivalence.
nl_theorem: Let I be a finite nonempty index type, let (W_i) for i in I be measurable spaces, put X equal to the product of the W_i, and let F be a measurable event family on X (a collection of subsets of X each of which is measurable). Then the following two statements are equivalent. First, F has finite linear VC dimension: there exists a natural number k such that every finite axis-parallel colinear set S (a set for which there is a coordinate index i so that any two of its points agree in every coordinate other than i) that is shattered by F (for every subset T of S there is a member of F whose intersection with S equals T) has cardinality at most k. Second, for every family P of probability measures on X that is uniformly box-continuous (for every real alpha greater than 0 there is a real beta greater than 0 such that for every measure P in the family and every measurable set E, if the P-measure of E is at least alpha then the measure of E under the product of the coordinate marginals of P is at least beta), the pair (F, P) is uniformly estimable: there exist a sample-complexity function and an event estimator so that for all epsilon and delta in (0,1), every P in the family, and every sample size m at least the sample complexity, the m-fold product measure assigns probability at most delta to the set of samples for which some member of F has estimation error exceeding epsilon.

core_claim: Under the stated assumptions, the cross-fitted doubly robust policy's regret obeys, with probability at least one minus four delta, both an explicit oracle-plus-grid-plus-nuisance bound and a coarse bound with a positive universal coefficient.

metainfo.paper: Wasserstein Policy Learning for Distributional Outcomes

nl_proof:
The paper proves the guarantee for the cross-fitted doubly robust learner in several stages, working throughout in quantile coordinates where the 2-Wasserstein distance between two laws equals the L2 distance between their quantile curves.

Reduction of regret to a uniform curve deviation. Using that the learned policy maximizes the estimated utility and that the utility is Lipschitz for the Wasserstein distance, the regret is first sandwiched by twice the worst-case Wasserstein distance between the estimated and population barycenters over the policy class. Because the monotone rearrangement is a non-expansive projection onto valid quantile curves, this distance is at most the L2 distance between the raw estimated quantile curve and the population quantile curve. Passing the supremum over policies inside the integral, the regret is bounded by twice the utility Lipschitz constant times the square root of the integral over the quantile index of the squared uniform-over-policies deviation of the raw curve. It therefore suffices to control this pointwise-in-index uniform deviation.

Decomposition of the pointwise deviation. At each index the deviation of the raw doubly robust curve from its target is split into three pieces: a term carrying the propensity-estimation error times the outcome residual, a term carrying the outcome-regression error times the centered inverse-propensity weight, and an oracle empirical-process term built from the true nuisances. The analysis conditions on the training folds so that the fitted nuisances behave as fixed functions when averaging over the held-out fold.

Neyman orthogonality. Two conditional-mean identities are recorded: the residual of the observed quantile around the true outcome regression is mean zero given action and context, and the centered inverse-propensity weight is mean zero given context. Consequently the first-order conditional means of the propensity and outcome pieces vanish, so the only non-centered bias is the product of the two nuisance errors; the individual errors appear only multiplied by the policy-complexity factor or the grid mesh.

Controlling each piece. For the two nuisance-dependent pieces and the oracle piece, the argument proceeds pointwise at grid nodes: for a fixed index, the number of distinct action labelings the policy class realizes on a fold is bounded through the multiclass growth function controlled by the Natarajan dimension, and Hoeffding's inequality together with a union bound over labelings gives a fixed-index deviation bound. A union bound over the finitely many grid nodes, combined with the assumed high-probability uniform nuisance-error bounds at confidence level delta over three times the number of folds, and a further union bound over folds, extends this to all nodes. The bounded and Lipschitz regularity of the true and fitted quantile curves in the index (the fitted Lipschitz constant being absorbed into the same constant) makes the deviation Lipschitz in the index, so a supremum-transfer lemma upgrades the finite-grid control to a uniform-over-index control, adding a deterministic discretization term proportional to the mesh. The oracle term is handled the same way with the outcome bound in place of the nuisance errors.

Assembling the explicit bound. Summing the fold averages and collecting the three high-probability events, each of failure probability at most delta, plus the nuisance event, a union bound leaves total failure probability at most four times delta. Grouping the resulting terms reproduces the stated oracle coefficient times the policy-complexity deviation factor, the grid coefficient times the mesh, and the nuisance remainder, whose leading standalone bias is the product of the two nuisance rates while the single-rate terms multiply the deviation factor or the mesh.

Coarse form. Finally, since the confidence argument lies in the admissible range the two nuisance rates are nonnegative and the outcome rate is at most one, so the triple product is dominated by the corresponding pair product. Bounding every coefficient in the explicit expression by its absolute-value counterpart yields a strictly positive constant, depending only on the utility Lipschitz constant, the outcome bound, the overlap lower bound, the index Lipschitz constant, the number of folds, and the number of actions, so that with the same probability the regret is at most this constant times the coarse rate expression combining the deviation factor, the mesh, the product of nuisance rates, and their cross terms with the deviation factor and mesh.
nl_theorem: Fix admissible numerical parameters p (confidence delta in (0,1/4); positive fold, grid, and action counts; Natarajan dimension between 1 and the sample size; nonnegative structural constants with positive overlap lower bound and nonnegative utility Lipschitz constant; nuisance-rate functions that are nonnegative and nonincreasing on (0,1) at the sample size, with the outcome rate at delta/(3L) at most 1). Let m be a cross-fitted logged-data model on a probability space satisfying the structural assumptions (finite action type with cardinality d, Natarajan dimension V of the represented policy class, measurable policies, foldwise i.i.d. logged observations, foldwise training sigma-algebras independent of the complete held-out vectors with jointly measurable nuisance evaluation, consistency, moment identities, overlap, boundedness, and quantile-regularity, valid square-integrable population/outcome/estimated quantile curves, an L_U-Lipschitz utility, a nonexpansive rearrangement, and exact population and learned maximizers) and the nuisance-rate assumptions (for each fold and each gamma in (0,1), with probability at least 1-gamma the fitted propensity and outcome-regression errors are uniformly bounded by their respective rate functions at gamma). Assume the simultaneous good event is measurable. Then, with probability at least 1 - 4*delta, the regret is at most the explicit bound C_or·V_N + C_grid·eta + Rem_nuis; and the coefficient C_coarse(L_U, M, overlap, U, L, d) is positive and, with the same probability, the regret is at most that coefficient times the coarse expression V_N + eta + r_f·r_m + r_f·V_N + r_m·V_N + r_f·eta.

core_claim: The wedge-sampling spectral tensor-completion estimator recovers a symmetric incoherent low-rank tensor with relative Frobenius error controlled by explicit universal constants, holding with high probability whenever the two sampling rates exceed the stated thresholds.

metainfo.paper: Wedge Sampling: Efficient Tensor Completion with Nearly-Linear Sample Complexity

nl_proof:
The paper proves the bound by controlling the estimator's two sources of error separately and then combining them.

Setup. Write A for the first-mode unfolding of T, so A is a rank-r, (mu1,mu2)-incoherent matrix of dimension n by n^{k-1}, with singular values sigma_1 >= ... >= sigma_r and condition number kappa. The algorithm forms the wedge-sampled Gram matrix, takes its top-r eigenvectors U-hat, and sets the projector Q = U-hat U-hat^T. It also forms the inverse-probability-weighted uniform observation Y and outputs T-hat, which in unfolded form is Q applied in every mode to Y. Introduce the intermediate object T* obtained by applying Q in every mode to the true A. The triangle inequality for the Frobenius norm gives ||T - T-hat||_F <= ||T - T*||_F + ||T* - T-hat||_F, and the two terms are bounded separately.

Ingredient 1: concentration of the wedge matrix. Writing the wedge Gram matrix minus AA^T as a sum of independent, centered, symmetric rank-structured matrices, the paper applies the matrix Bernstein inequality. Incoherence controls both the per-summand operator norm (through the maximal entry of A) and the variance proxy (through the mixed 2-infinity and infinity-2 norms of A). This yields, with probability 1 - O(n^{-a}), that ||Z - AA^T|| is at most a universal constant times (sqrt(a mu1 mu2 r^2 log n / (p n^k)) + a mu1 mu2 r^2 log n / (p n^k)) times ||A||^2. The lower bound on the wedge rate p (with C_0 large) makes this perturbation at most one quarter of the spectral gap sigma_r^2, so the first term dominates the second.

Ingredient 2: left singular subspace recovery. Because the perturbation is small relative to the gap, the Davis-Kahan theorem bounds the sine of the principal angles between the ranges of U-hat and the true left singular matrix U, giving an operator-norm subspace error of order kappa^2 sqrt(a mu1 mu2 r^2 log n / (p n^k)). A more delicate leave-one-out analysis (deleting the wedge contributions incident to each row, and using that the deleted matrix is independent of that row's noise) upgrades this to a row-wise (2-infinity) bound: after the optimal orthogonal alignment, ||U-hat sgn(H) - U||_{2,infinity} is at most order kappa^4 ||U||_{2,infinity} times the same square-root factor.

Ingredient 3: delocalization of the projector. Since sgn(H) is orthogonal, the row norms of U-hat equal those of U-hat sgn(H); combining the 2-infinity recovery bound with the triangle inequality and incoherence of U (||U||_{2,infinity} <= sqrt(mu1 r / n)) shows that, with high probability, ||Q||_{2,infinity} <= 2 kappa^2 sqrt(mu1 r / n).

Ingredient 4: concentration of the projected uniform noise. The unfolded error Q(Y-A)(Q tensor ... tensor Q) is written as a sum of independent rank-one matrices indexed by tensor entries. The per-summand norm and the variance proxy are controlled by the maximal entry of A (via incoherence) and by k factors of ||Q||_{2,infinity}. Matrix Bernstein then bounds the operator norm of this projected error by a constant times r ||A|| (prod ||Q||_{2,infinity}) sqrt(mu1 mu2) (sqrt(a(k-1) log n / q) + a(k-1) log n /(q) n^{-k/2}), and the lower bound on q makes the first term dominate.

Step 1 (projection bias, bounding ||T - T*||_F). Expanding the difference between A and its multilinear projection and telescoping over the k modes, using symmetry of T to identify all mode residuals, one gets ||T - T*||_F <= k times the maximal single-mode residual, and since rank A = r this is at most k sqrt(r) ||(I-Q)A||. Because AA^T = U Sigma^2 U^T, the operator norm ||(I-Q)A|| is controlled by the subspace distance ||UU^T - U-hat U-hat^T|| times ||A||, which via Davis-Kahan and Ingredient 1 is at most a constant times kappa^2 sqrt(a mu1 mu2 r^2 log n / (p n^k)) ||A||. Using ||A|| <= ||T||_F gives ||T - T*||_F <= C k sqrt(r) kappa^2 sqrt(a mu1 mu2 r^2 log n / (p n^k)) ||T||_F.

Step 2 (projected uniform error, bounding ||T* - T-hat||_F). Unfolding and using that the projected error has rank at most r, ||T* - T-hat||_F <= sqrt(r) ||Q(A-Y)(Q tensor ... tensor Q)||. Substituting the delocalization bound ||Q||_{2,infinity} <= 2 kappa^2 sqrt(mu1 r / n) into Ingredient 4 and collecting the powers of 2, r, kappa, mu1, mu2, n gives ||T* - T-hat||_F <= C 2^k r^{1.5 + k/2} kappa^{2k} sqrt(a(k-1) mu1^{k+1} mu2 log n / (q n^k)) ||T||_F.

Step 3 (assembly). All the required events hold simultaneously with probability 1 - O(n^{-a}) once the constants C_0 and C are chosen large enough. On their intersection, the triangle inequality adds the two bounds from Steps 1 and 2, producing exactly the claimed relative Frobenius error C ( k sqrt(r) kappa^2 sqrt(a mu1 mu2 r^2 log n / (p n^k)) + 2^k r^{1.5+k/2} kappa^{2k} sqrt(a(k-1) mu1^{k+1} mu2 log n / (q n^k)) ) ||T||_F, with the residual failure probability absorbed into a universal multiple of n^{-a}.
nl_theorem: There exist universal constants C₀, C > 0 and K ≥ 0 with the following property. Let (Ω, μ) be a probability space, let n ≥ 2 and d ≥ 1, and set the tensor order to k = d + 1. Let μ₁, μ₂ > 0 and κ ≥ 1, and let T be a symmetric (μ₁, μ₂)-incoherent order-k real tensor of mode dimension n whose first-mode unfolding has positive rank r and condition number κ. For sampling rates p, q with 0 < p ≤ 1 and 0 < q ≤ 1, let E be a wedge-spectral completion experiment for T at rates p and q (an Algorithm-2 experiment consisting of jointly Bernoulli wedge and uniform masks, a projector that is a measurable function of the wedge mask alone and, for every outcome, a leading rank-r spectral projector of the wedge-sampled Gram matrix, together with the inverse-probability-weighted uniform observation), and let its output be obtained by applying the learned projector in every mode to that observation. Then for every a ≥ 2, if p ≥ C₀·κ⁴·a·μ₁·μ₂·r²·log n / nᵏ and q ≥ a·(k−1)·log n / nᵏ, the probability that the Frobenius norm of the difference between T and the estimator output is at most C times (k·√r·κ²·√(a·μ₁·μ₂·r²·log n /(p·nᵏ)) + 2ᵏ·r^(3/2+k/2)·κ^(2k)·√(a·(k−1)·μ₁^(k+1)·μ₂·log n /(q·nᵏ))) times the Frobenius norm of T is at least 1 − K·n^(−a).
